children.title: Population-Risk Objectives
children.top_down_role: Population-risk formulations used in learning optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Population-Risk Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Statistical-learning objective defined on the data-generating distribution rather than a realized sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z\) be a measurable sample space, let \(P\) be a probability distribution on \(\mathcal Z\), let \(\Theta\) be a parameter set, and let \(\ell:\Theta\times\mathcal Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be measurable in its second argument. The population-risk objective is \[R(\theta):=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}[\ell(\theta;Z)]=\int_{\mathcal Z}\ell(\theta;z)\,dP(z),\qquad \theta\in\Theta,\] whenever the expectation is well defined. Population-risk minimization seeks an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta)\), or an \(\varepsilon\)-minimizer satisfying \(R(\theta)\leq\inf_{u\in\Theta}R(u)+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Population risk is the expected loss of a parameter under the data-generating distribution; learning seeks an exact or approximate minimizer of this expectation.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\sim P\) on a measurable space \(\mathcal Z\).
\(\ell(\theta;\cdot)\) is measurable and its expectation is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\theta)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}[\ell(\theta;Z)]\).

children.title: Expectation-Form Objectives
children.top_down_role: Expectation-indexed formulations over data or randomness.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-Form Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation representation used to connect learning objectives with stochastic first-order oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi\) be a random element with law \(P\), and let \(F:\Theta	imes\Xi	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be measurable in \(\xi\). An expectation-form objective is represented by \[f(	heta)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[F(	heta,\xi)].\] If \(F(\cdot,\xi)\) is differentiable almost surely and differentiation may be interchanged with expectation, then \[
abla f(	heta)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[
abla_	heta F(	heta,\xi)].\] Consequently, an independent draw \(\xi\sim P\) produces the unbiased stochastic-gradient observation \(g(	heta,\xi)=
abla_	heta F(	heta,xi)\) with \(\mathbb E[g(	heta,xi)]=
abla f(	heta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation objective averages a random component function. Under valid differentiation–expectation interchange, a component gradient is an unbiased gradient observation.
assumptions_latex: Differentiation under the expectation is valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\theta)=\mathbb E[F(\theta,\xi)]\) and \(\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta F(\theta,\xi)]=\nabla f(\theta)\).

children.title: Empirical Approximation Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural links from expectation objectives to sampled approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Approximation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-average interface between an inaccessible population objective and a finite optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For independent observations \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\sim P\) and population risk \(R(\theta)=\mathbb E[\ell(\theta;Z)]\), define the empirical approximation \[\widehat R_n(\theta):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta;Z_i).\] For each fixed \(\theta\) with \(\mathbb E|\ell(\theta;Z)|<\infty\), \(\widehat R_n(\theta)\to R(\theta)\) almost surely as \(n\to\infty\). If the losses are differentiable and differentiation commutes with expectation, then \(\mathbb E[\nabla\widehat R_n(\theta)]=\nabla R(\theta)\). Uniform convergence or additional stability conditions are required to transfer this pointwise approximation to empirical minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empirical average approximates population risk pointwise and may supply unbiased gradients, but optimization guarantees require stronger uniform or stability control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat R_n(\theta)\to R(\theta)\) almost surely for every fixed \(\theta\).

notation.meaning: empirical risk based on n samples

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Empirical-Risk Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite deterministic objective induced by a fixed training sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a fixed sample \(S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\), parameter domain \(\Theta\), and component losses \(f_i(	heta):=\ell(	heta;z_i)\), the finite-sum empirical-risk objective is \[F_S(	heta):= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(	heta),\qquad 	heta\in\Theta.\] Empirical-risk minimization returns an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{	heta\in\Theta}F_S(	heta)\), when one exists, or an \(\varepsilon\)-minimizer. If every \(f_i\) is differentiable, then \(
abla F_S(	heta)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
abla f_i(	heta)\); sampling an index uniformly therefore yields an unbiased component-gradient estimator of \(
abla F_S(	heta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical risk is the average of finitely many sample losses. Its gradient is the average component gradient, enabling uniform component sampling.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is differentiable for the gradient identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_S(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(\theta)\).

children.title: Overparameterized Regimes
children.top_down_role: Optimization geometry arising from excess parameter capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Overparameterized Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-relative condition based on effective parameter degrees of freedom, not parameter count alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m\) map parameters to all model outputs constrained by a training sample. A locally overparameterized regime at \(\theta\) satisfies \[\operatorname{rank}Dh(\theta)<p,\] so the output map has parameter directions that are locally unidentifiable. In the regular case, the constant-rank theorem gives a local fiber \(h^{-1}(h(\theta))\) of dimension \(p-\operatorname{rank}Dh(\theta)>0\). The common count condition \(p>m\) implies rank deficiency but is representation-dependent; rank or fiber dimension expresses the effective condition. Overparameterization alone makes no assertion that the target outputs lie in \(h(\mathbb R^p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is effectively overparameterized when the sample-output map has more parameter directions than locally identifiable constraints; this does not guarantee data interpolation.
assumptions_latex: The stated fiber-dimension conclusion is local to a constant-rank neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p-\operatorname{rank}Dh(\theta)>0\) measures local redundant parameter directions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank condition precisely describes local parameter redundancy under the stated constant-rank qualification, but treating it as the defining condition for an overparameterized regime is literature-dependent and narrower than common usage. An authoritative source must establish this intended local sense.

children.title: Interpolating Regimes
children.top_down_role: Training regimes admitting exact data fit.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolating Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fitting condition for nonnegative finite-sum losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_S(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)\), where every component loss satisfies \(\ell_i(\theta)\geq0\). The empirical problem is in an interpolating regime when there exists \(\theta_\star\in\Theta\) such that \[\ell_i(\theta_\star)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,n.\] Equivalently, \(F_S(\theta_\star)=0=\inf_{	heta\in\Theta}F_S(\theta)\). For supervised losses of the form \(\ell_i(\theta)=L(h_\theta(x_i),y_i)\), with \(L(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), interpolation is equivalent to \(h_{\theta_\star}(x_i)=y_i\) for all training examples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interpolation means one parameter simultaneously makes every nonnegative training loss zero, equivalently fitting every label exactly for a zero-only-at-equality loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\theta_\star\in\Theta\;\forall i,\ \ell_i(\theta_\star)=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exact empirical interpolation condition for nonnegative component losses
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interpolation condition is precise and the equivalence with zero empirical risk follows under nonnegative component losses. The condition kind fits the regime leaf, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Overparameterization–Interpolation Relationship
children.top_down_role: Cases where excess capacity does or does not yield interpolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Overparameterization–Interpolation Relationship
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-model boundary showing that overparameterization and interpolation are distinct conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider squared-loss linear regression \(F(w)=\|Xw-y\|_2^2/(2n)\) with \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\). Interpolation holds exactly when \(y\in\operatorname{range}(X)\). If \(p>n\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=n\), then every \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) is interpolable and the solution set has dimension at least \(p-n\). However, \(p>n\) does not imply interpolation when \(X\) is rank deficient and \(y\notin\operatorname{range}(X)\). Conversely, \(p\leq n\) does not preclude interpolation: any target \(y=Xw_0\) is interpolated by \(w_0\). Thus parameter-count overparameterization is neither necessary nor sufficient for a fixed dataset to interpolate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In linear regression, full row rank plus excess parameters guarantees interpolation, but parameter count alone is neither necessary nor sufficient for fitting fixed data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(w)=0\) is solvable if and only if \(y\in\operatorname{range}(X)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary linear-algebra characterization of exact least-squares interpolation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear-regression example correctly separates parameter-count overparameterization from interpolation, and failure_boundary is appropriate for this relationship leaf. No inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonstationary Objectives
children.top_down_role: Time-dependent objective behavior in learning optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-indexed optimization model whose objective may change during the decision sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a fixed feasible set and let \(f_t:\Theta\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be the loss objective presented at time \(t=1,\ldots,T\). The problem is nonstationary when the sequence is not constrained to satisfy \(f_t=f\) for all \(t\). An optimizer produces decisions \(\theta_t\in\Theta\), while a time-varying comparator may be chosen as \(\theta_t^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}f_t(\theta)\). Performance can be measured by dynamic regret \[\operatorname{Reg}^{\mathrm{dyn}}_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(f_t(\theta_t)-f_t(\theta_t^\star)\bigr),\] provided the per-time minima exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstationary problem has a time-varying objective sequence; dynamic regret compares each decision with a minimizer of the current objective.
assumptions_latex: Each comparator \(\theta_t^\star\) exists when dynamic regret is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Reg}^{\mathrm{dyn}}_T=\sum_{t=1}^T(f_t(\theta_t)-f_t(\theta_t^\star))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dynamic-regret formula is standard, but no source is supplied. The phrase 'when the sequence is not constrained to satisfy' defines a model class that permits variation rather than a property of a realized sequence; a sourced revision should distinguish those meanings.

children.title: Objective Drift Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gradual evolution of the optimization target.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Drift Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradual nonstationarity controlled by functional or minimizer-path variation budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For objectives \(f_1,\ldots,f_T:\Theta\to\mathbb R\), a bounded objective-drift regime may be specified by the functional variation budget \[V_T:=\sum_{t=2}^T\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lvert f_t(\theta)-f_{t-1}(\theta)\rvert\leq B_T.\] When minimizers \(\theta_t^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}f_t(\theta)\) are selected, an alternative path-length regime is \[P_T:=\sum_{t=2}^T\lVert\theta_t^\star-\theta_{t-1}^\star\rVert\leq C_T.\] These conditions are distinct: functional variation controls changes over the whole feasible set, whereas path length controls only a selected sequence of minimizers. Budgets that are sublinear in \(T\) describe variation that is sublinear relative to the time horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective drift can be bounded by the total uniform change of successive functions or by the path length of selected minimizers; these are distinct assumptions.
assumptions_latex: Minimizers \(\theta_t^\star\) exist when \(P_T\) is used, and a particular minimizer sequence is selected if minimizers are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_T\leq B_T\) or \(P_T\leq C_T\) defines the selected drift regime.

notation.meaning: functional variation accumulated by the objective sequence
path length of the selected minimizer sequence

children.title: Abrupt Objective Changes
children.top_down_role: Discrete target shifts, change points, and phase boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Abrupt Objective Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-stationary objective model with finitely many discrete change points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K<\tau_{K+1}=T+1\) be change-point boundaries. An objective sequence has at most \(K\) abrupt changes if there exist functions \(g_0,\ldots,g_K:\Theta\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \[f_t=g_j\quad\text{whenever }\tau_j\leq t<\tau_{j+1}.\] A genuine change at \(\tau_j\) additionally requires \(g_j\neq g_{j-1}\). When the segment functions are real-valued and their uniform difference is finite, this may be expressed by \[0<\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\lvert g_j(\theta)-g_{j-1}(\theta)\rvert<+\infty.\] Thus the objective is stationary within each segment and changes only at the designated boundaries; a minimum jump-size condition may additionally be imposed for change detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abrupt-change regime is piecewise stationary: the objective is constant within each segment and switches to a different function at designated change points.
assumptions_latex: Each segment function \(g_j\) has the common feasible domain \(\Theta\).
Real-valuedness and finite uniform differences are required only for the displayed supremum characterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_t=g_j\) for every \(t\) satisfying \(\tau_j\leq t<\tau_{j+1}\).

children.title: Deterministic Gradient Oracles
children.top_down_role: Exact first-order access for differentiable objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Gradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order oracle for differentiable objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and let \(f:U	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable. A deterministic gradient oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal O_f:U	o\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \[\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),
abla f(x))\] for every query \(x\in U\); when function values are not requested, the oracle may return only \(
abla f(x)\). Repeated queries at the same point return the same exact result. If, additionally, \(U\) is convex and \(f\) is convex on \(U\), then the returned gradient satisfies \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle\qquad	ext{for all }x,y\in U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic gradient oracle returns the exact function value and gradient at a query, with no sampling noise or query-to-query randomness. For a differentiable convex function on a convex domain, the returned gradient also gives the global supporting inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
Convexity of both the domain \(U\) and the function \(f\) is required only for the global supporting inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x))\).

notation.meaning: exact gradient at the query point

children.title: Deterministic Subgradient Oracles
children.top_down_role: Exact first-order access for nonsmooth objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Subgradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order oracle for proper convex, possibly nonsmooth objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex. At any query \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\), a deterministic subgradient oracle returns \[\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),g(x)),\qquad g(x)\in\partial f(x),\] where \[\partial f(x):=\{g\in\mathbb R^d: f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \text{for all }y\in\mathbb R^d\}.\] If the subdifferential contains multiple vectors, the oracle uses a fixed selection rule, so repeated queries at \(x\) return the same \(g(x)\). At differentiability points, \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic subgradient oracle returns an exact supporting subgradient selected consistently at each query; it reduces to the gradient oracle where the function is differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),g(x))\) with \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\).

children.title: Smoothness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation between differentiable and nonsmooth oracle regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact gradient-oracle models from subgradient models at loss of differentiability or Lipschitz gradient regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be open and convex, and let \(f:U	o\mathbb{R}\) be convex. The smooth first-order regime with constant \(L\geq 0\) requires differentiability and \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2\leq L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).\] An exact deterministic gradient oracle can then return \(
abla f(x)\). If \(f\) is nondifferentiable at some \(x\), that oracle is undefined there and must be replaced by an oracle returning \(g\in\partial f(x)\). If differentiability holds but no finite \(L\) satisfies the inequality, analyses requiring an \(L\)-smooth oracle do not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact gradient models require differentiability; smooth-method guarantees additionally require a Lipschitz gradient. Nondifferentiable points require subgradients, while an unbounded gradient Lipschitz constant lies outside smooth analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic \(L\)-smooth gradient-oracle model is valid exactly under differentiability and the displayed finite-\(L\) inequality; otherwise the indicated boundary is crossed.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x

knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Stochastic-Gradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses conditional unbiasedness, the form needed when oracle calls may depend on an algorithm’s past.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and let \(\mathcal F_t\) contain all information available before the query \(x_t\). An unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle returns an integrable random vector \(G_t=G(x_t,\xi_t)\) such that \[\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\quad\text{almost surely}.\] A bounded-noise version additionally supplies \(\sigma\geq0\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[\|G_t-\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\leq\sigma^2\). Unbiasedness defines the oracle type; the variance bound is an additional quantitative assumption used in convergence rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given the algorithm’s past, the oracle’s expected output equals the true gradient. A conditional second-moment bound may additionally quantify its noise.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(G_t\) is conditionally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_t\) is an unbiased stochastic-gradient estimate of \(\nabla f(x_t)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Component Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines component-gradient access and its unbiased importance-weighted stochastic realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable. A finite-sum component oracle accepts \((x,i)\) and returns \((f_i(x),
abla f_i(x))\), or only \(
abla f_i(x)\) when values are unnecessary. If \(I\) is sampled with probabilities \(p_i>0\), then \[G(x,I)= rac{1}{n p_I}
abla f_I(x)\] satisfies \(\mathbb E[G(x,I)\mid x]=
abla f(x)\). Uniform sampling gives \(G(x,I)=
abla f_I(x)\). Thus component access is stronger than receiving an unspecified stochastic gradient because the queried index is observable or selectable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component oracle returns one summand’s gradient. Sampling component i with positive probability and applying importance weighting yields an unbiased full-gradient estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[(n p_I)^{-1}\nabla f_I(x)\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\).

children.title: Biased First-Order Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle regimes with systematic directional error.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased First-Order Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bias conditionally on the optimization history and separates bounded from vanishing bias models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. For a query \(x_t\) measurable with respect to the past \(\mathcal F_t\), an integrable first-order oracle output \(G_t\) has conditional bias \[b_t=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]-\nabla f(x_t).\] It is a biased first-order oracle when \(b_t\neq0\) may occur with positive probability. A uniformly \(\delta\)-biased model requires \(\|b_t\|_2\leq\delta\) almost surely for every call; a vanishing-bias model instead requires a deterministic sequence \(\delta_t\downarrow0\) with \(\|b_t\|_2\leq\delta_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic first-order oracle is biased when its conditional mean differs from the true gradient. The discrepancy may be uniformly bounded or required to vanish over time.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(G_t\) is conditionally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \(b_t\) exactly measures the oracle’s conditional first-order bias.

children.title: Inexact First-Order Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle regimes with limited numerical or computational accuracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact First-Order Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the norm-bounded approximate-gradient model rather than a function-model or relative-error oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and fix a tolerance \(\delta\geq0\). A deterministic norm-inexact first-order oracle returns \(g_\delta(x)\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfying \[\|g_\delta(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_2\leq\delta\] at every admissible query \(x\). A stochastic norm-inexact oracle may return \(G_\delta(x,\xi)\) satisfying the same inequality almost surely. The case \(\delta=0\) recovers exact first-order access. This definition bounds total oracle error and, by itself, does not require the error to be unbiased, independent across calls, or adversarial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact oracle returns an approximate gradient whose norm error is at most a specified tolerance. The definition permits either systematic or random error.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta\geq0\) is fixed for the oracle call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned vector belongs to the closed ball \(\nabla f(x)+\delta\mathbb B_2\).

children.title: Bias–Accuracy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interaction between systematic error and approximation fidelity.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias–Accuracy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the conditional mean-square-error decomposition governing bias, variance, and attainable oracle accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_t\) be square-integrable conditionally on \(\mathcal F_t\), and define \(b_t=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]-\nabla f(x_t)\). Then the conditional oracle mean-square error decomposes as \[\mathbb E[\|G_t-\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t]=\mathbb E[\|G_t-\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t]+\|b_t\|_2^2.\] Consequently, an accuracy requirement with right-hand side at most \(\varepsilon^2\) forces both the conditional variance and squared bias to be at most \(\varepsilon^2\). Reducing variance alone cannot overcome a nonvanishing bias floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-square oracle error equals conditional variance plus squared bias. Therefore persistent bias creates an accuracy floor that cannot be removed merely by variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditional mean-square accuracy splits exactly into conditional variance and squared conditional bias.

children.title: Euclidean Parameter Geometry
children.top_down_role: Isotropic vector-space geometry for parameters and updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Parameter Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents an isotropic gradient step as a quadratic proximal minimization in Euclidean parameter space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with the inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^\top y\) and norm \(\|x\|_2\). The inner product identifies each covector \(g\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^*\) with a unique vector, permitting the update \[x^+=x-\eta g=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{\langle g,z\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta}\|z-x\|_2^2\right\},\qquad \eta>0.\] Thus Euclidean parameter geometry uses the identity Riesz map and penalizes all orthonormal directions equally. Under an orthogonal change of coordinates, the norm and this update retain the same form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean geometry identifies gradients with vectors through the standard inner product. A gradient step is equivalently a linearized objective minimized with an isotropic squared-distance penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euclidean gradient step equals the displayed quadratic proximal minimizer.

children.title: Coordinatewise Update Geometry
children.top_down_role: Axis-specific scaling and update structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Update Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents axis-aligned anisotropic steps using a positive diagonal metric or coordinate-specific learning rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\) with \(h_i>0\), and define \(\|u\|_H^2=u^\top Hu\). For \(x,g\in\mathbb{R}^d\), the coordinatewise metric step is \[x^+=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{\langle g,z\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta}\|z-x\|_H^2\right\}=x-\eta H^{-1}g.\] Equivalently, \(x_i^+=x_i-\eta_i g_i\) with \(\eta_i=\eta/h_i\). The geometry is tied to the chosen coordinate axes; unequal \(h_i\) assign different costs and effective learning rates to different coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal metric produces separate step sizes for separate coordinates. Unequal diagonal weights make the update anisotropic and dependent on the chosen axes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagonal-metric proximal step is exactly \(x^+=x-\eta H^{-1}g\).

children.title: Isotropy–Anisotropy Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transition between shared scaling and coordinate-specific scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Isotropy–Anisotropy Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a quadratic parameter metric treats every orthonormal direction identically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) be symmetric positive definite and let \(\|u\|_H^2=u^\top Hu\). The metric is isotropic precisely when it is invariant under every orthogonal coordinate transformation: \[\|Qu\|_H=\|u\|_H\quad\text{for all }u\in\mathbb{R}^d\text{ and all }Q\text{ with }Q^\top Q=I.\] This condition holds if and only if \(H=\alpha I\) for some \(\alpha>0\). Hence a diagonal metric is anisotropic exactly when two diagonal entries differ; its update then assigns direction-dependent effective step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic metric is invariant under every rotation exactly when its matrix is a positive scalar multiple of the identity. Unequal coordinate weights cross into anisotropic geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric is isotropic if and only if \(H=\alpha I\) for some \(\alpha>0\); otherwise it is anisotropic.

children.top_down_role: Parameter representations induced by mirror-coordinate choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror Parameter Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents parameter motion through primal coordinates and their dual mirror coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex, and let \(h:X	o\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be Legendre with \(
abla h\) invertible between \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) and \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\). Define the mirror coordinate \(y=
abla h(x)\). An unconstrained mirror step with covector \(g\) and \(\eta>0\) is \[y^+=y-\eta g,\qquad x^+=
abla h^*(y^+).\] Equivalently, \(x^+=(
abla h)^{-1}(
abla h(x)-\eta g)\). The choice of \(h\) therefore determines the nonlinear parameter geometry and the conversion between primal parameters and dual first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror geometry maps parameters into dual coordinates, takes an additive gradient step there, and maps back through the conjugate gradient. The mirror function determines this geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal mirror update is \(x^+=\nabla h^*(\nabla h(x)-\eta g)\).

children.title: Bregman Update Geometry
children.top_down_role: Update geometry organized through Bregman discrepancy.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Update Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses a constrained mirror step as minimization regularized by a directed Bregman divergence, with the required attainment condition made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(h\) be differentiable and strictly convex on an open set containing \(X\). Its Bregman divergence is \[D_h(z,x)=h(z)-h(x)-\langle
abla h(x),z-xangle.\] Given \(x\in X\), a covector \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(\eta>0\), assume that the following minimum is attained. The Bregman update is \[x^+\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X}\left\{\eta\langle g,zangle+D_h(z,x)ight\}.\] Strict convexity makes an attained minimizer unique. If \(h\) is strongly convex on \(X\), the objective is coercive and strongly convex on \(X\), so the minimizer exists and is unique. When \(X=\mathbb{R}^d\) and the minimizer exists, its first-order optimality condition is \(
abla h(x^+)=
abla h(x)-\eta g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman update minimizes a linear first-order model plus the divergence generated by a strictly convex mirror function. The update requires the minimum to be attained; strong convexity guarantees existence and uniqueness under the stated conditions. In the unconstrained case, its optimality condition gives the dual-coordinate mirror step.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and strictly convex on an open set containing \(X\).
The displayed minimum is attained unless strong convexity is invoked to guarantee attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed attained minimization defines a unique Bregman update; strong convexity of \(h\) guarantees existence and uniqueness under the stated conditions.

children.title: Primal–Dual Geometry Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between primal parameters and dual coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Geometry Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the Legendre correspondence, the dual form of Bregman divergence, and the admissibility condition for passing from a dual mirror update back to primal space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper closed Legendre convex function, with Fenchel conjugate \(h^*\). For \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) and \(y=
abla h(x)\), Fenchel equality and inverse-gradient duality give \[h(x)+h^*(y)=\langle x,yangle,\qquad x=
abla h^*(y).\] For every \(z\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), the corresponding Bregman divergences satisfy \[D_h(z,x)=D_{h^*}(
abla h(x),
abla h(z)).\] Thus a primal displacement measured by \(D_h\) is represented by a reversed dual displacement measured by \(D_{h^*}\). Given a covector \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\eta>0\), if \(y^+=y-\eta g\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), then the updated primal point is \(x^+=
abla h^*(y^+)\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed Legendre mirror function bijectively links interior primal points and interior dual coordinates. Primal Bregman divergence equals the conjugate divergence with reversed gradient arguments. An additive dual update can be mapped back to primal space whenever the updated dual coordinate remains in the conjugate domain’s interior.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, convex, and Legendre.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The maps \(
abla h\) and \(
abla h^*\) are inverse on the stated interiors, \(D_h(z,x)=D_{h^*}(
abla h(x),
abla h(z))\), and every admissible dual update returns to primal space through \(x^+=
abla h^*(y-\eta g)\).

children.title: Blockwise Parameter Geometry
children.top_down_role: Parameter partitions based on computational or structural blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Parameter Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space geometry induced by a fixed partition of the optimizer parameter vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\oplus\cdots\oplus X_B\) be a finite-dimensional real parameter space with block decomposition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_B)\). A blockwise parameter geometry is specified by symmetric positive-definite operators \(H_b:X_b\to X_b\) and the block-diagonal operator \(H=\operatorname{diag}(H_1,\ldots,H_B)\). Its inner product, norm, and dual norm are \[\langle u,v\rangle_H=\sum_{b=1}^B\langle u_b,H_bv_b\rangle,\qquad \|u\|_H^2=\sum_{b=1}^B\|u_b\|_{H_b}^2,\qquad \|g\|_{H^{-1}}^2=\sum_{b=1}^B\langle g_b,H_b^{-1}g_b\rangle.\] Consequently, the metric-scaled first-order direction is \(-H^{-1}g=(-H_1^{-1}g_1,\ldots,-H_B^{-1}g_B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blockwise geometry equips each parameter block with its own positive-definite metric; norms and metric-scaled gradient updates then decompose as sums and independent block directions.
assumptions_latex: \(X_b\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space for every \(b\).
\(H_b\) is symmetric positive definite for every \(b\).

notation.meaning: positive-definite metric operator on block b
block component of a gradient or first-order oracle output

children.title: Layerwise Parameter Geometry
children.top_down_role: Parameter partitions aligned with network layers.

knowledge_statements.title: Layerwise Parameter Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product geometry whose blocks are the ordered parameter tensors of a layered model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a model with ordered layers \(1,\ldots,L\) and parameter space \(X=X^{(1)}\oplus\cdots\oplus X^{(L)}\). A layerwise parameter geometry assigns to each layer a symmetric positive-definite operator \(H_\ell:X^{(\ell)}\to X^{(\ell)}\), possibly determined by that layer's dimensions or activations, while excluding off-diagonal metric terms. For \(u=(u^{(1)},\ldots,u^{(L)})\), \[\|u\|_H^2=\sum_{\ell=1}^L\langle u^{(\ell)},H_\ell u^{(\ell)}\rangle.\] Given layer gradients \(g^{(\ell)}\) and step size \(\eta>0\), the associated metric step is \[x_+^{(\ell)}=x^{(\ell)}-\eta H_\ell^{-1}g^{(\ell)},\qquad \ell=1,\ldots,L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layerwise geometry treats each model layer as a metric block, allowing layer-dependent scaling while retaining a block-diagonal update across layers.
assumptions_latex: \(X^{(\ell)}\) is finite dimensional for every layer \(\ell\).
\(H_\ell\) is symmetric positive definite for every layer \(\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_+^{(\ell)}=x^{(\ell)}-\eta H_\ell^{-1}g^{(\ell)}\) independently for each \(\ell\).

notation.meaning: parameter space associated with layer l
metric operator assigned to layer l

children.title: Cross-Block Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interactions that limit independent block or layer treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Off-diagonal metric structure coupling first-order updates across parameter blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\bigoplus_{b=1}^B X_b\) and let \(H:X\to X\) be symmetric positive definite, with block operators \(H_{bc}:X_c\to X_b\). The geometry has cross-block coupling exactly when \(H_{bc}\ne0\) for some \(b\ne c\). For a gradient \(g\), the metric direction \(d=-H^{-1}g\) satisfies \[\sum_{c=1}^B H_{bc}d_c=-g_b,\qquad b=1,\ldots,B.\] Hence a component \(d_b\) generally depends on gradient components outside block \(b\). Independent block scaling occurs precisely when \(H\) is block diagonal, equivalently when every off-diagonal operator \(H_{bc}\) vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Off-diagonal metric blocks couple the update equations, so one block's direction may depend on gradients from other blocks; independent scaling is equivalent to a block-diagonal metric.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\bigoplus_{b=1}^B X_b\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-block dependence occurs through \(H_{bc}\), and blockwise independence is equivalent to \(H_{bc}=0\) for all \(b\ne c\).

notation.meaning: metric operator mapping block c into block b
block b of the metric-scaled direction

children.title: Matrix Parameter Geometry
children.top_down_role: Row-column structure in matrix-valued parameter spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Parameter Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided quadratic geometry preserving the row-column structure of a matrix parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the parameter be \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Given symmetric positive-definite matrices \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), the associated two-sided matrix geometry is \[\langle U,V\rangle_{A,B}=\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}AVB),\qquad \|U\|_{A,B}^2=\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}AUB).\] Under column vectorization its metric matrix is \(B\otimes A\), since \(\|U\|_{A,B}^2=\operatorname{vec}(U)^{\mathsf T}(B\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(U)\). For a gradient matrix \(G\), the metric-scaled direction is \(D=-A^{-1}GB^{-1}\), equivalently the unique solution of \(ADB=-G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix geometry applies separate positive-definite metrics to row and column modes, yielding a Kronecker metric and the scaled direction obtained from a two-sided linear equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric is \(B\otimes A\), and its scaled gradient direction is \(D=-A^{-1}GB^{-1}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Kronecker representation of a two-sided matrix quadratic form
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided matrix metric, Kronecker representation, and scaled direction are mutually consistent and fit the leaf, but they lack a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Tensor Parameter Geometry
children.top_down_role: Multimode structure in higher-order parameter spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Parameter Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mode-separable quadratic geometry for an order-K tensor parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_K}\), and for each mode \(k\) let \(A_k\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times n_k}\) be symmetric positive definite. A mode-separable tensor geometry is the quadratic form whose matrix under a fixed vectorization convention is \[H=A_K\otimes\cdots\otimes A_1,\qquad \|\mathcal U\|_H^2=\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal U)^{\mathsf T}H\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal U).\] If \(\mathcal G\) is the gradient tensor, the metric direction \(\mathcal D\) is determined by \[\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal D)=-\bigl(A_K^{-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes A_1^{-1}\bigr)\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal G).\] Thus every tensor mode contributes a separate factor to the parameter and dual geometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable tensor geometry assigns one positive-definite factor to each tensor mode; the full metric and its inverse are Kronecker products of those factors.
assumptions_latex: \(K\ge2\) and each mode dimension \(n_k\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=A_K\otimes\cdots\otimes A_1\) and \(H^{-1}=A_K^{-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes A_1^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: positive-definite metric factor for mode k

children.title: Flattening-Sensitive Geometry
children.top_down_role: Dependence of optimizer structure on matrix or tensor reshaping.

knowledge_statements.title: Flattening-Sensitive Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry whose induced quadratic form depends on the chosen tensor matricization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a tensor and let \(F\) and \(F'\) be two bijective flattenings with permutation matrix \(P\) satisfying \(\operatorname{vec}(F'(\mathcal U))=P\operatorname{vec}(F(\mathcal U))\). Suppose a matrix-space rule assigns metric matrices \(M_F\) and \(M_{F'}\) after applying the two flattenings. The rule is flattening invariant when \[M_F=P^{\mathsf T}M_{F'}P.\] It is flattening sensitive when this equality fails for at least one tensor shape and pair \(F,F'\). In that case, some perturbation \(\mathcal U\) has unequal squared norms under the two induced geometries, even though both flattenings encode the same tensor entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tensor geometry is flattening sensitive if two equivalent matricizations induce quadratic forms that are not related by the corresponding coordinate permutation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(F'\) are bijective flattenings of the same finite-dimensional tensor space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flattening sensitivity is equivalent to the existence of \(F,F'\) for which \(M_F\ne P^{\mathsf T}M_{F'}P\).

children.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting by first-order oracle interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-indexed count of interactions with a specified first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm interact with an oracle \(\mathcal O\), where one call at a query point returns the output prescribed by the oracle model. For an accuracy predicate \(\mathsf{Acc}(x,\varepsilon)\), define the worst-case oracle-call complexity over an instance class \(\mathcal F\) by \[N_{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf\bigl\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\mathsf{Acc}(x_t,f,\varepsilon)\text{ holds}\bigr\}.\] The count increases by one per invocation of \(\mathcal O\), independently of the arithmetic cost of producing or processing its response. A claimed bound \(N_{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon)\le T(\varepsilon)\) is meaningful only after \(\mathcal O\), \(\mathcal F\), and \(\mathsf{Acc}\) have been fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity is the worst-case number of invocations of a specified oracle needed to meet a stated accuracy criterion, excluding internal arithmetic unless separately counted.
assumptions_latex: An instance class \(\mathcal F\), oracle model \(\mathcal O\), and accuracy predicate \(\mathsf{Acc}\) are fixed.
The algorithm produces an iterate \(x_t\) after \(t\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon)\) counts oracle invocations required for the prescribed accuracy, not arithmetic operations.

notation.meaning: worst-case oracle-call complexity at accuracy epsilon

children.title: Gradient-Evaluation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity accounting by full or component gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Evaluation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy-indexed count of individual component-gradient computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(t\) evaluates component gradients \(\nabla f_i(x_t)\) for indices in a multiset \(B_t\). If \(T_\varepsilon\) is the first iteration whose output satisfies the fixed accuracy predicate, define the gradient-evaluation complexity by \[N_{\nabla}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}|B_t|.\] A full gradient of \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) therefore costs \(n\) component-gradient evaluations, whereas a minibatch of size \(b_t\) costs \(b_t\). This resource can differ from oracle-call complexity because a single batched oracle invocation may return multiple component gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-evaluation complexity totals individual component gradients, so a batch of size b costs b evaluations even when obtained through one oracle call.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) and component gradients are the atomic resource.
The stopping iteration \(T_\varepsilon\) is defined by a fixed accuracy predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\nabla}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{t<T_\varepsilon}|B_t|\), which need not equal the number of batched oracle calls.

notation.meaning: multiset of component indices evaluated at iteration t

children.title: Batch Accounting Conventions
children.top_down_role: Normalization choices for comparing calls across batch sizes.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch Accounting Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit conversion between batched calls, examples processed, and component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let iteration \(t\) use a batch multiset \(B_t\) of size \(b_t\), and let \(T\) iterations be executed. Under call accounting, one simultaneous request for the batch contributes one oracle call, so \(N_{\mathrm{call}}=T\). Under sample or component-gradient accounting, every occurrence in every batch is counted, so \[N_{\mathrm{sample}}=N_{\nabla}=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t.\] With constant batch size \(b\), this becomes \(N_{\mathrm{sample}}=bN_{\mathrm{call}}\). Repeated indices are counted with multiplicity. Therefore complexity comparisons involving batching must state which resource is counted and whether parallel evaluation changes elapsed depth without changing total sample work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One batched request counts as one call but as b sample or component-gradient evaluations; repeated samples count with multiplicity, and parallel execution does not erase total work.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration issues exactly one batch request.
Every sampled component gradient is assigned unit sample work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{call}}=T\) and \(N_{\mathrm{sample}}=N_{\nabla}=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t\).

notation.meaning: batch cardinality at iteration t, including multiplicity

children.title: Arithmetic Work Complexity
children.top_down_role: Operation-count costs of optimizer computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Work Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total scalar-operation cost required to attain a prescribed optimization accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a scalar-operation model in which additions, multiplications, divisions, comparisons, and specified elementary functions have declared unit or weighted costs. If an execution reaching accuracy \(\varepsilon\) performs operations \(o_1,\ldots,o_m\) with costs \(c(o_j)\), its arithmetic work is \[W(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j=1}^m c(o_j).\] For an iterative method with \(T_\varepsilon\) iterations, per-iteration local work \(w_t\), and oracle-response work \(q_t\) included by convention, \[W(\varepsilon)=\sum_{t=0}^{T_\varepsilon-1}(w_t+q_t).\] Work counts all executed arithmetic operations, including operations performed concurrently, and therefore differs from parallel depth and communication volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic work is the total weighted count of scalar operations needed for the target accuracy; concurrent operations still contribute separately to total work.
assumptions_latex: The accuracy predicate and stopping index \(T_\varepsilon\) are fixed.
A scalar-operation cost model specifies whether oracle-response computation is included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(\varepsilon)\) is the sum of all included operation costs and is not reduced merely by parallel execution.

notation.meaning: arithmetic work required for accuracy epsilon
included local arithmetic work at iteration t

children.title: Parallel Depth Complexity
children.top_down_role: Critical-path costs under parallel execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Depth Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path length of an accuracy-achieving parallel computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the computation producing an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output by a finite directed acyclic graph whose vertices are unit-time arithmetic, oracle, or communication operations under a declared parallel machine model, and whose edges encode dependencies. The parallel depth is \[D(\varepsilon)=\max_{p}\sum_{v\in p}\tau(v),\] where the maximum ranges over directed paths \(p\) and \(\tau(v)\) is the latency assigned to vertex \(v\). With unlimited processors and no omitted resource constraints, the execution time is at least \(D(\varepsilon)\). Always \(D(\varepsilon)\le W(\varepsilon)\) when every included vertex has unit cost in both measures, with equality for a completely sequential dependency graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel depth is the weighted critical-path length of the computation; it lower-bounds parallel time and never exceeds unit-cost total work under consistent accounting.
assumptions_latex: The accuracy-achieving computation is represented by a finite dependency DAG.
Operation latencies and the parallel machine model are fixed.
Work and depth include the same unit-cost vertices for the comparison \(D\le W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\varepsilon)\) is the critical-path cost and satisfies \(D(\varepsilon)\le W(\varepsilon)\) under consistent unit-cost accounting.

notation.meaning: parallel depth required for accuracy epsilon

children.title: Communication Overhead
children.top_down_role: Synchronization and data-movement costs affecting parallel scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional distributed cost measured by messages, transmitted data, and synchronization rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution attaining accuracy \(\varepsilon\) on \(P\) workers, let \(m_r\) be the number of messages and \(v_r\) the number of transmitted scalar words in communication round \(r\), for \(r=1,\ldots,R_\varepsilon\). Its communication resources are \[M(\varepsilon)=\sum_{r=1}^{R_\varepsilon}m_r,\qquad V(\varepsilon)=\sum_{r=1}^{R_\varepsilon}v_r,\qquad R(\varepsilon)=R_\varepsilon.\] In an \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) latency-bandwidth model, a serialized upper accounting is \[C_{\mathrm{comm}}(\varepsilon)=\alpha M(\varepsilon)+\beta V(\varepsilon),\] with synchronization or congestion costs added when the machine model requires them. Communication overhead must be reported separately from arithmetic work unless those costs are explicitly incorporated into one common time model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication overhead records message count, transmitted words, and rounds; a latency-bandwidth model combines messages and volume, with synchronization added when required.
assumptions_latex: A distributed execution and its communication rounds are fixed.
The \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) model assigns latency \(\alpha\) per message and transfer cost \(\beta\) per scalar word.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}(\varepsilon)=\alpha M(\varepsilon)+\beta V(\varepsilon)\) under serialized latency-bandwidth accounting.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Memory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-memory coordinate for comparing first-order learning optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an iterative optimizer, let \(x_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be the current model and let \(s_t\in\mathcal S_t\) collect every quantity retained from iterations preceding \(t\), excluding fixed hyperparameters and the current oracle response. A memoryless method has \(\mathcal S_t=\{\varnothing\}\) and \(M_t=0\); retaining \(k\) dense vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(q\) scalars gives \(M_t=kd+q\). The model vector \(x_t\) may be reported separately as unavoidable iterate storage.

children.title: Optimization Progress Measures
children.top_down_role: Quantities used to track optimization advancement.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Progress Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar measures used to quantify first-order optimization progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(X\subseteq E\), let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\neq\varnothing\), and let \(f^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x)>-\infty\). For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), standard progress measures include the objective gap \(\Delta_f(x)=f(x)-f^*\) and the solution distance \(d_*(x)=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}\lVert x-x^*\rVert\). In the unconstrained case \(X=E\), when \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), a stationarity measure is \(r(x)=\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_*\). The objective gap and solution distance vanish at every minimizer, and the gradient residual vanishes at every differentiable unconstrained minimizer; converses require additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common progress measures are objective suboptimality and distance to the solution set. In differentiable unconstrained optimization, the gradient norm is also a stationarity measure. Equivalence or converse implications require additional structural assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(X\subseteq E\).
The gradient residual is used only when \(X=E\) and \(f\) is differentiable at the point under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x^*\in X^*\), \(\Delta_f(x^*)=0\) and \(d_*(x^*)=0\); if additionally \(X=E\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\), then \(r(x^*)=0\).

notation.meaning: distance from x to the solution set
dual-norm gradient residual in the differentiable unconstrained setting

children.title: Optimization Certificate Types

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Certificate Types
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable witnesses associated with common optimization guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimizing \(f\) over \(X\), an \(\varepsilon\)-certificate is data \(C(x)\), computable or checkable from declared problem information, whose validity implies a stated tolerance. Principal types are: a value certificate \(U(x)-L\le\varepsilon\), where \(U(x)=f(x)\) and \(L\le f^*\); a stationarity certificate \(R(x)\le\varepsilon\), where \(R(x)=0\) expresses the relevant first-order condition; and a feasibility certificate \(V(x)\le\varepsilon\), where \(V\) measures constraint violation. A primal-dual certificate may jointly bound feasibility and a primal-dual gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificates are checkable witnesses of value accuracy, stationarity, feasibility, or a combined primal-dual guarantee; each type requires a declared residual and tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Every reported bound or residual is computable from the declared certificate data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validity of \(C(x)\) implies its declared value, stationarity, feasibility, or primal-dual tolerance.

notation.meaning: certified lower bound on the optimal value

children.title: Progress–Certificate Matching
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between a progress measure and its reported certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Progress–Certificate Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between a reported rate and its terminating certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be the progress measure appearing in an optimizer guarantee, and let \(C:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a checkable certificate residual. The pair is matched on a problem class \(\mathcal F\) if there exists a known nondecreasing function \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\), with \(\phi(0)=0\), such that for every instance in \(\mathcal F\) and every admissible \(x\), \(C(x)\le\varepsilon\) implies \(P(x)\le\phi(\varepsilon)\). It is rate-matched if a stated certificate rate \(C(x_t)\le b_t\) therefore yields \(P(x_t)\le\phi(b_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A progress measure and certificate match when a known uniform implication converts certificate tolerance into the claimed progress tolerance over the entire problem class.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(C\) are defined on every admissible iterate in the problem class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(x_t)\le b_t\Longrightarrow P(x_t)\le\phi(b_t)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Sample Stochastic Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One independent stochastic first-order sample per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), and a stochastic first-order oracle \(G(x,\xi)\), for \(t=0,1,\ldots,T-1\), draw one sample \(\xi_t\) conditionally independently of the past, set \(g_t=G(x_t,\xi_t)\), and update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t g_t\). For constrained optimization over a closed convex set \(X\), replace the update by \(x_{t+1}=\Pi_X(x_t-\eta_tg_t)\). Stop after \(T\) oracle calls and output the declared last iterate or an explicitly weighted average of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, draw one sample, evaluate one stochastic gradient, take a stepsize-scaled gradient step, and optionally project onto the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tG(x_t,\xi_t)\), or \(x_{t+1}=\Pi_X(x_t-\eta_tG(x_t,\xi_t))\) under constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Minibatch Stochastic Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaged stochastic-gradient update using multiple samples per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), batch sizes \(b_t\ge1\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), and a stochastic oracle \(G\), iteration \(t\) draws conditionally independent samples \(\xi_{t,1},\ldots,\xi_{t,b_t}\), forms \(\bar g_t=b_t^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_t}G(x_t,\xi_{t,j})\), and sets \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\bar g_t\). For a closed convex feasible set \(X\), use \(x_{t+1}=\Pi_X(x_t-\eta_t\bar g_t)\). After \(T\) iterations, output the declared last or averaged iterate; the total sample-gradient cost is \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minibatch SGD averages several stochastic gradients at the same iterate before updating; its sample cost is the sum of all batch sizes.
assumptions_latex: Samples within each batch are conditionally independent with finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar g_t=b_t^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b_t}G(x_t,\xi_{t,j})\) and \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\bar g_t\).

children.title: Without-Replacement Sampling
children.top_down_role: Sampling schemes that avoid repeated components within a draw cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population sampling with no repeated index inside a sampling unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A length-\(b\) index sequence \((i_1,\ldots,i_b)\), where \(1\le b\le n\), is sampled without replacement if its entries are almost surely distinct. Uniform ordered sampling without replacement assigns probability \(1/(n)_b\) to every distinct ordered sequence, where \((n)_b=n!/(n-b)!\). Equivalently, draw a uniform random permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\) and take \(i_j=\pi(j)\) for \(1\le j\le b\). Although each \(i_j\) is marginally uniform, the indices are dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without-replacement sampling selects distinct finite-sum indices. Uniform sampling is equivalent to taking a prefix of a random permutation, producing dependent but marginally uniform indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P((i_1,\ldots,i_b)=(j_1,\ldots,j_b))=1/(n)_b\) for every distinct ordered \((j_1,\ldots,j_b)\).

notation.meaning: finite index set from 1 through n
uniform random permutation of the index set

children.title: Random-Reshuffling Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Reshuffling Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum incremental gradients in a fresh random order each epoch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), initialize \(x_0^0\in\mathbb R^d\). At epoch \(k\), draw a permutation \(\pi_k\) uniformly from all permutations of \([n]\), set \(x_k^0\) to the preceding epoch's endpoint, and for \(j=0,\ldots,n-1\) update \(x_k^{j+1}=x_k^j-\eta_{k,j}\nabla f_{\pi_k(j+1)}(x_k^j)\). Set \(x_{k+1}^0=x_k^n\). After \(K\) epochs, output \(x_K^0\) or another prespecified epoch/iterate average. Each epoch evaluates every component gradient exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random reshuffling randomly permutes all finite-sum components each epoch and performs one incremental-gradient update per component without replacement.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\pi_k\) is uniform; its dependence across epochs is declared by the method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}^0=x_k^n\), where \(x_k^{j+1}=x_k^j-\eta_{k,j}\nabla f_{\pi_k(j+1)}(x_k^j)\).

children.title: Ordering Effects
children.top_down_role: Optimizer behavior attributable to component presentation order.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncommuting incremental updates make epoch endpoints depend on component order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stepsize \(\eta\), define the component update map \(T_i(x)=x-\eta\nabla f_i(x)\). An epoch ordered by permutation \(\pi\) applies \(T_{\pi(n)}\circ\cdots\circ T_{\pi(1)}\); hence its endpoint can depend on \(\pi\) whenever the maps do not commute. Concretely, on \(\mathbb R\), take \(f_1(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2\) and \(f_2(x)=\tfrac12(x+1)^2\). Then \(T_2(T_1(x))=(1-\eta)^2x-\eta^2\), whereas \(T_1(T_2(x))=(1-\eta)^2x+\eta^2\). Thus every \(\eta\neq0\) produces different endpoints for the two orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental component-gradient maps generally do not commute, so two permutations of the same components can yield different epoch endpoints, even for smooth convex quadratics.
assumptions_latex: A common nonzero stepsize \(\eta\) is used for both component updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_2\circ T_1\neq T_1\circ T_2\) for the displayed quadratic components whenever \(\eta\neq0\).

notation.meaning: gradient update map for component i

children.title: Importance Sampling

knowledge_statements.title: Importance Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased finite-sum gradient estimation using inverse-probability weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose probabilities \(p_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\). At iteration \(t\), draw \(I_t\) with \(\mathbb P(I_t=i)=p_i\), form \(g_t=(np_{I_t})^{-1}\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\), and update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t\), or project this point onto a declared convex feasible set. Stop after a prescribed number of samples and output the declared last or averaged iterate. Conditional on \(x_t\), the estimator satisfies \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance-sampled SGD draws components with chosen positive probabilities and divides each sampled component gradient by its finite-sum probability weight to preserve unbiasedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_t=(np_{I_t})^{-1}\nabla f_{I_t}(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb E[g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\).

children.title: Probability-Weighting Interface
children.top_down_role: Interaction between selection probabilities and gradient scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Weighting Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact weighting condition for unbiased finite-sum gradient estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let each \(f_i:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, and let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i f_i(x)\), where \(a_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=1\). Draw \(I\in[n]\) with probabilities \(p_i\ge0\), where \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\) and \(p_i>0\) whenever \(a_i>0\), and use \(g(x,I)=w_I\nabla f_I(x)\). For every \(x\in D\), this estimator is unbiased for \(\nabla F(x)\) for every possible collection of component-gradient values if and only if \(p_iw_i=a_i\) for every \(i\). Thus, on every sampled component with \(p_i>0\), \(w_i=a_i/p_i\); for the uniform average \(a_i=1/n\), this becomes \(w_i=1/(np_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For differentiable weighted finite sums, sampling probability times gradient weight must equal the corresponding objective coefficient. For a uniform finite sum, every sampled component therefore receives weight one over n times its sampling probability.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and each \(f_i:D\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
The unbiasedness identity is required to hold for arbitrary admissible component-gradient values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g(x,I)]=\nabla F(x)\) for all admissible component-gradient values if and only if \(p_iw_i=a_i\) for every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Stochastic-Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projected stochastic subgradient iteration for a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x;\xi)]\) be finite on \(C\). Given \(x_1\in C\), positive stepsizes \((\eta_t)_{t\geq1}\), and samples \(\xi_t\), obtain \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial F(x_t)\), and update \[x_{t+1}=\Pi_C(x_t-\eta_t g_t),\qquad \Pi_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\|x-z\|_2.\] After \(T\) oracle calls, output either \(x_{T+1}\) or the weighted average \(\bar x_T=(\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t x_t)/(\sum_{t=1}^T\eta_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take a stochastic subgradient step, project it onto the feasible set, and return the last iterate or a stepsize-weighted average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\in C\) for every \(t\), and the stated last-iterate or averaged output is well defined.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Mirror-Descent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained stochastic mirror descent with a strongly convex distance-generating function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space, and let \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and strongly convex. Define \(D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\). Starting from \(x_1\in C\), choose \(\eta_t>0\), obtain a stochastic subgradient \(g_t\) with \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial F(x_t)\), and set \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{\eta_t\langle g_t,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_t)\right\}.\] After \(T\) iterations, output \(x_{T+1}\) or a prescribed weighted average of \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize the stochastic objective and regularize the step by a Bregman divergence adapted to the feasible geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and strongly convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update minimizes the stochastic linear model plus the Bregman displacement penalty over \(C\).
