knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Dual-Averaging Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite regularized dual averaging using accumulated stochastic gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty and closed convex, let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x;\xi)]+r(x)\), and let \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be strongly convex. Initialize \(s_0=0\). For positive weights \(a_t\), set \(A_t=\sum_{i=1}^t a_i\), obtain \(g_t\) with \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial\mathbb{E}[f(x_t;\xi)]\), form \(s_t=s_{t-1}+a_tg_t\), and compute \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{\langle s_t,x\rangle+A_t r(x)+\beta_t h(x)\right\},\] where \(\beta_t>0\). Output the last iterate or \(A_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T a_t x_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulate weighted stochastic gradients and recover each iterate by minimizing their aggregate linearization plus composite and strongly convex regularization.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(h\) is strongly convex.
\(a_t>0\), \(\beta_t>0\), and the smooth-part oracle is conditionally unbiased.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) is the regularized primal point associated with the accumulated dual vector \(s_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Regularized dual averaging has several materially different weighting and regularization conventions. No source supports this particular placement of the composite term and beta sequence, and the stated properties of h do not clearly ensure that every displayed argmin is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Proximal-Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-backward stochastic iteration for a smooth-plus-convex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=f(x)+r(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(r\) is proper, closed, and convex. Given \(x_1\in\operatorname{dom}r\) and \(\eta_t>0\), obtain \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\), and update \[x_{t+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta_t r}(x_t-\eta_tg_t),\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\eta r}(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}\left\{r(x)+\frac{1}{2\eta}\|x-z\|_2^2\right\}.\] Stop according to a prescribed iteration or oracle budget and return the last iterate or a specified average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take a stochastic gradient step on the differentiable term and a proximal step on the nonsmooth convex term.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and \(r\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is a stochastic forward step for \(f\) followed by the backward proximal step for \(r\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the scaled regularizer
unbiased stochastic gradient of the differentiable term

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

source_witnesses.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward-backward update fits the stochastic proximal-gradient container, but the cited deterministic proximal-gradient chapter does not specifically support the conditionally unbiased stochastic extension or the proposed output choices. A stochastic proximal-gradient locator is required.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 12: acceleration and when acceleration accelerates

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Ball Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical heavy-ball recurrence with deterministic or stochastic first-order directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), choose \(x_0,x_1\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), and momentum coefficients \(\beta_t\). At iteration \(t\geq1\), obtain \(g_t\), equal to \(\nabla F(x_t)\) in the deterministic case or satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\) in the stochastic case, and set \[x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1}).\] Equivalently, with \(v_t=x_t-x_{t-1}\), use \(v_{t+1}=\beta_tv_t-\eta_tg_t\) and \(x_{t+1}=x_t+v_{t+1}\). Return the iterate selected by the stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball momentum adds a scaled previous displacement to the current first-order step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next displacement equals the current first-order displacement plus \(\beta_t\) times the preceding displacement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence is a standard heavy-ball form, but the record blends deterministic heavy-ball and stochastic momentum under one algorithm without a source establishing that scope. A specific authoritative locator should fix the intended stochastic convention and admissible momentum parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Nesterov-Type Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Look-ahead momentum form commonly used in learning optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\). Initialize \(x_0=x_1\), prescribe \(\eta_t>0\) and \(\beta_t\), and define the extrapolated point \(y_t=x_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1})\). Obtain \(g_t\), equal to \(\nabla F(y_t)\) or satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid y_t]=\nabla F(y_t)\), and update \[x_{t+1}=y_t-\eta_tg_t.\] Thus the first-order direction is evaluated at the extrapolated point rather than at \(x_t\). After the prescribed budget, return the last iterate or an explicitly selected averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extrapolate using the previous displacement, evaluate the gradient at that look-ahead point, and then take a first-order step.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\) is exact or conditionally unbiased at \(y_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=x_t+\beta_t(x_t-x_{t-1})-\eta_tg_t\), with \(g_t\) evaluated at the extrapolated point.

notation.meaning: gradient estimate evaluated at the look-ahead point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Nesterov-type momentum denotes multiple inequivalent recurrences. No citation supports this particular look-ahead-gradient variant, its stochastic extension, or its output rule, so the mathematical version cannot be selected reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Acceleration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth convex stochastic-oracle regime separating deterministic acceleration from noise-limited convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing a convex function \(F\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient over a convex set containing a minimizer \(x^*\), with \(\|x_1-x^*\|_2\leq R\). Suppose a stochastic oracle returns \(g(x)\) with \(\mathbb{E}[g(x)]=\nabla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}\|g(x)-\nabla F(x)\|_2^2\leq\sigma^2\). In the standard stochastic first-order oracle model, accelerated methods can attain expected error of order \[\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat x_T)-F(x^*)]=O\!\left(\frac{LR^2}{T^2}+\frac{\sigma R}{\sqrt{T}}\right).\] Equivalently, accuracy \(\varepsilon\) requires order \(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}+\sigma^2R^2/\varepsilon^2\) oracle calls, up to constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration improves the smooth deterministic term to order inverse-square iterations, while stochastic noise retains an inverse-square-root limitation.
assumptions_latex: The oracle is unbiased with variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic component admits accelerated decay \(O(LR^2/T^2)\), whereas the stochastic component remains \(O(\sigma R/\sqrt{T})\).

notation.meaning: initial distance bound to a minimizer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed deterministic-plus-noise rate is plausible for a smooth convex stochastic-oracle regime and complexity_bound is the correct role, but such a nontrivial rate requires a precise theorem or lower/upper-bound locator. The feasible-set geometry, oracle independence/conditioning, algorithm class, and output estimator also need source-backed specification.

children.title: Scheduled Momentum
children.top_down_role: Momentum policies with time-varying coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduled Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Momentum iteration whose coefficient and stepsize vary according to prescribed schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), initialize \(x_1\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(v_1=0\), and prescribe sequences \(\eta_t>0\) and \(\beta_t\). At time \(t\), obtain \(g_t\), either an exact gradient or a stochastic gradient estimate at \(x_t\), and compute \[v_{t+1}=\beta_t v_t+g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t v_{t+1}.\] The schedules may depend on \(t\) and predetermined hyperparameters but, in the nonadaptive form, not on future oracle observations. Stop at a prescribed horizon \(T\) and output \(x_{T+1}\) or a specified average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply momentum with time-varying momentum coefficients and stepsizes fixed by a schedule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The influence of \(g_i\) on \(v_{t+1}\) is multiplied by \(\prod_{j=i+1}^{t}\beta_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Scheduled Momentum, and the stated influence product follows from the chosen accumulator recurrence. However, momentum normalization conventions differ substantially, and no authoritative source locates this specific scheduled form or its stochastic-oracle assumptions.

children.title: Damped Momentum
children.top_down_role: Momentum policies emphasizing controlled persistence or dissipation.

knowledge_statements.title: Damped Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Momentum recurrence parameterized by an explicit damping sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), initialize \(x_1\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(v_1=0\), and choose \(\eta_t>0\) and damping coefficients \(\gamma_t\in(0,1]\). Given a deterministic or stochastic gradient direction \(g_t\) at \(x_t\), update \[v_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_t)v_t+g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t v_{t+1}.\] Larger \(\gamma_t\) suppresses the previous accumulator more strongly; \(\gamma_t=1\) removes momentum entirely under this convention. Stop at the prescribed horizon and return the selected iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Damped momentum geometrically attenuates the previous accumulator before adding the current gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained fraction of the previous momentum is \(1-\gamma_t\), and zero retention occurs when \(\gamma_t=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence consistently defines damping as one minus momentum retention, but that convention is not universal. A specific source is needed to support the parameterization, stochastic scope, and identification of gamma_t=1 with removal of momentum.

children.title: Schedule–Damping Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where coefficient schedules alter effective damping.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule–Damping Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact constant-parameter stability condition for a scalar positive quadratic mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\tfrac12\lambda x^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), consider the constant-parameter recurrence \[x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta\lambda x_t+\beta(x_t-x_{t-1}),\qquad \beta=1-\gamma.\] Its characteristic polynomial is \(p(r)=r^2-(1+\beta-\eta\lambda)r+\beta\). Both characteristic roots lie strictly inside the unit disk if and only if \[0\leq\beta<1\quad\text{and}\quad 0<\eta\lambda<2(1+\beta).\] Equivalently, for \(0<\gamma\leq1\), stability holds exactly when \(0<\eta\lambda<2(2-\gamma)\). Thus admissible stepsize and damping cannot be selected independently on this quadratic mode.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar quadratic, damping changes the exact stable stepsize interval through the retained momentum coefficient.
assumptions_latex: Stability means both characteristic roots have modulus strictly below one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stability is equivalent to \(0\leq\beta<1\) and \(0<\eta\lambda<2(1+\beta)\).

notation.meaning: damping coefficient equal to one minus retained momentum

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate for the interaction leaf, but the asserted if-and-only-if statement is false unless beta is explicitly restricted to the nonnegative damping regime: stable negative beta values are otherwise omitted. The result also treats constant parameters, not scheduled time-varying interaction. An authoritative stability locator and an explicit parameter domain are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak–Ruppert Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging of stochastic-approximation iterates after a diminishing-step recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t g_t\) be a stochastic-approximation recursion in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with \(\eta_t>0\) and a conditionally unbiased first-order direction \(g_t\). Initialize the running average by \(\bar x_1=x_1\), and for \(t\geq2\) update \[\bar x_t=\bar x_{t-1}+\frac1t(x_t-\bar x_{t-1})=\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^t x_i.\] After \(T\) stochastic updates, return \(\bar x_T\), rather than necessarily returning the terminal raw iterate. Weighted variants replace \(1/t\) by normalized deterministic positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return the uniform running average of stochastic-approximation iterates instead of the final raw iterate.
assumptions_latex: The first-order direction is conditionally unbiased for the target mean field or gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reported point is \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Uniform running averaging is algorithmically well defined and fits the terminal container, but Polyak–Ruppert averaging conventionally carries specific stochastic-approximation and diminishing-step context. No authoritative locator supports the chosen scope or the inclusion of unspecified weighted variants.

children.title: Tail Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging restricted to late-stage iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging restricted to a terminal window of the iterate trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\), choose a tail length \(m\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\). Define the tail-averaged output by \[\bar x_{T,m}^{\mathrm{tail}}=\frac1m\sum_{t=T-m+1}^{T}x_t.\] Equivalently, if a burn-in index \(b\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\) is specified, take \(m=T-b\) and average \(x_{b+1},\ldots,x_T\). The averaging rule does not alter generation of the raw iterates; it only changes the reported estimator. The case \(m=T\) reduces to full-trajectory uniform averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard an initial trajectory segment and return the uniform average of the final window of iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x_{T,m}^{\mathrm{tail}}=m^{-1}\sum_{t=T-m+1}^{T}x_t\), with full averaging recovered when \(m=T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal-window averaging formula and algorithm kind fit Tail Averaging, but no source is supplied. In addition, the assumptions contain `ldots` rather than the intended LaTeX command `\ldots` in both displayed domains; this should be repaired once a source-backed replacement is prepared.

children.title: Suffix Averaging
children.top_down_role: Averaging over a selected terminal trajectory segment.

knowledge_statements.title: Suffix Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging over a terminal block of stochastic iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and choose a suffix length \(m\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\). The suffix-averaged output is
\[
\bar x_{T,m}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{t=T-m+1}^{T}x_t.
\]
Equivalently, for a suffix fraction \(\rho\in(0,1]\), set \(m=\lceil \rho T\rceil\). Only the last \(m\) iterates receive positive weight, and their weights sum to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suffix averaging returns the uniform mean of the final chosen block of iterates, discarding all earlier iterates.
review_flags: Authoritative source specifically defining suffix averaging was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise, internally consistent, and appropriate for the Suffix Averaging leaf, but no source with an inspectable locator is cited.

children.title: Averaging-Window Selection
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing the retained terminal window.

knowledge_statements.title: Averaging-Window Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility and bias-memory criteria for selecting a suffix window.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\), an averaging window is specified by integers \(s_T,m_T\) satisfying
\[
1\le s_T\le T,\qquad 1\le m_T\le T-s_T+1,
\]
and produces \(m_T^{-1}\sum_{t=s_T}^{s_T+m_T-1}x_t\). A suffix window additionally satisfies \(s_T=T-m_T+1\). An asymptotically expanding suffix regime obeys \(m_T\to\infty\); it discards an asymptotically nonvanishing initial fraction when \(m_T/T\to\rho\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid window lies within the trajectory; an expanding suffix uses increasingly many terminal iterates and may discard a fixed initial fraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_T=T-m_T+1\) characterizes suffix windows, while \(m_T\to\infty\) characterizes expanding-window schedules.

notation.meaning: first index of the averaging window
number of iterates in the window

review_flags: No supplied locator supports a canonical statistical criterion for window selection.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The admissibility conditions and asymptotic regimes are coherent and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the proposed window-selection characterization has no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Exponential Iterate Averaging
children.top_down_role: Recency-weighted aggregation of iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Iterate Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive exponentially weighted averaging of an optimization trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given iterates \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\in\mathbb{R}^d\), initialize \(z_0=x_0\). For parameters \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\), update
\[
z_t=\beta_t z_{t-1}+(1-\beta_t)x_t,
\qquad t\ge1.
\]
After \(T\) iterations output \(z_T\). For constant \(\beta_t=\beta\), expansion gives
\[
z_T=\beta^T x_0+(1-\beta)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta^{T-t}x_t,
\]
so the weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a running convex combination that assigns geometrically decreasing weight to older iterates, then return the final running average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(z_T\) is a convex combination of \(x_0,\ldots,x_T\).
review_flags: The recursion is standard, but no supplied source locator specifically supports iterate EMA.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursion and constant-coefficient expansion are correct, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind, but no source with a specific locator supports exponential iterate averaging in this optimization context.

children.title: Trajectory Averaging
children.top_down_role: Aggregation across selected portions of the optimization path.

knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General weighted representation encompassing uniform, suffix, and exponential averages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a trajectory \(x_0,\ldots,x_T\in\mathbb{R}^d\), any nonnegative normalized weights \(w_{T,t}\) define the trajectory average
\[
\bar x_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T}w_{T,t}x_t,
\qquad w_{T,t}\ge0,
\qquad \sum_{t=0}^{T}w_{T,t}=1.
\]
Thus \(\bar x_T\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_0,\ldots,x_T\}\). Uniform averaging uses \(w_{T,t}=1/(T+1)\); suffix and exponential averaging arise from terminal-uniform and geometrically decaying weights, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trajectory averaging forms a convex combination of generated iterates; different weight systems recover uniform, suffix, and exponential averages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x_T\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_0,\ldots,x_T\}\).

notation.meaning: weight assigned at horizon T to iterate t

review_flags: No supplied source explicitly covers the general weighted-trajectory representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-combination representation is correct and representation fits the Trajectory Averaging leaf, but the general weighted-trajectory formulation and its named special cases lack cited support.

children.title: Weighting-Memory Regimes
children.top_down_role: Effective memory horizons induced by averaging weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighting-Memory Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative memory measures for constant-coefficient exponential averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constant \(\beta\in[0,1)\), the weight of \(x_{T-k}\) in the exponential average is \((1-\beta)\beta^k\) for \(0\le k<T\), apart from the initialization mass. Its infinite-horizon mean lag and squared-weight effective sample size are
\[
\ell(\beta)=\frac{\beta}{1-\beta},
\qquad
n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\beta)=\frac{1}{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-\beta)^2\beta^{2k}}=\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}.
\]
Both diverge as \(\beta\uparrow1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger exponential memory coefficient lengthens the average's mean lag and increases its effective number of contributing iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell(\beta)=\beta/(1-\beta)\) and \(n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\beta)=(1+\beta)/(1-\beta)\).

notation.meaning: mean age of the geometric weights
inverse sum of squared normalized weights

review_flags: The formulas are algebraically standard, but a domain-specific optimization source was not supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Clipping Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm clipping of stochastic directions before a first-order update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a stochastic direction \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\), threshold \(c_t>0\), and step size \(\eta_t\ge0\), define
\[
\widetilde g_t=g_t\min\left\{1,\frac{c_t}{\lVert g_t\rVert_2}\right\},
\]
with \(\widetilde g_t=0\) when \(g_t=0\), and update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\widetilde g_t\). The clipped direction satisfies \(\lVert\widetilde g_t\rVert_2\le c_t\) and preserves the direction of every nonzero \(g_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cap each stochastic gradient's Euclidean norm at a chosen threshold before taking the first-order step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\widetilde g_t\rVert_2\le c_t\) and \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\widetilde g_t\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator specifically addresses stochastic gradient clipping.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm-clipping update and norm bound are correct, and algorithm is suitable for this family container, but no cited source with a specific locator supports the formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized-Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order updates using only a direction's Euclidean orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a direction \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and step length \(\alpha_t\ge0\), set
\[
d_t=\begin{cases}g_t/\lVert g_t\rVert_2,&g_t\ne0,\\0,&g_t=0,\end{cases}
\qquad
x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t d_t.
\]
Stop according to a prescribed iteration, stationarity, or budget rule and return the selected iterate. Whenever \(g_t\ne0\), the displacement has norm \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2=\alpha_t\), independently of \(\lVert g_t\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize each nonzero gradient and use the step parameter as the displacement length, eliminating sensitivity to gradient magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(g_t\ne0\), then \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2=\alpha_t\).
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports normalized-gradient updates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized-direction update and displacement identity are correct, and the algorithm kind fits the method-family container, but the record has no supporting source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise sign transformation of a stochastic gradient direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_t,g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\eta_t\ge0\), define \(s_t\in\{-1,0,1\}^d\) coordinatewise by \((s_t)_i=\operatorname{sign}((g_t)_i)\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(0)=0\), and update
\[
x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t s_t.
\]
After a prescribed stopping rule, return the selected iterate. If \(k_t\) coordinates of \(g_t\) are nonzero, then \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_\infty=\eta_t\) when \(k_t>0\), and \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2=\eta_t\sqrt{k_t}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each gradient coordinate by its sign, so every active coordinate receives the same-magnitude update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\operatorname{sign}(g_t)\).

notation.meaning: number of nonzero coordinates of the direction

review_flags: No supplied source locator specifically covers sign-gradient methods.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise sign update and stated norm identities are correct, and algorithm fits the method-family container, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Gradient-Aggregation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface separating robust aggregation from the optimizer update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(t\), let worker or sample directions be \(g_{t,1},\ldots,g_{t,b_t}\in\mathbb{R}^d\). A robust gradient-aggregation interface is a map
\[
\mathcal A_t:(\mathbb{R}^d)^{b_t}\to\mathbb{R}^d,
\qquad
\widehat g_t=\mathcal A_t(g_{t,1},\ldots,g_{t,b_t}),
\]
followed by the optimizer update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\widehat g_t\). Permutation invariance requires \(\mathcal A_t(g_{t,\pi(1)},\ldots,g_{t,\pi(b_t)})=\mathcal A_t(g_{t,1},\ldots,g_{t,b_t})\) for every permutation \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust aggregation interface maps a batch of directions to one direction, which the optimizer consumes without depending on sample ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat g_t=\mathcal A_t(g_{t,1},\ldots,g_{t,b_t})\) is the sole direction passed to the update.
review_flags: Robustness guarantees depend on the contamination model and aggregator; no such source or model was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The map defines an aggregation interface and states permutation invariance precisely, but neither permutation invariance nor the bare map makes the aggregator robust. A contamination or adversarial model, a robustness property, and supporting source are required to substantiate the title's local sense.

children.title: Finite-Sum Noise-Reduction Interface
children.top_down_role: Named interfaces retained for optimizer navigation; detailed variance-reduction analysis belongs to the dedicated stochastic-approximation chapter.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: methods that diminish noise in stochastic directions

children.title: Batch-Growth Methods
children.top_down_role: Policies that increase per-update batch cardinality during training.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Growth Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-batch stochastic-gradient updates with a nondecreasing batch schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), choose \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), step sizes \(\eta_t\ge0\), and integers \(1\le b_t\le n\) satisfying \(b_{t+1}\ge b_t\). At iteration \(t\), sample \(B_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B_t|=b_t\), compute
\[
g_t=\frac{1}{b_t}\sum_{i\in B_t}\nabla f_i(x_t),
\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t g_t,
\]
and stop under a prescribed budget or accuracy rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run mini-batch gradient steps while increasing or retaining the batch size, thereby spending more component-gradient work on later updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update costs \(b_t\) component-gradient evaluations and uses their arithmetic mean.
review_flags: The supplied first-order textbook locators do not specifically document adaptive batch growth.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nondecreasing mini-batch schedule is a suitable algorithmic description of Batch-Growth Methods. However, the sampling law for the subsets is unspecified and no source with a relevant locator supports this particular method family.

children.title: Sample-Size Methods
children.top_down_role: Policies that vary the amount of sampled data used by the optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Size Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive selection of stochastic-gradient sample size using a variance tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x_t\), draw independent gradients \(G_{t,1},G_{t,2},\ldots\in\mathbb{R}^d\). For candidate size \(b\ge2\), form
\[
\bar G_{t,b}=\frac1b\sum_{j=1}^{b}G_{t,j},
\qquad
S_{t,b}^2=\frac1{b-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b}\lVert G_{t,j}-\bar G_{t,b}\rVert_2^2.
\]
Choose the first admissible \(b_t\) satisfying \(S_{t,b_t}^2/b_t\le\tau_t^2\), then update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t\bar G_{t,b_t}\). If no candidate satisfies the test, use a prescribed maximum batch size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increase the sample size until the estimated mean-gradient variance meets a tolerance, then update with that sample mean.
assumptions_latex: Conditional on \(x_t\), the sampled gradients are independent with finite second moments.
\(\tau_t>0\), \(\eta_t\ge0\), and a maximum batch size are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected estimator satisfies the empirical test \(S_{t,b_t}^2/b_t\le\tau_t^2\), unless the maximum batch size is reached.

notation.meaning: sample total variance at candidate size b

review_flags: Several inequivalent adaptive sample-size tests exist; this empirical-variance version needs a supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent empirical-variance sample-size algorithm, but this is only one of several inequivalent adaptive tests. Its exact stopping test, maximum-batch behavior, and interpretation require a supporting source with a specific locator.

children.title: Work–Accuracy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Computational consequences of increasing sampled information.

knowledge_statements.title: Work–Accuracy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance-work relation for independent mini-batch gradient estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_b\) be conditionally independent unbiased estimators of \(\nabla F(x)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E\lVert G_j-
abla F(x)\rVert_2^2\le\sigma^2\). For \(\bar G_b=b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{b}G_j\),
\[
\mathbb E\lVert\bar G_b-
abla F(x)\rVert_2^2\le\frac{\sigma^2}{b}.
\]
Thus guaranteeing root-mean-square gradient error at most \(\varepsilon>0\) by this bound requires \(b\ge\lceil\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\) component-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging independent unbiased gradients reduces mean-square error inversely with batch size, so halving RMS error requires roughly four times the work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\mathbb E\lVert\bar G_b-
abla F(x)\rVert_2^2\le\sigma^2/b\), and \(b\ge\lceil\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\) suffices for RMS error at most \(\varepsilon\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator specifically supports the mini-batch variance-work relation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated conditional independence, unbiasedness, and variance assumptions, the mini-batch mean-square bound and sufficient batch size are correct. Property fits the Work–Accuracy Tradeoffs leaf, but no supporting source or locator is cited.

children.title: Snapshot Reference Methods
children.top_down_role: Variance-reduction families organized around stored reference points.

knowledge_statements.title: Snapshot Reference Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum snapshot method with an exact reference gradient and stochastic inner iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where every \(f_i\) is differentiable. Given a snapshot \(\widetilde{x}\), compute \(\mu=
abla F(\widetilde{x})\), initialize \(x_0=\widetilde{x}\), and, for \(t=0,\ldots,m-1\), sample \(i_t\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and set \[v_t=
abla f_{i_t}(x_t)-
abla f_{i_t}(\widetilde{x})+\mu,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta v_t.\] For \(\eta>0\) and prescribed inner-loop length \(m\), output either \(x_m\) or an iterate sampled from \(\{x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\}\) according to a declared output convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a full gradient at a snapshot, then reuse it in stochastic control-variate updates throughout an inner loop.
assumptions_latex: \(i_t\) is sampled uniformly at each inner iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_m\), or a declared random inner iterate, is the output of the snapshot-reference epoch.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf and the displayed update is a recognizable SVRG-type snapshot epoch. A source with a precise algorithm, theorem, section, or page locator is required to support the exact initialization, inner-loop sampling, and alternative output conventions.

children.title: Control-Variate Gradient Estimators
children.top_down_role: Gradient estimators using correlated correction terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Control-Variate Gradient Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased snapshot control variate for uniformly sampled finite-sum gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), fix a reference point \(y\) and sample \(I\) uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The snapshot control-variate estimator is \[G(x;y,I)=
abla f_I(x)-
abla f_I(y)+
abla F(y).\] Its conditional mean, with \(x\) and \(y\) fixed, satisfies \[\mathbb{E}_I[G(x;y,I)]=
abla F(x).\] Moreover, \(G(y;y,I)=
abla F(y)\) for every sampled index, so its sampling variance is zero when the current and reference points coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract the sampled gradient at a reference point and add the reference full gradient; the resulting estimator is unbiased and exact at the reference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}_I[G(x;y,I)]=\nabla F(x)\) and \(G(y;y,I)=\nabla F(y)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expectation follows directly from uniform finite-sum sampling
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Reference-Refresh Regimes
children.top_down_role: Timing choices for renewing snapshot information.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Refresh Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epochwise and randomized refresh rules for snapshot control-variate methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Maintain a current point \(x_t\), reference \(y_t\), and stored full gradient \(\mu_t=
abla F(y_t)\). An epochwise regime selects boundaries \(0=	au_0<	au_1<\cdots\) and sets \(y_t=x_t\), \(\mu_t=
abla F(x_t)\) exactly when \(t=	au_k\); between boundaries it retains the previous pair. A loopless regime independently draws \(B_t\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\): after producing \(x_{t+1}\), set \((y_{t+1},\mu_{t+1})=(x_{t+1},
abla F(x_{t+1}))\) if \(B_t=1\), and otherwise retain \((y_t,\mu_t)\). In either regime, stochastic updates use the currently stored reference pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refresh the reference deterministically at epoch boundaries or randomly with fixed probability, retaining it between refreshes.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) has a computable full gradient.
For the randomized regime, \(p\in(0,1]\) and refresh draws are independent of current component sampling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method generates a specified reference process \((y_t,\mu_t)\) for use by snapshot control-variate estimators.

notation.meaning: stored reference point and its full gradient

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard epochwise and loopless snapshot-refresh conventions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the refresh-regime leaf, but deterministic epochwise and loopless randomized refresh conventions have method-dependent timing and independence details. A precise source locator is needed for the stated post-update Bernoulli refresh convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Table Variance-Reduction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SAGA-type finite-sum method maintaining one stored gradient per component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). Initialize \(x_0\), table entries \(a_i^0=
abla f_i(\phi_i^0)\), and \( ar a^0=n^{-1}\sum_i a_i^0\). At iteration \(t\), sample \(I_t\) uniformly, form \[v_t=
abla f_{I_t}(x_t)-a_{I_t}^t+ ar a^t,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_t v_t,\] then replace \(a_{I_t}^t\) by \(
abla f_{I_t}(x_t)\), leave other table entries unchanged, and update their average accordingly. Conditional on the stored table and \(x_t\), \(\mathbb{E}[v_t]=
abla F(x_t)\). Output the final or a declared sampled iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store one gradient per component, correct a sampled gradient by its stale table value, and add the table average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update uses a conditionally unbiased gradient-table estimator: \(\mathbb{E}[v_t\mid x_t,(a_i^t)_{i=1}^n]=\nabla F(x_t)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SAGA-type table update is internally consistent, conditionally unbiased, and appropriately classified as an algorithm. The exact table initialization, update ordering, and output convention nevertheless require an inspectable algorithm or section citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Gradient-Estimator Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SARAH/SPIDER-type estimator updated by recursive component-gradient differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), choose \(x_0\) and initialize \(v_0\) by a full gradient or a declared batch average; set \(x_1=x_0-\eta_0v_0\). For \(t\ge1\), sample a batch \(B_t\) and compute \[v_t=v_{t-1}+\frac{1}{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\bigl(\nabla f_i(x_t)-\nabla f_i(x_{t-1})\bigr),\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tv_t.\] At prescribed reset times, replace \(v_t\) by a fresh full-gradient or large-batch estimate. Stop after a prescribed number of updates and output the final or a declared sampled iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively update a gradient estimate using component-gradient differences, with occasional fresh estimates preventing accumulated error.
assumptions_latex: Each \(B_t\) follows the declared component-sampling rule.
Learning rates, batch sizes, reset times, and output convention are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursion produces iterates \((x_t)\) and difference-corrected estimators \((v_t)\) between successive resets.

children.title: Constant Learning-Rate Schedules
children.top_down_role: Training policies using a fixed learning rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Learning-Rate Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally constant positive step-size sequence for a first-order iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A learning-rate schedule \((\eta_t)_{t\ge0}\) is constant if there exists a scalar \(\eta>0\) such that \[\eta_t=\eta\qquad\text{for every integer }t\ge0.\] For an iteration \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t\), this schedule applies the same multiplier to every search direction \(g_t\). If the run has a finite horizon \(T\), the defining equality is required for \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant schedule uses one fixed positive learning rate at every optimization step.
assumptions_latex: The iteration index is \(t\in\mathbb{N}_0\), or \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\) for a finite run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_t=\eta\) throughout the schedule domain.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct standard definition of a constant scalar schedule
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Piecewise-Constant Learning-Rate Schedules
children.top_down_role: Training policies using staged fixed learning rates.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Constant Learning-Rate Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-size sequence constant on successive integer iteration blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive sequence \((\eta_t)_{t\ge0}\) is piecewise constant if there are integer boundaries \[0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\] and positive levels \((\alpha_k)\) such that \[\eta_t=\alpha_k\quad\text{whenever}\quad \tau_k\le t<\tau_{k+1}.\] For a finite horizon, the final boundary equals the horizon and only finitely many blocks occur. Adjacent blocks with equal levels may be merged; requiring \(\alpha_{k+1}\ne\alpha_k\) therefore gives the minimal boundary representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-constant schedule holds the learning rate fixed within iteration blocks and changes it only at declared boundaries.
assumptions_latex: All boundaries \(\tau_k\) are integers and strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule is constant on each half-open integer block \([\tau_k,\tau_{k+1})\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of a piecewise-constant sequence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Schedule Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Placement and effects of changes between constant-rate phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Transition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact iteration indices at which a piecewise-constant learning rate changes level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a piecewise-constant schedule with integer boundaries \(0=\tau_0<\cdots<\tau_K=T\) and levels \(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{K-1}\), an interior index \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\) is a transition boundary precisely when \[\eta_{t-1}\ne\eta_t.\] In the minimal representation, this is equivalent to \(t=\tau_k\) for some \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K-1\}\), with \(\eta_{t-1}=\alpha_{k-1}\) and \(\eta_t=\alpha_k\). The schedule convention assigns the new level beginning at the boundary index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transition boundary is an iteration where the learning rate differs from the immediately preceding iteration; the new block starts there.
assumptions_latex: The schedule has finite horizon \(T\) and is piecewise constant.
The boundary representation is minimal, so adjacent levels differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\) is a transition boundary if and only if \(\eta_{t-1}\ne\eta_t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: boundary predicate follows from the minimal block representation

children.title: Polynomial Learning-Rate Decay
children.top_down_role: Learning-rate schedules with polynomial time dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Learning-Rate Decay
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive learning-rate sequence decreasing as a negative power of shifted time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomially decaying learning-rate schedule has parameters \(\eta_0>0\), scale \(\tau>0\), and exponent \(p>0\), and is defined for integers \(t\ge0\) by \[\eta_t=\eta_0\left(1+\frac{t}{\tau}\right)^{-p}.\] It begins at \(\eta_0\), is nonincreasing, and satisfies \(\eta_t\sim \eta_0\tau^p t^{-p}\) as \(t\to\infty\). Equivalent parameterizations \(a(b+t)^{-p}\), with \(a,b>0\), describe the same schedule family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial decay reduces the learning rate proportionally to a negative power of shifted iteration time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_t=\eta_0(1+t/\tau)^{-p}\) and \(\eta_t=\Theta(t^{-p})\) as \(t\to\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard shifted polynomial schedule parameterization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Inverse-Time Learning-Rate Decay
children.top_down_role: Reciprocal-time specializations of decaying learning rates.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Time Learning-Rate Decay
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exponent-one specialization of polynomial learning-rate decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inverse-time learning-rate schedule is the polynomial-decay specialization with exponent \(p=1\). Given \(\eta_0>0\) and \(\tau>0\), define \[\eta_t=\frac{\eta_0}{1+t/\tau}=\frac{\eta_0\tau}{t+\tau},\qquad t\in\mathbb{N}_0.\] The sequence is positive and decreasing, begins at \(\eta_0\), and satisfies \(t\eta_t\to\eta_0\tau\). Equivalently, it may be written \(a/(b+t)\) with positive constants \(a\) and \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-time decay divides the initial learning rate by a quantity growing linearly with the iteration index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_t=\eta_0\tau/(t+\tau)\) and \(t\eta_t\to\eta_0\tau\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exponent-one specialization of polynomial decay
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Decay-Exponent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Qualitative schedule behavior across decay-exponent choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Decay-Exponent Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summability regimes for polynomially decaying positive learning rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\eta_t=a(b+t)^{-p}\) for integers \(t\ge0\), with \(a,b,p>0\). Then the learning rates vanish for every \(p>0\), and the p-series criteria give \[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\eta_t=\infty\iff 0<p\le1,\qquad \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\eta_t^2<\infty\iff p>\frac12.\] Consequently, both nonsummability and square summability hold exactly in the regime \(1/2<p\le1\). At \(p=1/2\) the squared series diverges, while for \(p>1\) the learning-rate series itself converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial rates are nonsummable through exponent one and square summable above one-half; both properties hold exactly when one-half is below the exponent and at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_t\eta_t=\infty\) and \(\sum_t\eta_t^2<\infty\) hold simultaneously if and only if \(1/2<p\le1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct application of classical p-series convergence criteria
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Cosine Learning-Rate Schedules
children.top_down_role: Learning-rate variation following cosine-shaped phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Cosine Learning-Rate Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon monotone cosine interpolation between maximum and minimum learning rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a horizon \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) and levels \(0\le\eta_{\min}\le\eta_{\max}\). The cosine learning-rate schedule on \(t=0,\ldots,T\) is \[\eta_t=\eta_{\min}+\frac{\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min}}{2}\left(1+\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{T}\right)\right).\] It satisfies \(\eta_0=\eta_{\max}\), \(\eta_T=\eta_{\min}\), and is nonincreasing over the horizon. When updates are indexed only through \(T-1\), the terminal value specifies the limiting endpoint of the prescribed schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cosine schedule smoothly decreases the learning rate from a maximum to a minimum over a fixed horizon using half a cosine wave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_t\) interpolates monotonically from \(\eta_{\max}\) to \(\eta_{\min}\) according to a half-cosine profile.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed half-cosine schedule is internally correct and the definition role fits the leaf. However, cosine schedules use differing horizon, endpoint, minimum-rate, and update-index conventions; an authoritative locator is needed for this exact finite-horizon convention and its terminal-endpoint interpretation.

children.title: Cyclic Learning-Rate Schedules
children.top_down_role: Repeated learning-rate variation within bounded cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Learning-Rate Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines deterministic periodic modulation of a first-order method's learning rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cyclic learning-rate schedule is a sequence \((\eta_t)_{t\ge 0}\) determined by bounds \(0\le \eta_{\min}<\eta_{\max}\), a cycle length \(P\in\mathbb N\), and a profile \(q:[0,1)\to[0,1]\) through
\[\eta_t=\eta_{\min}+(\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min})q\!\left(\frac{t\bmod P}{P}\right).\]
Thus \(\eta_{t+P}=\eta_t\) for every \(t\ge0\). The profile may be triangular, cosine-shaped, or otherwise prescribed; cyclicity requires periodic repetition, not monotonicity within a cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cyclic schedule repeatedly applies a fixed bounded learning-rate profile over consecutive periods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_{t+P}=\eta_t\) for all \(t\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent, properly delimited, and appropriate for the leaf, but it has no citation. An inspectable source defining cyclic learning-rate schedules or periodic learning-rate policies is required.

children.title: Restart Learning-Rate Schedules
children.top_down_role: Schedules that renew or reset decay phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Learning-Rate Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines phase resets at prescribed iteration boundaries, allowing cycle lengths and amplitudes to vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) be restart times and let \(T_k=\tau_{k+1}-\tau_k\). A restart learning-rate schedule assigns each \(t\in[\tau_k,\tau_{k+1})\cap\mathbb N\) the value
\[\eta_t=\eta_{k,\min}+(\eta_{k,\max}-\eta_{k,\min})q_k\!\left(\frac{t-\tau_k}{T_k}\right),\]
where \(q_k:[0,1)\to[0,1]\) is the phase-\(k\) profile. At \(t=\tau_{k+1}\) the local phase is reset to zero; the next length, bounds, and profile may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restart schedule resets its within-cycle clock at specified boundaries and may change the next cycle's length, range, or profile.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every \(\tau_{k+1}\), the schedule begins a new local phase with index \(k+1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The phase-reset formulation is internally consistent and fits a definition container, but no evidence supports this generalized restart definition, particularly the allowance for phase-dependent lengths, bounds, and profiles.

children.title: Cycle–Restart Relationship
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between periodic cycling and phase renewal.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle–Restart Relationship
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates periodic cycles to the broader class of phase-reset schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every cyclic schedule with period \(P\) is a restart schedule by choosing \(\tau_k=kP\) and using identical bounds and profiles in every phase. Conversely, a restart schedule is cyclic with period \(P\) if \(T_k=P\) and the complete phase data are independent of \(k\). If lengths, bounds, or profiles vary with \(k\), the schedule retains phase restarts but is generally not periodic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed identical restarts produce a cyclic schedule; variable restart lengths, ranges, or profiles generally destroy periodicity.
assumptions_latex: The schedule is indexed by integer iterations \(t\ge0\).
Restart phases are specified by their lengths, bounds, and normalized profiles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical fixed-length restart phases are equivalent to periodic cycles; variable phase data need not be cyclic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated relationship is coherent: identical fixed-length restart phases yield periodicity, while variable phase data need not. A specific source is nevertheless required to support this characterization and its terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Learning-Rate Warmup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear startup warmup followed by an arbitrary prescribed base schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given warmup length \(W\in\mathbb N\), initial rate \(\eta_{\mathrm{init}}\ge0\), target rate \(\eta_{\mathrm{base}}(0)>0\), and a post-warmup schedule \(\eta_{\mathrm{base}}\), set
\[\eta_t=\begin{cases}\eta_{\mathrm{init}}+\dfrac{t}{W}\bigl(\eta_{\mathrm{base}}(0)-\eta_{\mathrm{init}}\bigr),&0\le t<W,\\ \eta_{\mathrm{base}}(t-W),&t\ge W.\end{cases}\]
Use \(\eta_t\) in the optimizer's ordinary update at iteration \(t\). The output and stopping rule are those of the underlying optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warmup gradually raises the learning rate during the first W iterations, then hands control to the ordinary schedule.
assumptions_latex: The underlying optimizer accepts a time-varying learning rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The learning rate transitions from \(\eta_{\mathrm{init}}\) to the base schedule over the startup interval.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a valid algorithmic convention, but warmup endpoint and indexing conventions vary. A source must establish the intended convention, including the use of t/W for t<W and the handoff to the base schedule at t=W.

children.title: Momentum-Coefficient Warmup
children.top_down_role: Startup policies for gradually introducing momentum persistence.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum-Coefficient Warmup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ramps the momentum coefficient while retaining the underlying momentum recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(W>0\) and \(0\le\beta_{\mathrm{init}}\le\beta_{\mathrm{target}}<1\), define
\[\beta_t=\beta_{\mathrm{init}}+\min\!\left\{\frac{t}{W},1\right\}(\beta_{\mathrm{target}}-\beta_{\mathrm{init}}).\]
Starting from \(v_0=0\), update \(v_{t+1}=\beta_t v_t+(1-\beta_t)g_t\) and apply the underlying parameter step using \(v_{t+1}\). After iteration \(W\), keep \(\beta_t=\beta_{\mathrm{target}}\) unless a later policy changes it; stopping and output follow the underlying optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Momentum-coefficient warmup interpolates from a startup coefficient to the target coefficient while updating the usual momentum state.
assumptions_latex: A gradient or stochastic gradient \(g_t\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta_t=\beta_{\mathrm{target}}\) for every \(t\ge W\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coefficient ramp and momentum recursion are well-defined and algorithm is the correct role, but momentum-coefficient warmup is convention-dependent and the specific increasing-beta policy requires authoritative support.

children.title: Moment-Estimate Warmup
children.top_down_role: Startup policies for stabilizing adaptive moment states.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Estimate Warmup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias-corrected exponential moments compensate for zero-initialization during startup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m_0=v_0=0\) and let coefficients satisfy \(0\le\beta_{1,t},\beta_{2,t}<1\). For gradients \(g_t\), define
\[m_t=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_{2,t}v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2,t})g_t^{\odot2}.\]
The startup-corrected estimates are
\[\widehat m_t=\frac{m_t}{1-\prod_{i=1}^t\beta_{1,i}},\qquad \widehat v_t=\frac{v_t}{1-\prod_{i=1}^t\beta_{2,i}}.\]
For constant coefficients these denominators reduce to \(1-\beta_1^t\) and \(1-\beta_2^t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moment warmup removes zero-initialization shrinkage by dividing exponential first and second moments by their accumulated weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat m_t\) and \(\widehat v_t\) normalize the accumulated exponential weights during startup.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-coefficient bias-correction formulas correctly normalize zero-initialized exponential weights, and representation is an acceptable role. A source is required both for the formulas and for treating bias correction as 'Moment-Estimate Warmup.'

children.title: Initialization Transients
children.top_down_role: Early-training effects caused by immature optimizer state.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Transients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies startup bias caused by zero-initialized exponential state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(m_0=0\) and \(m_t=\beta m_{t-1}+(1-\beta)g_t\) with \(0\le\beta<1\). If \(\mathbb E[g_t]=\mu\) for every \(t\), then
\[\mathbb E[m_t]=(1-\beta^t)\mu.\]
Hence the uncorrected estimate is multiplicatively attenuated during startup, with residual bias \(-\beta^t\mu\). The transient vanishes geometrically, but for \(\beta\) near one it can persist for many iterations; dividing by \(1-\beta^t\) removes this mean bias under the stated stationarity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-initialized exponential averages underestimate a stationary nonzero mean by a factor that decays geometrically as beta to the t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[m_t]-\mu=-\beta^t\mu\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation and residual-bias formulas are correct under the stated constant-mean assumption, and failure_boundary fits the startup-transient phenomenon. No supporting citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Optimizer Switching
children.top_down_role: Policies for replacing one optimizer family with another.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer Switching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Switches update rules at prescribed iterations while explicitly mapping optimizer state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0=\tau_0<\cdots<\tau_K\) be switching times. For phase \(k\), let \(U_k(x,s,g,t)\) return the next parameter-state pair. Initialize \((x_0,s_0)\). At each boundary \(t=\tau_k\) with \(k>0\), set \(s_t=\Phi_k(s_{t^-},x_t)\); then, while \(\tau_k\le t<\tau_{k+1}\), compute \(g_t\) and apply
\[(x_{t+1},s_{t+1})=U_k(x_t,s_t,g_t,t).\]
Stop by the prescribed global criterion and return the final iterate or designated phase output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizer switching applies different update maps in successive intervals and uses an explicit state-transfer map at each boundary.
assumptions_latex: Switching times \(\tau_k\) are strictly increasing integers.
Each update map \(U_k\) is defined on its phase state.
Each transfer map \(\Phi_k\) produces a valid state for phase \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates follow \(U_k\) on phase \(k\) with boundary states supplied by \(\Phi_k\).

notation.meaning: optimizer update map in phase k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract switching algorithm fits the leaf, but the discrete pre-boundary state notation s_{t^-} and the state-transfer convention require a source that defines the boundary semantics and supports this generalized formulation.

children.title: Phased Training
children.top_down_role: Training programs divided into optimizer-specific phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Phased Training
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines training as an ordered partition with phase-specific objectives, data, or update policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A phased training policy consists of boundaries \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K\) and phase specifications \(\mathcal P_k=(F_k,D_k,U_k,H_k)\). For every iteration \(t\in[\tau_k,\tau_{k+1})\cap\mathbb N\), the objective or loss \(F_k\), data rule \(D_k\), update map \(U_k\), and hyperparameter policy \(H_k\) are those of phase \(k\). At least one component changes at each genuine boundary; the terminal output is selected by the global training protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phased training partitions iterations into ordered intervals, each with its own objective, data rule, optimizer, or hyperparameter policy.
assumptions_latex: Each phase specification is well-defined throughout its interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration is governed by exactly one phase specification \(\mathcal P_k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently partitions iterations into phase specifications and uses an appropriate content kind. Its four-component phase tuple and genuine-boundary condition appear synthesized and require an authoritative source.

children.title: Optimizer-State Transfer
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of accumulated state across optimizer transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when a boundary map yields a valid state for the receiving optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose optimizer \(A\) has state space \(S_A\) and optimizer \(B\) has state space \(S_B\). A valid state transfer at parameter value \(x\) is a map \(\Phi_{A\to B}:S_A\times X\to S_B\) such that \(s_B=\Phi_{A\to B}(s_A,x)\) lies in the domain of the next \(B\)-update and satisfies all invariants required by \(B\), including dimensional compatibility and positivity of denominator or preconditioner state. Reinitialization is the special case \(\Phi_{A\to B}(s_A,x)=s_B^0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-transfer map is valid when it produces a dimensionally compatible receiving state satisfying every invariant required by the next optimizer update.
assumptions_latex: The receiving update rule specifies a state domain and invariants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{A\to B}(s_A,x)\in S_B\) and the next optimizer-\(B\) update is well-defined.

notation.meaning: source and receiving optimizer state spaces
default initial state of optimizer B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the appropriate role and the abstract validity requirement is coherent. However, admissible state domains and invariants are optimizer-specific, so a source is needed to support the general condition and representative invariants.

children.title: Phase-Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instabilities or discontinuities near training-phase changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Phase-Transition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a well-posed transition between consecutive training phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a boundary \(\tau_k\) between phases \(k-1\) and \(k\), a transition is well-posed if the parameter passed forward is unambiguous, \(x_{\tau_k}^{+}=x_{\tau_k}^{-}\) unless an explicit parameter map is declared; the incoming optimizer state belongs to the next update's domain; and schedules are evaluated using a declared clock convention, either global time \(t=\tau_k\) or reset local time \(r=0\). Evaluation, checkpointing, and stopping events at the boundary must have a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A phase boundary must define parameter continuity or mapping, valid incoming optimizer state, schedule-clock semantics, and event ordering.
assumptions_latex: Two consecutive phases meet at integer iteration \(\tau_k\).
The receiving phase declares its update-state domain.
Boundary events have a declared execution order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first update of phase \(k\) is uniquely defined at \(\tau_k\).

notation.meaning: parameters immediately before and after transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition appropriately identifies state validity, clock semantics, parameter transfer, and event ordering as boundary requirements. The combined well-posedness criterion is unsupported by any cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak-Type Stepsizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical target-value Polyak step for projected convex subgradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and suppose the optimal value \(f_*\) is known. Starting from \(x_0\in C\), choose \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). If \(g_t=0\), stop and return \(x_t\); otherwise set
\[\eta_t=\frac{f(x_t)-f_*}{\lVert g_t\rVert_2^2},\qquad x_{t+1}=\Pi_C(x_t-\eta_t g_t).\]
Stop under a prescribed accuracy or iteration criterion and return the selected iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Polyak step divides the current objective gap to a known target value by the squared subgradient norm.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex and has known optimal value \(f_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(g_t\ne0\), the projected update uses \(\eta_t=(f(x_t)-f_*)/\lVert g_t\rVert_2^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected convex subgradient algorithm with the known optimal-value Polyak stepsize is precise, correctly scoped, and uses the correct content kind. A specific textbook section, theorem, or original-paper locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Line-Search Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-batch backtracking with an independently sampled acceptance test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given differentiable sample losses \(f(\cdot;\xi)\), an iterate \(x_t\in\mathbb R^d\), an initial trial \(\bar\alpha_t>0\), a contraction \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and \(c\in(0,1)\), form \(g_t=|B_t|^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in B_t}\nabla f(x_t;\xi)\). For \(j=0,1,\ldots\), set \(\alpha_{t,j}=\rho^j\bar\alpha_t\) and draw an evaluation batch \(C_{t,j}\) independent of \(B_t\). Accept the first \(j\) satisfying \[\widehat F_{C_{t,j}}(x_t-\alpha_{t,j}g_t)\leq \widehat F_{C_{t,j}}(x_t)-c\alpha_{t,j}\lVert g_t\rVert^2,\] where \(\widehat F_C(x)=|C|^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in C}f(x;\xi)\), and output \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_{t,j}g_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking contracts a trial step until an independent mini-batch estimates sufficient loss decrease along the stochastic-gradient direction.
assumptions_latex: The gradient and acceptance-test batches are independent conditional on \(x_t\).
A finite maximum number of trials or a fallback step is specified in implementations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t\) with \(\alpha_t\) selected by the stated stochastic sufficient-decrease test.
review_flags: Exact stochastic acceptance tests and resampling conventions vary across line-search families.
Provided line-search locator supports deterministic line search but not this stochastic formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the independently resampled Armijo test is a specific stochastic line-search variant with no supporting citation. Under the stated differentiability assumptions, acceptance need not occur because the search direction is computed from a different batch; the mentioned finite-trial fallback is not actually defined in the algorithm or conclusion.

children.title: Loss-Feedback Policies
children.top_down_role: Stepsize control driven by observed loss behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Feedback Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Causal stepsize policies driven by observed objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) be the information filtration of a first-order optimization process, and let \(\ell_t\in\mathbb R\) be a loss estimate observed at iteration \(t\). A loss-feedback stepsize policy is a sequence of measurable maps \(\pi_t\) for which \[\alpha_t=\pi_t(\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_t;s_t)>0,\] where \(s_t\) is an internal state satisfying \(s_{t+1}=U_t(s_t,\ell_t)\), and \(\alpha_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. The resulting first-order update is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t\), with \(g_t\) an available gradient or stochastic-gradient estimate. The definition excludes policies whose current step uses future losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loss-feedback policy causally maps the observed loss history and internal state to a positive first-order stepsize.
assumptions_latex: The policy and state update are measurable with respect to the available information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_t\) is a positive causal function of observed loss feedback.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically defines loss-feedback learning-rate policies.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and causal formulation fit Loss-Feedback Policies, but no inspectable source establishes this proposed umbrella definition, its timing convention, or its inclusion of both exact and estimated losses.

children.title: Gradient-Feedback Policies
children.top_down_role: Stepsize control driven by gradient-derived signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Feedback Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Causal stepsize policies driven by gradients and gradient-derived statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_t\in\mathbb R^d\) be the gradient or stochastic-gradient estimate observed at iteration \(t\), and let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\) denote the process filtration. A gradient-feedback stepsize policy is a sequence of measurable maps \(\pi_t\) such that \[\alpha_t=\pi_t(g_0,\ldots,g_t;s_t)>0,\qquad s_{t+1}=U_t(s_t,g_t),\] and \(\alpha_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. The update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t\) may therefore depend on norms, inner products, coordinatewise accumulators, or moving moments computed from current and past gradients, but not on future gradient observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient-feedback policy causally chooses a positive stepsize from observed gradients, derived statistics, and an internal state.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\) is observed before the step is chosen.
The policy and state update are measurable with respect to current information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_t\) is a positive causal function of the observed gradient history.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically defines gradient-feedback learning-rate policies.

children.title: Feedback-Signal Coupling
children.top_down_role: Policies combining or reconciling multiple feedback signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Feedback-Signal Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint state-space representation of loss and gradient feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_t=(\ell_t,g_t)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\) collect the loss and gradient signals available at iteration \(t\). A coupled feedback policy admits the causal state-space representation \[s_{t+1}=U_t(s_t,z_t),\qquad \alpha_t=\Pi_t(s_t,z_t)>0,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t.\] Coupling is nonseparable when no maps \(a_t,b_t\) exist such that \(\Pi_t(s,(\ell,g))=a_t(s,\ell)+b_t(s,g)\) throughout the policy domain. Thus mixed statistics, such as a loss gap divided by a squared gradient norm, constitute genuine loss-gradient coupling rather than independent aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled controller jointly processes current loss and gradient signals; nonseparability distinguishes genuine interaction from adding two independent policies.
assumptions_latex: Both \(\ell_t\) and \(g_t\) are available when \(\alpha_t\) is selected.
\(U_t\) and \(\Pi_t\) are measurable on their stated domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimizer is represented by a causal joint-signal controller and a first-order state update.
review_flags: The nonseparability convention is mathematically precise but lacks a supplied optimizer-specific source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Feedback-Signal Coupling and the variables are introduced consistently. However, additive nonseparability is a particular proposed convention rather than an established optimizer-family definition, and no source supports either that convention or the resulting classification claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Coin-Betting Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional wealth-potential template underlying parameter-free online first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For online linear losses \(g_tw\) with \(g_t\in[-1,1]\), initialize wealth \(W_0=\epsilon>0\). At round \(t\), choose a predictable betting fraction \(\beta_t\in[-1,1]\), play \(w_t=\beta_tW_{t-1}\), observe \(g_t\), and update \[W_t=W_{t-1}-g_tw_t=W_{t-1}(1-\beta_tg_t).\] The constraint \(|\beta_t|\leq1\) guarantees \(W_t\geq0\). A coin-betting optimization method selects \(\beta_t\) from past gradients so that \(W_t\) lower-bounds a prescribed potential of the cumulative signed gradient; the played points, or their online-to-batch average, are the optimizer outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coin-betting converts past gradients into bounded betting fractions, preserves nonnegative wealth, and uses a wealth potential to obtain parameter-free iterates.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta_t\) depends only on feedback observed before round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_t\geq0\) for every \(t\), and \(w_t=\beta_tW_{t-1}\) defines the parameter-free online iterate.
review_flags: No supplied source locator covers coin-betting optimization or its multidimensional reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-over-Gradients Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected DoG template with distance numerator and accumulated-gradient denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Given \(x_0\in K\) and \(r_\epsilon>0\), observe \(g_t\) at \(x_t\), define \[r_t=\max\!\left\{r_\epsilon,\max_{0\leq i\leq t}\lVert x_i-x_0\rVert_2\right\},\qquad G_t=\sum_{i=0}^{t}\lVert g_i\rVert_2^2,\qquad \eta_t=\frac{r_t}{\sqrt{G_t}},\] whenever \(G_t>0\), and update \(x_{t+1}=\operatorname{proj}_K(x_t-\eta_tg_t)\). If \(G_t=0\), set \(x_{t+1}=x_t\). After \(T\) iterations, output a specified last iterate or weighted average; convergence guarantees depend on that output convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DoG scales each projected gradient step by the traveled distance divided by the root accumulated squared-gradient norm.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_t\) is an available gradient or stochastic-gradient estimate at \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}=\operatorname{proj}_K(x_t-(r_t/\sqrt{G_t})g_t)\) when \(G_t>0\).

notation.meaning: Running displacement radius from the initial point.

review_flags: DoG variants differ in stabilization, averaging, and stochastic assumptions.
No supplied locator supports the exact distance-over-gradients update.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the terminal container, but the precise radius, stabilization, projection, and output conventions distinguish DoG variants. No source supports this exact recurrence, so its intended mathematical version cannot be confirmed.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Free Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition based on absence of a time-prescribed decay schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a first-order method with state \(s_t\), observed feedback \(z_t\), and update \[s_{t+1}=U(s_t,z_t;\theta),\qquad x_{t+1}=V(s_{t+1};\theta),\] where \(\theta\) is fixed before optimization. The method is schedule-free with respect to learning-rate decay if neither \(U\) nor \(V\) receives the iteration index \(t\), a horizon \(T\), or an externally prescribed sequence \((\eta_t)\) as an input; any effective step variation must instead arise from the evolving state and observed feedback. This definition does not mean hyperparameter-free: fixed scale, averaging, or interpolation parameters may remain in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule-free method varies its effective steps through optimizer state and feedback, without an externally prescribed time or horizon-dependent decay sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(z_t\) contains only information available by iteration \(t\).
\(\theta\) is fixed independently of the iteration counter and optimization horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective update has no explicit dependence on \(t\), \(T\), or a prescribed decay schedule.
review_flags: Schedule-free optimization has named algorithm-specific meanings; the supplied sources do not determine a canonical update.
A primary source is required to align this operational definition with the intended family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition can fit this family-level leaf, but the proposed absence-of-index criterion is not source-backed and may be stricter than named schedule-free methods, whose state updates or averaging weights can still have explicit iteration dependence. A primary source is needed to determine the intended family meaning.

children.title: Diagonal Adaptive Optimization
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise scaling based on cumulative or exponentially weighted gradient statistics.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: 5.6 Adaptive Gradient Descent

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar AdaGrad
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean AdaGrad with one accumulator shared by all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_1\in\mathbb R^d\), scale \(\eta>0\), and stabilizer \(\epsilon>0\), initialize \(S_0=0\). At iteration \(t\geq1\), obtain a gradient or stochastic-gradient estimate \(g_t\in\mathbb R^d\), update \[S_t=S_{t-1}+\lVert g_t\rVert_2^2,\qquad \alpha_t=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{S_t}+\epsilon},\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tg_t.\] For a nonempty closed convex constraint set \(K\), replace the final equality by \(x_{t+1}=\operatorname{proj}_K(x_t-\alpha_tg_t)\). The algorithm outputs the last iterate or a prespecified average after the stopping rule is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar AdaGrad divides a global learning-rate scale by the root cumulative squared norm of all observed gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All coordinates use the common adaptive stepsize \(\alpha_t=\eta/(\sqrt{S_t}+\epsilon)\).
