knowledge_statements.title: Eigendecomposition-Based Matrix Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal spectral matrix functions for real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) be symmetric with eigendecomposition \(A=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)Q^\top\), where \(Q^\top Q=I_d\). For a scalar function \(f\) defined on the spectrum of \(A\), its spectral matrix function is \[f(A)=Q\operatorname{diag}\bigl(f(\lambda_1),\ldots,f(\lambda_d)\bigr)Q^\top.\] In particular, if \(A\) is positive semidefinite, its principal root is \(A^\alpha=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i^\alpha)Q^\top\) for \(\alpha>0\); if \(A\) is positive definite, the same formula defines \(A^{-\alpha}\). The result is independent of the orthonormal basis chosen inside repeated eigenspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix function is computed by applying the scalar function to its eigenvalues and reconstructing with the eigenvectors.
assumptions_latex: The scalar function \(f\) is defined at every eigenvalue of \(A\).
Negative powers are used only when all eigenvalues are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(A)=Q\operatorname{diag}(f(\lambda_i))Q^\top\).

notation.meaning: spectral matrix function induced by f

review_flags: A precise authoritative locator for the spectral functional calculus is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the spectral matrix-function container, and the statement correctly distinguishes positive-semidefinite positive powers from positive-definite negative powers. No citation is attached, however; an authoritative matrix-functions source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is required.

children.title: Iterative Matrix-Root Approximations
children.top_down_role: Iterative computation families targeting positive matrix roots.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Matrix-Root Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Denman–Beavers iteration for the principal square root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a real symmetric positive-definite matrix \(A\), initialize \(Y_0=A\) and \(Z_0=I\). For \(j=0,1,\ldots\), compute \[Y_{j+1}=\tfrac12\bigl(Y_j+Z_j^{-1}\bigr),\qquad Z_{j+1}=\tfrac12\bigl(Z_j+Y_j^{-1}\bigr).\] Stop when a declared residual, such as \(\lVert Y_j^2-A\rVert/\lVert A\rVert\), is at most \(\tau\), or when an iteration limit is reached; return \(Y_j\) as the square-root approximation. In exact arithmetic the iterates commute with \(A\), remain positive definite, and converge to \(A^{1/2}\), while \(Z_j\) converges to \(A^{-1/2}\). Practical implementations solve linear systems rather than forming explicit inverses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Denman–Beavers coupled iteration approximates a positive-definite matrix square root and inverse square root until a residual tolerance is met.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) is symmetric positive definite.
Linear solves defining the updates are performed exactly for the stated convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In exact arithmetic, \(Y_j\to A^{1/2}\) and \(Z_j\to A^{-1/2}\).
review_flags: The supplied matrix-inversion locator is indirect; an exact Denman–Beavers convergence locator is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Iterative Matrix-Root Approximations, and the Denman–Beavers iteration and exact-arithmetic SPD convergence claim are stated coherently. The inventory's matrix-inversion locator does not specifically establish this coupled iteration or its convergence, so an exact Denman–Beavers locator is required.

children.title: Iterative Matrix-Inverse-Root Approximations
children.top_down_role: Iterative computation families targeting inverse fractional matrix powers.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Matrix-Inverse-Root Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled Newton–Schulz iteration for the inverse square root of a symmetric positive-definite matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\), choose \(\alpha>0\) such that \(\lVert I-\alpha A\rVert_2<1\). Initialize \(Y_0=\alpha A\) and \(Z_0=I\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots,K-1\), compute \[T_k=\tfrac12(3I-Z_kY_k),\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_kT_k,\qquad Z_{k+1}=T_kZ_k.\] Return \(B_K=\sqrt{\alpha}\,Z_K\) as the approximation to \(A^{-1/2}\). In exact arithmetic, the commuting iterates satisfy \(Y_k\to(\alpha A)^{1/2}\) and \(Z_k\to(\alpha A)^{-1/2}\); an implementation may stop when \(\lVert I-Z_kY_k\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the positive-definite matrix, jointly iterate square-root and inverse-root factors, and stop when their product is sufficiently close to the identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_K=\sqrt{\alpha}\,Z_K\approx A^{-1/2}\), with \(B_K\to A^{-1/2}\) in exact arithmetic.
review_flags: Exact inverse-root iteration and convergence basin require a directly supporting matrix-functions source; the supplied matrix-inversion locator is insufficient.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and Newton–Schulz scaling are mathematically appropriate for this leaf, but the exact coupled iteration, convergence basin, and limit claims require a directly supporting matrix-functions source with a specific locator.

children.title: Matrix-Function Approximation Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Accuracy limits arising from truncation, conditioning, and finite precision.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Function Approximation Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certificate for an approximate inverse square root in the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) be symmetric positive definite and let \(\widehat B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\). Define the inverse-root residual \(R=I-A^{1/2}\widehat B\). If \(\lVert R\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\), then \[\lVert\widehat B-A^{-1/2}\rVert_2\leq \lVert A^{-1/2}\rVert_2\,\varepsilon=\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(A)}}.\] Consequently, every vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies \(\lVert(\widehat B-A^{-1/2})v\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\lVert v\rVert_2/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(A)}\). Thus this residual, when it can be evaluated or bounded, together with a lower spectral bound for \(A\), certifies absolute operator and action accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small inverse-root residual certifies approximation error, amplified by the reciprocal square root of the matrix's smallest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\widehat B-A^{-1/2}\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(A)}\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the positive-definite matrix.
Upper bound on the residual norm.

children.title: Preconditioner Refresh Cadence

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioner Refresh Cadence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic lifecycle policy for recomputing a matrix preconditioner during first-order optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a refresh period \(q\in\mathbb{N}\), an initialization \(x_0\), and a rule \(\mathcal P(S)\) mapping accumulated optimizer state \(S\) to a positive-definite preconditioner. At iteration \(t\), update the state to \(S_t\). If \(t=0\) or \(t\equiv0\pmod q\), set \(P_t=\mathcal P(S_t)\); otherwise set \(P_t=P_{t-1}\). For a gradient estimate \(g_t\), perform \[x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tP_tg_t.\] Stop under a prescribed optimization criterion and return the final iterate. Exactly one refresh is scheduled in every complete block of \(q\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompute the preconditioner every fixed number of optimizer steps and reuse the most recently computed matrix between scheduled refreshes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_t=\mathcal P(S_t)\) when \(q\mid t\), and otherwise \(P_t=P_{t-1}\).

notation.meaning: Number of optimizer iterations between scheduled refreshes.
Accumulated state used to construct the preconditioner.

children.title: Preconditioner Reuse Horizon
children.top_down_role: Policies controlling how long a computed preconditioner remains active.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioner Reuse Horizon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum age of a cached preconditioner under a specified refresh schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_0<r_1<\cdots\) be refresh iterations, and define the most recent refresh time at iteration \(t\) by \(r(t)=\max\{r_j:r_j\leq t\}\). A preconditioner-reuse policy has horizon \(H\in\mathbb{N}_0\) if \[0\leq t-r(t)\leq H\] for every iteration at which the cached preconditioner is applied. Its minimal reuse horizon is \(H_* = \sup_t(t-r(t))\). For periodic refresh every \(q\geq1\) iterations, \(H_*=q-1\). A horizon bounds cache age only; without assumptions on state variation, it does not bound the numerical discrepancy between cached and current preconditioners.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reuse horizon is the greatest number of elapsed optimizer steps since the preconditioner was last recomputed; periodic cadence q has horizon q−1.
assumptions_latex: \(r(t)=\max\{r_j:r_j\leq t\}\) exists at every considered iteration
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_*=\sup_t(t-r(t))\), and periodic cadence \(q\) gives \(H_*=q-1\).

notation.meaning: Most recent refresh iteration no later than t.
Minimal uniform bound on cache age.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the horizon is a direct discrete-time cache-age definition.
No supplied source directly defines this lifecycle quantity.

children.title: Staleness-Triggered Refresh
children.top_down_role: Refresh policies driven by detected drift in curvature or optimizer state.

knowledge_statements.title: Staleness-Triggered Refresh
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-triggered refresh based on relative change in the matrix state underlying a cached preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t\succ0\) be the current matrix state and let \(S_{r(t)}\succ0\) be the state used for the cached preconditioner. For a threshold \(\tau>0\), define the relative staleness score \[\delta_t=\bigl\lVert S_{r(t)}^{-1/2}(S_t-S_{r(t)})S_{r(t)}^{-1/2}\bigr\rVert_2.\] Refresh at iteration \(t\) exactly when \(\delta_t>\tau\), optionally also enforcing a hard horizon \(H\) through the disjunction \(t-r(t)>H\). Otherwise retain the cached preconditioner. This predicate is invariant under multiplying both matrix states by the same positive scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refresh when the current matrix state differs too much from the state behind the cached preconditioner, or when an optional age limit is exceeded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{refresh}_t\iff(\delta_t>\tau)\lor(t-r(t)>H)\), with the second clause omitted when no hard horizon is imposed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relative congruence-normalized matrix change gives a checkable event-trigger policy.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Function Numerical Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ill-conditioning of inverse matrix powers as the positive-definite spectrum approaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p>0\), consider \(f(A)=A^{-p}\) on symmetric positive-definite matrices. The scalar family \(A_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(\delta,1)\), with \(\delta>0\), satisfies \[\lVert f(A_\delta)\rVert_2=\delta^{-p}.\] For the perturbation \(E_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(\delta,0)\), one has \(A_\delta+E_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(2\delta,1)\) and \[\lVert f(A_\delta+E_\delta)-f(A_\delta)\rVert_2=(1-2^{-p})\delta^{-p}.\] Hence perturbations whose absolute norm tends to zero can produce unbounded absolute output error as \(\lambda_{min}(A_\delta)\downarrow0\). Uniform absolute stability therefore requires a positive spectral floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse matrix powers become absolutely unstable near singularity: vanishing input perturbations can cause unbounded output changes unless eigenvalues stay uniformly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert E_\delta\rVert_2\to0\) but \(\lVert(A_\delta+E_\delta)^{-p}-A_\delta^{-p}\rVert_2\to\infty\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioner Staleness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning failure caused by applying a cached preconditioner to a substantially changed curvature matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the curvature surrogate at refresh time be \(A_s=I_2\), so the cached inverse preconditioner is \(P_s=A_s^{-1}=I_2\). At a later iteration, let \(A_t=\operatorname{diag}(M,M^{-1})\) for \(M\geq1\). The preconditioned matrix then obeys \[\kappa_2(P_s^{1/2}A_tP_s^{1/2})=\kappa_2(A_t)=M^2.\] Thus a preconditioner that was exact when constructed can become arbitrarily ineffective when reused after anisotropic state drift. A finite reuse age alone cannot prevent this failure; control requires a bound on relative spectral change or a staleness-triggered refresh.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An initially exact cached preconditioner can become arbitrarily poor after anisotropic curvature drift, even if it has been reused for only a few steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Partition Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss from discarding cross-block coupling under a fixed block-diagonal preconditioner model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two blocks of equal size, let \[A_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}I&\rho I\\ \rho I&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0\leq\rho<1.\] The block-diagonal approximation induced by the displayed partition is \(D=\operatorname{blkdiag}(A_\rho)=I\). Although \(D^{-1}\) exactly represents both within-block components, it omits all cross-block coupling, and \[\kappa_2(D^{-1/2}A_\rho D^{-1/2})=\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}.\] The condition number diverges as \(\rho\uparrow1\). Therefore block scaling can fail when the chosen partition separates strongly coupled coordinates, despite each diagonal block being individually well conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal model can miss strong interactions between blocks; its preconditioned condition number diverges as cross-block coupling approaches the positive-definiteness boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Tensor-Factorization Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative error of approximating a tensor-structured positive-definite matrix by one Kronecker product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\succ0\) act on \(\mathbb{R}^{d_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbb{R}^{d_m}\). Its relative single-factorization mismatch in a matrix norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) is \[\mu_{\otimes}(A)=\inf_{P_j\succ0}\frac{\left\lVert A-\bigotimes_{j=1}^mP_j\right\rVert}{\lVert A\rVert}.\] Exact tensor factorization holds precisely when \(\mu_{\otimes}(A)=0\) and the infimum is attained. For a diagonal two-mode \(2\times2\) array with positive diagonal entries \(d_{11},d_{12},d_{21},d_{22}\), exact Kronecker separability requires \(d_{11}d_{22}=d_{12}d_{21}\); violation of this cross-product identity is a concrete tensor-factorization mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tensor-factorization mismatch is the best relative error of representing a positive-definite operator by one Kronecker product; nonseparable diagonal arrays violate a cross-product identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_{\otimes}(A)=0\) characterizes exact representability by the prescribed Kronecker factorization when the infimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Factorization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative propagation of factorwise perturbations through a Kronecker-structured preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\bigotimes_{j=1}^mP_j\) and \(\widetilde P=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m(P_j+E_j)\), where every \(P_j\neq0\) and \(\lVert E_j\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon_j\lVert P_j\rVert_2\). By multiplicativity of the spectral norm on Kronecker products and multilinear expansion, \[\frac{\lVert\widetilde P-P\rVert_2}{\lVert P\rVert_2}\leq\prod_{j=1}^m(1+\varepsilon_j)-1.\] Hence small errors across several factors accumulate approximately additively to first order, \(\sum_j\varepsilon_j\), but include higher-order cross terms. Sensitivity therefore grows with both factor count and factorwise approximation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative perturbations in tensor factors combine multiplicatively; their first-order effects add, while cross terms increase sensitivity as more factors are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\widetilde P-P\rVert_2/\lVert P\rVert_2\leq\prod_{j=1}^m(1+\varepsilon_j)-1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Scaling Resource Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense and block-structured storage and arithmetic costs for maintaining matrix preconditioners.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Divergence Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order local representation of a smooth statistical divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{p_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\}\) be a regular statistical model and let \(D(\theta,\theta')\) be a twice continuously differentiable divergence satisfying \(D(\theta,\theta)=0\) and \(D(\theta,\theta')\geq 0\). Its local metric is \(G(\theta)=\left.\nabla^2_{\theta'}D(\theta,\theta')\right|_{\theta'=\theta}\). For every perturbation \(\delta\to0\), \[D(\theta,\theta+\delta)=\tfrac12\delta^\top G(\theta)\delta+o(\|\delta\|_2^2).\] For the Kullback--Leibler divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta'})\), regularity permits differentiation under the integral and gives \(G(\theta)=F(\theta)\), the expected Fisher information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth divergence induces a local quadratic metric through its diagonal Hessian; for KL divergence this metric is the expected Fisher information.

\(D\) is twice continuously differentiable near the diagonal.

knowledge_statements.title: Steepest Descent under Information Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural gradient as the metric-constrained local steepest-descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a differentiable objective \(L:\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), a point \(\theta_k\), and a symmetric positive-definite information matrix \(F_k\), define \(g_k=\nabla L(\theta_k)\). The unit \(F_k\)-norm steepest-descent direction solves \[v_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v^\top F_kv\leq1}g_k^\top v,\qquad v_k=-\frac{F_k^{-1}g_k}{\sqrt{g_k^\top F_k^{-1}g_k}}\] when \(g_k\neq0\). Equivalently, the penalized local model yields \(s_k=-\alpha_kF_k^{-1}g_k\). Update \(\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+s_k\) and stop when a prescribed stationarity test, such as \(g_k^\top F_k^{-1}g_k\leq\varepsilon^2\), holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural gradient is steepest descent measured in the Fisher metric: precondition the gradient by the inverse information matrix and apply a chosen step size.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha_k>0\) is selected by a prescribed step rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_k=-\alpha_kF_k^{-1}\nabla L(\theta_k)\) is the information-metric steepest-descent step.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected Fisher Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-expectation definition for a regular parametric conditional distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\) be a differentiable parametric conditional distribution, let \(X\sim q\), and conditionally let \(Y\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid X)\). With score \(s_\theta(X,Y)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(Y\mid X)\), the expected Fisher information is \[F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{X\sim q,\,Y\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid X)}\!\left[s_\theta(X,Y)s_\theta(X,Y)^\top\right].\] If the support is parameter-independent and differentiation under the expectation is valid, then \(\mathbb E[s_\theta]=0\) and \(F(\theta)=-\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta^2\log p_\theta(Y\mid X)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected Fisher information is the model-distribution expectation of the score outer product; under regularity it equals the negative expected log-likelihood Hessian.
assumptions_latex: The conditional model has parameter-independent support.
Differentiation and integration may be interchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[s_\theta s_\theta^\top]=-\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta^2\log p_\theta(Y\mid X)]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and regularity-qualified Hessian identity are standard and internally consistent, but the record supplies no authoritative statistics source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Fisher Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observed-label outer-product matrix used as a Fisher surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For observations \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) and a differentiable conditional model \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\), define individual observed-label scores \(s_i(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)\). The empirical Fisher information is \[\widehat F_{\mathrm{emp}}(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n s_i(\theta)s_i(\theta)^\top.\] It is positive semidefinite, but it generally differs from the expected Fisher because the labels are fixed observed data rather than fresh draws from \(p_\theta(\cdot\mid x_i)\). Equality requires additional distributional or averaging conditions and is not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empirical Fisher averages outer products of observed-label scores. It is positive semidefinite but generally is not the expected Fisher.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat F_{\mathrm{emp}}(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_i s_i(\theta)s_i(\theta)^\top\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Score evaluated at observed example i

knowledge_statements.title: Score-Covariance Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monte Carlo estimation of Fisher information from sampled scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), draw independently \(y_{ij}\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid x_i)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,r\), and compute \(s_{ij}=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(y_{ij}\mid x_i)\). Form \[\widehat F=\frac1{mr}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^r s_{ij}s_{ij}^\top.\] Conditional on the inputs, \(\widehat F\) is positive semidefinite and unbiased for \(m^{-1}\sum_i F(\theta\mid x_i)\). If the inputs are themselves independent draws from \(q\), it is unbiased for the joint expected Fisher. Output \(\widehat F\), or its prescribed structured projection, after the fixed sample budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample labels from the model, compute their scores, and average score outer products to obtain a positive-semidefinite unbiased Fisher estimator.
assumptions_latex: The score has a finite second moment.
Any random inputs are independent draws from \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat F\mid x_1,\ldots,x_m]=m^{-1}\sum_i F(\theta\mid x_i)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Gauss–Newton Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-space curvature pullback and its Fisher specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a model produce \(z=f_\theta(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(\ell(z,y)\) be twice differentiable and convex in \(z\). With \(J_\theta(x)=\partial f_\theta(x)/\partial\theta\) and \(H_\ell(z,y)=\nabla_z^2\ell(z,y)\succeq0\), the generalized Gauss--Newton matrix is \[G(\theta)=\mathbb E\!\left[J_\theta(X)^\top H_\ell(f_\theta(X),Y)J_\theta(X)\right]\succeq0.\] When \(\ell(z,y)=-\log p(y\mid z)\), the expectation over \(Y\sim p(\cdot\mid z)\) and standard likelihood regularity identify the corresponding output-space curvature with output Fisher information, so its parameter-space pullback equals the expected Fisher.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Fisher Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise approximation retaining only Fisher diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric positive-semidefinite Fisher matrix \(F\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\), its diagonal approximation is \[D=\operatorname{Diag}(\operatorname{diag}F),\qquad D_{ii}=F_{ii},\quad D_{ij}=0\ \text{for }i\neq j.\] With damping \(\lambda>0\), an approximate natural-gradient step for gradient \(g\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[s=-\alpha(D+\lambda I)^{-1}g,\qquad s_i=-\alpha\frac{g_i}{F_{ii}+\lambda}.\] The construction preserves nonnegative coordinate curvatures and permits linear-time storage and application, but discards every cross-coordinate coupling and is generally coordinate-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal Fisher Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-partition approximation retaining within-block Fisher couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the parameter indices into disjoint nonempty blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_K\). For a Fisher matrix \(F\succeq0\), define the block-diagonal approximation \[F_{\mathrm{bd}}=\operatorname{blockdiag}(F_{B_1B_1},\ldots,F_{B_KB_K}).\] If \(g=(g_{B_1},\ldots,g_{B_K})\), damping \(\lambda>0\) gives the approximate natural-gradient step \[s_{B_k}=-\alpha(F_{B_kB_k}+\lambda I)^{-1}g_{B_k},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.\] Each retained principal block is positive semidefinite, so the damped system is positive definite. The approximation preserves within-block interactions but sets all between-block Fisher interactions to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Layerwise Kronecker Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: K-FAC block representation for a fully connected affine layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an affine layer with weight matrix \(W\), augmented input activation \(a\), preactivation \(s=Wa\), and back-propagated score derivative \(\delta=\partial\log p_\theta(Y\mid X)/\partial s\), the vectorized weight score is \(g_W=\operatorname{vec}(\delta a^\top)=a\otimes\delta\). Hence its Fisher block is \[F_W=\mathbb E[(aa^\top)\otimes(\delta\delta^\top)].\] The layerwise Kronecker approximation replaces expectation of the Kronecker product by the product of expectations: \[F_W\approx A\otimes G,\qquad A=\mathbb E[aa^\top],\quad G=\mathbb E[\delta\delta^\top].\] When invertible, \((A\otimes G)^{-1}=A^{-1}\otimes G^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully connected layer’s Fisher block is approximated by the Kronecker product of activation and back-propagated score second moments.
assumptions_latex: The layer is affine in its augmented input.
The relevant second moments are finite.
The factorization approximation separates activation and derivative second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_W\approx A\otimes G\), with inverse \(A^{-1}\otimes G^{-1}\) when both factors are invertible.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenbasis-Corrected Kronecker Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal correction in the eigenbasis of Kronecker factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a layer curvature block have a Kronecker approximation \(A\otimes G\), with eigendecompositions \(A=Q_A\Lambda_AQ_A^\top\) and \(G=Q_G\Lambda_GQ_G^\top\). Define the Kronecker eigenbasis \(Q=Q_A\otimes Q_G\). For a target positive-semidefinite curvature matrix \(F\), the eigenbasis-corrected approximation is \[\widetilde F=Q\operatorname{Diag}(d)Q^\top,\qquad d=\operatorname{diag}(Q^\top FQ).\] Thus \(\widetilde F\) retains the Kronecker eigenvectors but replaces the separable eigenvalues by directional second moments. With \(d_i+\lambda>0\), its damped inverse action is \((\widetilde F+\lambda I)^{-1}g=Q\operatorname{Diag}((d+\lambda\mathbf1)^{-1})Q^\top g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain Kronecker-factor eigenvectors but estimate a separate curvature value in each joint eigen-direction, then invert the corrected diagonal with damping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde F=Q\operatorname{Diag}(\operatorname{diag}(Q^\top FQ))Q^\top\) has an efficiently applicable damped inverse in basis \(Q\).

notation.meaning: Eigenvector matrices of the Kronecker factors

knowledge_statements.title: Convolutional Kronecker Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-weight Kronecker approximation for a convolutional layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convolutional layer, let \(a_t\) be the vectorized input patch, including any bias coordinate, and let \(\delta_t\) be the score derivative with respect to the preactivation at spatial location \(t\in\mathcal T\). The shared-kernel score has the form \[g_W=\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\operatorname{vec}(\delta_ta_t^\top)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}a_t\otimes\delta_t.\] A convolutional Kronecker variant approximates its Fisher block by \[F_W\approx c\,A\otimes G,\qquad A=\mathbb E_t[a_ta_t^\top],\quad G=\mathbb E_t[\delta_t\delta_t^\top],\] where the normalization \(c>0\) is fixed consistently with whether spatial sums or averages define the gradient and factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convolutional K-FAC uses shared-kernel patch and preactivation-derivative moments, with normalization determined by spatial sum or average conventions.
assumptions_latex: The convolution uses a kernel shared across spatial locations.
Patch and derivative second moments are finite.
The chosen variant neglects or homogenizes specified cross-location correlations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_W\approx c\,A\otimes G\) under a stated spatial normalization and cross-location approximation.

notation.meaning: Vectorized input patch at spatial location t
Score derivative at spatial location t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record captures the shared-kernel score structure, but the constant c and treatment of cross-location correlations are variant-dependent and insufficiently specified without a primary convolutional K-FAC source.

children.title: Recurrent Kronecker Variants
children.top_down_role: Kronecker approximations specialized to recurrent temporal structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Recurrent Kronecker Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A time-shared recurrent-layer K-FAC approximation that discards cross-time Fisher correlations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a recurrent parameter matrix \(W\), let the per-sequence gradient be \(G_W=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t z_t^{\mathsf T}\), where \(z_t\) is the recurrent-layer input and \(\delta_t\) is the corresponding preactivation derivative. A recurrent Kronecker approximation replaces the Fisher block \(F_W=\mathbb E[\operatorname{vec}(G_W)\operatorname{vec}(G_W)^{\mathsf T}]\) by \(\widetilde F_W=T(A\otimes B)\), with \(A=\mathbb E[z_tz_t^{\mathsf T}]\) and \(B=\mathbb E[\delta_t\delta_t^{\mathsf T}]\), using a specified distribution over sequences and time indices. With damping \(\lambda>0\), the approximate natural-gradient direction solves \((\widetilde F_W+\lambda I)\operatorname{vec}(D_W)=-\operatorname{vec}(G_W)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recurrent K-FAC variant factors a time-shared Fisher block into input and derivative covariances, neglecting cross-time correlations, then solves a damped Kronecker-structured system.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is shared across the \(T\) recurrent time steps.
The approximation neglects cross-time terms and factorizes same-time second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_W\approx T(A\otimes B)\), enabling a structured damped metric solve.

notation.meaning: Input to the recurrent affine transformation at time t.
Derivative with respect to recurrent preactivation at time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the recurrent-variant leaf and is internally coherent under stationarity, discarded cross-time terms, and same-time moment factorization. A recurrent K-FAC source is required to confirm the factor convention, averaging law, and factor T.

children.title: Architecture-Specific Factorization Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by spatial, temporal, or sharing assumptions that do not match the model.

knowledge_statements.title: Architecture-Specific Factorization Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of architecture-specific Kronecker factorizations when the aggregate omitted-correlation and moment-factorization residual is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a shared parameter has gradient \(G=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i z_i^{\mathsf T}\), then its exact Fisher block is \[F=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb E[(z_i z_j^{\mathsf T})\otimes(\delta_i\delta_j^{\mathsf T})].\] Consider the diagonal, separated approximation \[\widetilde F=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb E[z_i z_i^{\mathsf T}]\otimes\mathbb E[\delta_i\delta_i^{\mathsf T}].\] Its aggregate error is \[R=F-\widetilde F=\sum_{i\ne j}\mathbb E[(z_i z_j^{\mathsf T})\otimes(\delta_i\delta_j^{\mathsf T})]+\sum_i\Bigl(\mathbb E[(z_i z_i^{\mathsf T})\otimes(\delta_i\delta_i^{\mathsf T})]-\mathbb E[z_i z_i^{\mathsf T}]\otimes\mathbb E[\delta_i\delta_i^{\mathsf T}]\Bigr).\] The approximation is exact if and only if \(R=0\); therefore it fails whenever this aggregate residual is nonzero. Weight sharing, correlated spatial locations, recurrent dependence, attention coupling, and conditional heteroscedasticity can generate such a residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal, separated Kronecker approximation is exact exactly when the aggregate of its discarded cross-index correlations and retained moment-factorization errors vanishes; architecture-induced dependence can make that aggregate residual nonzero.
assumptions_latex: The parameter is reused at \(m\) architectural locations or times.
\(\widetilde F\) is the displayed diagonal, separated approximation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximation is exact if and only if \(R=F-\widetilde F=0\), and it loses fidelity whenever \(R\neq0\).

notation.meaning: Architectural locations, tokens, or recurrent times.
Aggregate approximation residual, including cross-index and moment-separation errors.

children.title: Low-Rank Fisher Approximations
children.top_down_role: Fisher representations restricted to a selected low-dimensional subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Fisher Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best rank-budget approximations of a finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite Fisher matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite with eigendecomposition \(F=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_p)U^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_p\geq0\). For a rank budget \(r<p\), the truncated approximation is \(F_r=U_r\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)U_r^{\mathsf T}\). A damped inverse action is represented by \[(F_r+\lambda I)^{-1}g=U_r\operatorname{diag}((\sigma_i+\lambda)^{-1})U_r^{\mathsf T}g+\lambda^{-1}(I-U_rU_r^{\mathsf T})g,\] for \(\lambda>0\). Thus only the leading Fisher subspace receives curvature-dependent scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A low-rank Fisher approximation preserves the leading eigen-directions; damping supplies a uniform inverse scale on the omitted subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite-dimensional symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_r\) retains the leading \(r\) Fisher eigenpairs and permits the displayed damped inverse action.

notation.meaning: Matrix of the leading r orthonormal Fisher eigenvectors.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically correct for a finite-dimensional symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix, and the damped inverse formula is consistent with the stated eigenspace decomposition. An authoritative source with a specific locator is absent.

children.title: Sketch-Based Fisher Approximations
children.top_down_role: Compressed Fisher representations produced through randomized or structured sketches.

knowledge_statements.title: Sketch-Based Fisher Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sample-space sketch producing a rank-bounded empirical Fisher approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given per-sample gradients \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^p\), form \(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) with row \(i\) equal to \(g_i^{\mathsf T}\), so \(\widehat F=n^{-1}G^{\mathsf T}G\). Choose a sketch \(S\in\mathbb R^{s\times n}\), with \(s<n\), and compute \(Y=SG/\sqrt n\). Store \(Y\) and define \(\widetilde F=Y^{\mathsf T}Y=n^{-1}G^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}SG\), whose rank is at most \(s\). For a query gradient \(g\) and damping \(\lambda>0\), output \(d=-(\widetilde F+\lambda I)^{-1}g\), evaluated through a low-dimensional Woodbury solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sketch the matrix of sample gradients, form a rank-at-most-s empirical Fisher surrogate, and apply its damped inverse through a small Woodbury system.
assumptions_latex: \(S\in\mathbb R^{s\times n}\) is a chosen random or deterministic sketch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output uses \(\widetilde F=n^{-1}G^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T}SG\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde F)\leq s\).

notation.meaning: Matrix whose rows are per-sample gradients.
Sketch dimension and rank upper bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, and the rank bound follows from the displayed construction. A source is needed for this particular sample-space Fisher sketch and its Woodbury implementation; no accuracy guarantee is claimed, so the unspecified sketch distribution is not itself a mathematical error.

children.title: Rank-Budget Fidelity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between retained curvature information and representation budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Budget Fidelity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp spectral and Frobenius fidelity limits imposed by a rank budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite with eigenvalues \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_p\geq0\). For every matrix \(B\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq r<p\), \[\|F-B\|_2\geq\sigma_{r+1},\qquad \|F-B\|_{\mathrm F}\geq\left(\sum_{i=r+1}^{p}\sigma_i^2\right)^{1/2}.\] The truncated eigendecomposition \(F_r\) attains both bounds. Hence a rank-\(r\) Fisher representation cannot uniformly reproduce curvature below the discarded spectral tail; if \(\sigma_{r+1}>0\), exact recovery is impossible, and inverse actions require damping or an additional full-rank component on the omitted subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r Fisher surrogate cannot beat the discarded spectral tail; exact recovery requires the true Fisher rank to be at most r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal rank-\(r\) errors are \(\sigma_{r+1}\) in spectral norm and \((\sum_{i>r}\sigma_i^2)^{1/2}\) in Frobenius norm.

notation.meaning: Ordered eigenvalues of the Fisher matrix.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and the spectral- and Frobenius-norm rank limits are stated correctly for a finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite matrix. The theorem has no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Metric Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct solution of a regularized positive-definite metric system by Cholesky factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a gradient \(g\in\mathbb R^p\), a symmetric positive-semidefinite metric \(M\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\), and \(\lambda>0\). Form \(H=M+\lambda I\), compute a Cholesky factorization \(H=LL^{\mathsf T}\), solve \(Ly=-g\), and then solve \(L^{\mathsf T}d=y\). Output \(d\), which is the unique minimizer of \(g^{\mathsf T}u+\tfrac12u^{\mathsf T}Hu\). A stopping check may verify the relative residual \(\|Hd+g\|_2/\max\{\|g\|_2,1\}\leq\varepsilon\). Dense factorization requires \(O(p^3)\) arithmetic and \(O(p^2)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularize the metric, factor it by Cholesky decomposition, and use two triangular solves to obtain the unique metric-scaled direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns \(d=-(M+\lambda I)^{-1}g\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Metric Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-gradient computation of a regularized metric direction using only matrix-vector products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(g\in\mathbb R^p\), damping \(\lambda>0\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and an oracle returning \(Mv\) for a symmetric positive-semidefinite metric \(M\). Apply conjugate gradients to \(Hd=-g\), where the oracle action is \(Hv=Mv+\lambda v\), starting from \(d_0=0\). At iteration \(k\), update the standard residual, search direction, and step coefficient using one call to the oracle. Stop when \(\|Hd_k+g\|_2\leq\varepsilon\|g\|_2\), or at a prescribed iteration limit, and output \(d_k\). No explicit metric matrix or factorization is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use conjugate gradients and metric-vector products to approximate the damped natural-gradient direction without storing or factoring the metric.
assumptions_latex: The oracle computes \(Mv\) accurately enough for the residual test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned iterate approximately solves \((M+\lambda I)d=-g\) to the stated relative residual tolerance.

children.title: Metric Regularization Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Structural modifications used to stabilize estimated metric operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Regularization Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive, spectral-floor, and convex-shrinkage regularizations of a positive-semidefinite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric positive-semidefinite metric \(M=Q\operatorname{diag}(\mu_i)Q^{\mathsf T}\), three full-rank regularizations are: additive damping \(M_{\lambda}=M+\lambda I\); spectral flooring \(M_{\tau}=Q\operatorname{diag}(\max\{\mu_i,\tau\})Q^{\mathsf T}\); and shrinkage \(M_{\rho,\alpha}=(1-\rho)M+\rho\alpha I\), where \(\lambda>0\), \(\tau>0\), \(0<\rho\leq1\), and \(\alpha>0\). Each regularized metric is positive definite, so \(d=-M_{m reg}^{-1}g\) exists uniquely. Their eigenvalue transformations differ, and therefore they need not produce identical scaled directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Damping, eigenvalue flooring, and identity shrinkage make a semidefinite metric invertible through distinct eigenvalue transformations.
assumptions_latex: All regularization parameters satisfy the displayed positivity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed \(M_{\rm reg}\) is positive definite and defines a unique direction \(d=-M_{\rm reg}^{-1}g\).

notation.meaning: Any one of the displayed regularized metrics.

children.title: Metric Damping Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fixed, scheduled, or adaptive regimes for controlling metric damping.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Damping Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenwise behavior of additive metric damping in weak-, intermediate-, and strong-damping regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=Q\operatorname{diag}(\mu_i)Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), write \(g=\sum_i\gamma_iq_i\), and set \(d_{\lambda}=-(M+\lambda I)^{-1}g=-\sum_i\gamma_i(\mu_i+\lambda)^{-1}q_i\). If \(\lambda\ll\mu_i\), the component approaches natural-metric scaling \(-\gamma_i/\mu_i\). If \(\lambda\) is comparable to \(\mu_i\), curvature and damping jointly determine the scale. If \(\lambda\gg\mu_i\), the component equals \(-\gamma_i/\lambda+O(\mu_i/\lambda^2)\), so the direction approaches a uniformly scaled negative gradient. Nullspace components always receive scale \(1/\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small damping preserves curvature scaling, comparable damping interpolates, and large damping approaches a scaled gradient; metric-nullspace components are controlled entirely by damping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each eigencomponent is scaled by \((\mu_i+\lambda)^{-1}\), yielding the stated damping regimes.

notation.meaning: Gradient coefficient along the i-th metric eigenvector.

children.title: Bias–Conditioning Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Interaction between solve stability and distortion of the natural-gradient direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias–Conditioning Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how additive damping improves conditioning while attenuating the undamped inverse metric action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\succ0\) have eigenvalues \(0<\mu_{\min}\leq\mu_{[1~max}\), and define \(d_0=-M^{-1}g\) and \(d_\lambda=-(M+\lambda I)^{-1}g\) for \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\kappa_2(M+\lambda I)=\frac{\mu_{[1~max}+\lambda}{\mu_{\min}+\lambda}\leq\kappa_2(M).\] Along an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\mu_i\), damping changes the inverse scale from \(1/\mu_i\) to \(1/(\mu_i+\lambda)\), giving relative attenuation \(\lambda/(\mu_i+\lambda)\) with respect to the undamped scale. Thus increasing \(\lambda\) monotonically improves spectral conditioning while increasing attenuation of the undamped metric direction, with greater relative attenuation for smaller \(\mu_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing additive damping lowers the metric condition number but increasingly attenuates the undamped inverse action, especially along small-eigenvalue directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Damping reduces \(\kappa_2\) while imposing eigenwise relative attenuation \(\lambda/(\mu_i+\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: Smallest and largest eigenvalues of the metric.
Undamped and additively damped metric directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a metric trust-region linear model and a scaled metric-gradient direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\succ0\), \(g\neq0\), and \(\Delta>0\). The metric trust-region problem \[\min_d\; g^{\mathsf T}d\quad\text{subject to}\quad \tfrac12d^{\mathsf T}Md\leq\Delta\] has the unique solution \[d^*=-\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta}{g^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}g}}\,M^{-1}g.\] Equivalently, for its positive Lagrange multiplier \(\eta\), \(d^*=-\eta^{-1}M^{-1}g\). More generally, minimizing \(g^{\mathsf T}d+\tfrac12d^{\mathsf T}(M+\lambda I)d\) yields \(d=-(M+\lambda I)^{-1}g\), which is the trust-region solution for the radius equal to that direction's metric norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric-scaled gradient is exactly the optimizer of a linear model over an ellipsoidal trust region; regularization changes the defining metric and radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trust-region optimizer is a positive scalar multiple of \(-M^{-1}g\).

notation.meaning: Trust-region radius measured as half the squared metric norm.
Positive multiplier of the active quadratic constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic-Model Training
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural-gradient training for a differentiable conditional probabilistic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a data distribution \(P_{\rm data}\), a differentiable model \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\), the loss \(L(\theta)=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P_{\rm data}}[-\log p_\theta(y\mid x)]\), step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\), and damping parameters \(\lambda_k>0\), initialize \(\theta_0\). At iteration \(k\), estimate \(g_k=\nabla L(\theta_k)\) and the conditional-model Fisher \[F(\theta_k)=\mathbb E_{x\sim P_{\rm data},\,\widetilde y\sim p_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid x)}[s_ks_k^{\mathsf T}],\qquad s_k=\nabla_\theta\log p_{\theta_k}(\widetilde y\mid x).\] Solve \((F(\theta_k)+\lambda_k I)d_k=-g_k\), set \(\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\alpha_kd_k\), and stop under a prescribed gradient, validation, or iteration criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Train a differentiable conditional probabilistic model by preconditioning the likelihood gradient with a damped model Fisher estimated using outcomes sampled from the current model.
assumptions_latex: \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\) is differentiable in \(\theta\) on the parameter domain.
The score has a finite second moment under the displayed sampling law.
\(\lambda_k>0\) makes the metric solve well posed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update uses the damped natural-gradient direction \(d_k=-(F(\theta_k)+\lambda_k I)^{-1}g_k\).

notation.meaning: Conditional-model score evaluated at the current parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inference Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Fisher geometry of a smooth variational family and its natural-gradient direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{q_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\}\) be a regular variational family with score \(s_\theta(z)=\nabla_\theta\log q_\theta(z)\) and Fisher matrix \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{q_\theta}[s_\theta s_\theta^\top]\). Then
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\theta\Vert q_{\theta+\delta})=\tfrac12\delta^\top F(\theta)\delta+o(\|\delta\|_2^2).
\]
For a differentiable evidence lower bound \(\mathcal L\), if \(F(\theta)\succ0\), the unit-radius steepest-ascent direction in this local geometry is
\[
d_\star=\frac{F(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal L(\theta)}{\sqrt{\nabla\mathcal L(\theta)^\top F(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal L(\theta)}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fisher matrix is the quadratic local metric induced by KL divergence, and Fisher-preconditioned ELBO ascent is steepest ascent under that metric.
assumptions_latex: \(q_\theta\) has parameter-independent support and is twice differentiable near \(\theta\).
Differentiation and integration may be interchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\theta\Vert q_{\theta+\delta})=\tfrac12\delta^\top F(\theta)\delta+o(\|\delta\|_2^2)\), with steepest direction proportional to \(F(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal L(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: Fisher information matrix of the variational family.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports variational-family KL geometry and the normalized natural-gradient representation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the variational-inference geometry container and the KL expansion is standard, but no inspectable source is supplied. The normalized direction also requires \(\nabla\mathcal L(\theta)\ne0\); otherwise its denominator vanishes.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Policy Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Fisher-preconditioned ascent for a differentiable stochastic-policy objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a differentiable policy \(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\), objective \(J(\theta)\), step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\), and initial parameter \(\theta_0\), define
\[
F(\theta_k)=\mathbb E_{(s,a)\sim\mu_{\theta_k}}\!\left[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_{\theta_k}(a\mid s)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_{\theta_k}(a\mid s)^\top\right].
\]
At iteration \(k\), compute \(g_k=\nabla J(\theta_k)\), solve \(F(\theta_k)d_k=g_k\), and update \(\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\alpha_k d_k\). Stop under a prescribed gradient, step, or iteration criterion and return the final policy parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural policy gradient updates policy parameters along the objective gradient preconditioned by the policy Fisher information matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\) are differentiable on the iterates.
\(F(\theta_k)\succ0\), or a specified regularized or pseudoinverse solve replaces the exact solve.
The sampling distribution \(\mu_{\theta_k}\) is fixed explicitly by the policy-objective convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\alpha_kF(\theta_k)^{-1}\nabla J(\theta_k)\).

notation.meaning: State-action distribution used to define the policy Fisher matrix.

review_flags: The supplied inventory has no policy-gradient source locator.
Sampling-distribution conventions vary across natural policy-gradient formulations.

The conclusion uses an ordinary inverse even though the assumptions also permit regularized or pseudoinverse solves, so the exact algorithmic variant remains unresolved.

children.title: Singular Fisher Metrics
children.top_down_role: Metric degeneracy with exact rank loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Fisher Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of a finite-dimensional Fisher information matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a regular parametric model \(p_\theta(x)\), let \(s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)\) and \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{p_\theta}[s_\theta s_\theta^\top]\). The Fisher metric is singular at \(\theta\) precisely when \(F(\theta)\) is not positive definite. Equivalently, there exists \(v\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
v^\top F(\theta)v=\mathbb E_{p_\theta}\!\left[(v^\top s_\theta(X))^2\right]=0.
\]
Thus \(v^\top s_\theta(X)=0\) almost surely under \(p_\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fisher metric is singular when some nonzero parameter direction has zero score variance and therefore zero Fisher quadratic length.
assumptions_latex: The score has a finite second moment under \(p_\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\theta)\) is singular if and only if \(\ker F(\theta)\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Null space of the Fisher matrix.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly treats Fisher information or its degeneracy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly characterizes singularity of the positive-semidefinite Fisher matrix and fits the terminal container, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Nearly Singular Fisher Metrics
children.top_down_role: Ill-conditioned metric regimes dominated by very small spectral components.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Singular Fisher Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thresholded spectral condition for an ill-conditioned positive-definite Fisher metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(\theta)\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\) be a Fisher information matrix and fix a relative degeneracy threshold \(\tau\in(0,1)\). The metric is \(\tau\)-nearly singular when
\[
\frac{\lambda_{\min}(F(\theta))}{\lambda_{\max}(F(\theta))}\le\tau,
\]
or equivalently when its spectral condition number satisfies \(\kappa_2(F(\theta))\ge\tau^{-1}\). This definition is scale invariant: multiplying \(F(\theta)\) by any positive scalar does not change the condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite Fisher matrix is nearly singular when its smallest eigenvalue is tiny relative to its largest, equivalently when its condition number is large.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\min}(F)/\lambda_{\max}(F)\le\tau\iff\kappa_2(F)\ge\tau^{-1}\).

children.title: Fisher Null-Space Consequences
children.top_down_role: Optimization consequences associated with unidentifiable or weakly represented directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fisher Null-Space Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvability and nonuniqueness consequences of Fisher null directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\in\mathbb S_+^d\) and \(g\in\mathbb R^d\). The natural-gradient equation \(Fd=g\) is solvable if and only if \(g\in\operatorname{range}(F)\), equivalently \(g\perp\ker(F)\). When solvable, every solution has the form
\[
d=F^\dagger g+v,\qquad v\in\ker(F),
\]
and \(F^\dagger g\) is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm solution. Moreover, adding a null vector does not change the Fisher quadratic model because \((d+v)^\top F(d+v)=d^\top Fd\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fisher null directions cause nonunique natural-gradient solves; incompatible gradients yield no exact solve, while the pseudoinverse selects the minimum-norm solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Fd=g\) is solvable exactly when \(g\perp\ker(F)\), and then \(\{d:Fd=g\}=F^\dagger g+\ker(F)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical-Fisher Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-observation Bernoulli example separating empirical and model Fisher matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) with logit parameter \(\theta\), so \(p=(1+e^{-\theta})^{-1}\) and \(\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(Y)=Y-p\). The model Fisher information is
\[
F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{Y\sim p_\theta}[(Y-p)^2]=p(1-p).
\]
For one observed label \(y\), the empirical outer-product quantity is \(\widehat F_{\mathrm{emp}}=(y-p)^2\). At \(p=0.8\) and \(y=1\), \(F=0.16\) whereas \(\widehat F_{\mathrm{emp}}=0.04\). Hence the empirical Fisher need not equal the model Fisher, even in a correctly specified model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Bernoulli logistic likelihood, a single observed-score square generally differs from the model-averaged Fisher information.
assumptions_latex: The empirical Fisher is defined from the observed score outer product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(1-p)\ne(y-p)^2\) in general; specifically, \(0.16\ne0.04\) when \(p=0.8\) and \(y=1\).

notation.meaning: Observed-score outer product for one sample.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Factorization Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral control of inverse-metric error under an approximate factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F,\widetilde F\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\) and suppose their relative factorization error satisfies
\[
\left\|F^{-1/2}(\widetilde F-F)F^{-1/2}\right\|_2\le\varepsilon<1.
\]
Then
\[
(1-\varepsilon)F\preceq\widetilde F\preceq(1+\varepsilon)F
\]
and inversion reverses the Loewner order, giving
\[
\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}F^{-1}\preceq\widetilde F^{-1}\preceq\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}F^{-1}.
\]
Thus a relative metric-factorization error approaching one can amplify the preconditioned step without bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative spectral factorization error below one yields explicit inverse-metric bounds; the upper amplification diverges as the error approaches one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1+\varepsilon)^{-1}F^{-1}\preceq\widetilde F^{-1}\preceq(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}F^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: Metric reconstructed from an approximate factorization.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Estimation Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiasedness and mean-square error of an independent sample metric estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) be independent identically distributed random symmetric matrices with \(\mathbb E\|Z_1\|_F^2<\infty\), and define \(F=\mathbb E[Z_1]\) and \(\widehat F_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m Z_i\). Then \(\widehat F_m\) is unbiased and
\[
\mathbb E\|\widehat F_m-F\|_F^2=\frac{1}{m}\mathbb E\|Z_1-F\|_F^2.
\]
For a sampled Fisher metric one may take \(Z_i=s_i s_i^\top\). Thus its root-mean-square Frobenius estimation error decays exactly as \(m^{-1/2}\) when the displayed second moment is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent sample-average metric is unbiased, and its root-mean-square Frobenius error decreases at the standard inverse-square-root sample rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat F_m]=F\) and \(\mathbb E\|\widehat F_m-F\|_F^2=m^{-1}\mathbb E\|Z_1-F\|_F^2\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports matrix-valued metric-estimation variance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unbiasedness and exact Frobenius mean-square identity are correct for iid matrix-valued samples with finite second moment, and the property fits the container. No inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Metric-State Memory Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-State Memory Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage costs for dense, diagonal, and low-rank metric states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a real-RAM storage model, an arbitrary symmetric metric \(F\in\mathbb S^d\) has \(d(d+1)/2\) independent entries, so exact unstructured storage requires \(\Theta(d^2)\) scalar words. A diagonal metric requires exactly \(d\) scalar words. A diagonal-plus-rank-\(r\) representation
\[
F=D+UU^\top,
\]
with diagonal \(D\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) and \(U\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\), requires \(d+dr=\Theta(dr+d)\) words. Consequently, linear-memory metric state requires diagonal, fixed-rank, implicit, or comparably structured representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense metric state needs quadratic memory, while diagonal or fixed-rank structured metrics can be stored with linear memory in the parameter dimension.
assumptions_latex: Each stored real scalar occupies one memory word.
The dense metric is arbitrary and symmetric.
The low-rank factor has rank parameter \(r\le d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mathrm{dense}}=\Theta(d^2)\), \(M_{\mathrm{diag}}=\Theta(d)\), and \(M_{\mathrm{diag+rank}\text{-}r}=\Theta(dr+d)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Solve Compute Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense direct-solve cost and condition-dependent conjugate-gradient cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\), a dense Cholesky factorization of \(F\) costs \(\Theta(d^3)\) arithmetic operations and \(\Theta(d^2)\) storage; each subsequent triangular solve costs \(\Theta(d^2)\). Alternatively, conjugate gradients applied to \(Fd=g\) uses one multiplication by \(F\) per iteration and, from an arbitrary initial iterate, satisfies
\[
\frac{\|d_k-d_\star\|_{F,\mathrm{en}}}{\|d_0-d_\star\|_{F,\mathrm{en}}}\le 2\left(\frac{\sqrt\kappa-1}{\sqrt\kappa+1}\right)^k,
\]
where \(\|x\|_{F,\mathrm{en}}=(x^\top Fx)^{1/2}\) and \(\kappa=\kappa_2(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense exact metric solves have cubic setup cost; conjugate gradients replace factorization by matrix-vector products but deteriorate with the square root of conditioning.
assumptions_latex: Dense direct arithmetic uses no exploitable structure.
Conjugate gradients is evaluated in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense factorization costs \(\Theta(d^3)\), while conjugate-gradient energy-norm error contracts by at most \(2((\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1))^k\).

notation.meaning: Exact solution of the metric linear system.

children.title: Distributed Metric-Solve Overhead

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Metric-Solve Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication payloads for dense aggregation and distributed matrix-free metric solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(P\) workers hold additive local metrics \(F_p\in\mathbb S^d\) and the global metric is \(F=\sum_{p=1}^P F_p\). Materializing \(F\) by a symmetric all-reduce communicates a payload of \(d(d+1)/2=\Theta(d^2)\) scalars per collective. In a matrix-free Krylov solve, if each product is formed as
\[
Fv=\sum_{p=1}^P F_pv,
\]
then every iteration requires reduction of at least one \(d\)-vector, giving \(\Theta(kd)\) reduced scalar payload over \(k\) iterations, in addition to synchronization latency and any scalar inner-product reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed dense metric assembly communicates quadratic-size payloads; matrix-free iterative solves reduce this to vector-size payloads per iteration but add repeated synchronization.
assumptions_latex: Workers use an additive partition \(F=\sum_{p=1}^P F_p\).
Collective payload counts exclude implementation-dependent routing multiplicities.
The Krylov method performs \(k\) distributed metric-vector products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense aggregation has \(\Theta(d^2)\) collective payload, whereas \(k\) matrix-free products have \(\Theta(kd)\) vector-reduction payload plus latency.

knowledge_statements.title: Isotropic Parameter Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean perturbation set used by isotropic sharpness-aware optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameter vector \(\theta\in\mathbb R^d\) and radius \(\rho\ge0\), the isotropic parameter neighborhood is the closed Euclidean ball
\[
\mathcal N_2(\theta,\rho)=\{\theta+\delta:\delta\in\mathbb R^d,\ \|\delta\|_2\le\rho\}.
\]
For a loss \(L:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), the associated isotropic sharpness-aware objective is
\[
\Phi_\rho(\theta)=\sup_{\|\delta\|_2\le\rho}L(\theta+\delta).
\]
The same radius is applied in every orthonormal coordinate direction, so the neighborhood contains no parameterwise or learned anisotropic scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isotropic parameter neighborhood is a Euclidean ball of perturbations with one common radius; sharpness is the worst loss inside that ball.
assumptions_latex: The supremum is taken only where \(L\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_2(\theta,\rho)=\theta+\rho\mathbb B_2^d\) and \(\Phi_\rho(\theta)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal N_2(\theta,\rho)}L(u)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Dependent Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation sets defined by an arbitrary norm and used in sharpness-aware objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and let \(\rho\ge 0\). The norm-dependent neighborhood of \(w\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is \[\mathcal N_{\rho,\|\cdot\|}(w)=\{w+\delta:\delta\in\mathbb{R}^d,\ \|\delta\|\le\rho\}.\] Its associated robust or sharpness-aware objective is \[F_{\rho,\|\cdot\|}(w)=\sup_{\|\delta\|\le\rho}f(w+\delta).\] If \(f\) is differentiable at \(w\), the linearized inner maximization has value \(f(w)+\rho\|\nabla f(w)\|_*\), where \(\|\cdot\|_*\) is the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-dependent neighborhood is a translated norm ball. Linearizing the loss makes its worst-case increase equal to the radius times the gradient’s dual norm.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at the point used for the linearized formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N_{\rho,\|\cdot\|}(w)=w+\rho B_{\|\cdot\|}\) and the linearized worst-case increase is \(\rho\|\nabla f(w)\|_*\).

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the perturbation norm.
Norm-dependent neighborhood centered at the parameter vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and dual-norm linearization are mathematically precise and fit the neighborhood-geometry leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied for either the sharpness-aware objective or its linearized formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterwise Adaptive Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-scaled perturbation geometry whose radii depend on the current parameter vector or optimizer state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \(\rho\ge0\), and let \(s(w)\in(0,\infty)^d\) be a vector of parameterwise scales. For \(p\in[1,\infty]\), define \[\mathcal N_{\rho,s,p}(w)=\{w+s(w)\odot u:\|u\|_p\le\rho\}=\{w+\delta:\|\delta\oslash s(w)\|_p\le\rho\}.\] Thus coordinate \(i\) has effective perturbation scale \(\rho s_i(w)\). For differentiable \(f\), a maximizer of the linearized loss solves \(\max_{\|u\|_p\le\rho}\langle s(w)\odot\nabla f(w),u\rangle\), whose value is \(\rho\|s(w)\odot\nabla f(w)\|_q\), with \(1/p+1/q=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterwise adaptive neighborhood rescales each perturbation coordinate by a positive, state-dependent factor; its linearized sharpness is measured by the corresponding scaled dual norm.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(w\) for the linearized formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The neighborhood is a diagonally scaled \(\ell_p\)-ball, and its linearized worst-case increase is \(\rho\|s(w)\odot\nabla f(w)\|_q\).

notation.meaning: Positive vector of parameterwise perturbation scales.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonally scaled ell_p neighborhood and Holder-dual linearization are internally consistent and appropriate as a definition, but the record has no cited source establishing this parameterwise adaptive sharpness geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Pass Sharpness-Aware Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical update using one gradient to construct a perturbation and another at the perturbed parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given differentiable losses \(f_t:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), radii \(\rho_t\ge0\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), and a perturbation map \(A_t\), initialize \(w_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). At iteration \(t\), compute the first-pass gradient \(g_t=\nabla f_t(w_t)\), choose \(\delta_t\in A_t(g_t)\) with \(\delta_t\) feasible for the prescribed sharpness neighborhood, compute the second-pass gradient \(h_t=\nabla f_t(w_t+\delta_t)\), and update \[w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t h_t.\] Stop according to a specified iteration, gradient, or validation criterion and output the selected iterate. The method uses two gradient evaluations per iteration when both passes use the same loss batch.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update direction is \(\nabla f_t(w_t+\delta_t)\), obtained after a separate gradient evaluation used to construct \(\delta_t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Pass Sharpness Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-new-gradient approximation to a two-pass sharpness-aware update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(w_t\), stepsize \(\eta_t>0\), and state \(z_t\) available before iteration \(t\), form a predicted perturbation \(\widehat\delta_t=\Phi_t(w_t,z_t)\) without evaluating \(\nabla f_t(w_t)\), subject to the chosen neighborhood constraint. Evaluate one new gradient \[\widehat h_t=\nabla f_t(w_t+\widehat\delta_t),\] update \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t\widehat h_t\), and set \(z_{t+1}=\Psi_t(z_t,w_t,\widehat h_t)\). Stop by a prescribed criterion and output the selected iterate. It is a single-pass approximation precisely when computing \(\Phi_t\) and \(\Psi_t\) requires no additional current-iteration gradient evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-pass approximation predicts the perturbation from stored state, evaluates one fresh gradient at the predicted perturbed point, and updates both parameters and state.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi_t\) produces a feasible perturbation using only information available before the new gradient call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one new gradient evaluation is required at iteration \(t\), namely \(\nabla f_t(w_t+\widehat\delta_t)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Fidelity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error boundary for replacing the exact perturbed gradient by a one-pass approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\delta_t\) and \(\widehat\delta_t\) be the exact and approximate feasible perturbations at \(w_t\). Then \[\|\nabla f(w_t+\widehat\delta_t)-\nabla f(w_t+\delta_t)\|_2\le L\|\widehat\delta_t-\delta_t\|_2.\] Hence an approximation guarantee \(\|\widehat\delta_t-\delta_t\|_2\le\varepsilon_t\) transfers to a direction error at most \(L\varepsilon_t\). Without gradient continuity, perturbation closeness alone gives no vanishing direction error: for \(f(x)=|x|\), arbitrarily close points on opposite sides of zero have gradients \(-1\) and \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a Lipschitz gradient, perturbation error controls update-direction error. Without gradient continuity, arbitrarily close perturbations can produce gradients separated by a fixed amount.
assumptions_latex: For the upper bound, \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on a set containing both perturbed points.
For the counterexample, gradients are evaluated away from the nondifferentiable point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direction fidelity follows from perturbation fidelity only under suitable gradient regularity; absent continuity, no bound tending to zero is generally valid.
review_flags: The inequality is standard smooth analysis, but no supplied locator directly supports this sharpness-approximation boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lipschitz-gradient bound and the absolute-value counterexample are mathematically correct, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. No cited source with a specific locator supports the bound or its sharpness-approximation interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermittent Sharpness-Aware Updates

Update \[w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t d_t.\] Stop according to a specified criterion and output the selected iterate. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((s_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a prescribed binary schedule with \(s_t\in\{0,1\}\). Initialize \(w_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). knowledge_statements.title: Update-Mode Switching Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent boundary when switching between ordinary and approximate sharpness-aware directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(g_t=\nabla f(w_t)\), and write the selected direction as \(d_t=g_t+e_t\). For \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t d_t\), the descent lemma gives \[f(w_{t+1})\le f(w_t)-\eta_t\langle g_t,d_t\rangle+\frac{L\eta_t^2}{2}\|d_t\|_2^2.\] Thus strict one-step descent is certified when \(\langle g_t,d_t\rangle>(L\eta_t/2)\|d_t\|_2^2\). Switching can cross the descent boundary when approximation or stale-state error makes this inequality fail; in particular, \(d_t=-g_t\) is an ascent direction whenever \(g_t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mode switching preserves a certified descent step only while the chosen direction remains sufficiently aligned with the current gradient relative to the stepsize and smoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on the update segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The switching boundary is \(\langle g_t,d_t\rangle=(L\eta_t/2)\|d_t\|_2^2\); crossing to the smaller-alignment side removes this descent certificate.

notation.meaning: Difference between the selected direction and current gradient.

review_flags: The smooth descent inequality is standard, but the supplied sources do not locate this update-mode switching interpretation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The descent-lemma inequality and stated sufficient strict-descent certificate are correct under segment-wise L-smoothness; the equality is properly interpreted as the boundary of that certificate. The record nevertheless lacks a source for the result and its update-mode-switching interpretation.

children.title: Parameter-Subset Sharpness Updates
children.top_down_role: Sharpness-aware perturbations restricted to selected parameter subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Subset Sharpness Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness perturbation restricted to a selected subset of parameter coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(M_{S_t}\) be its diagonal coordinate mask. Given \(w_t\), compute \(g_t=\nabla f_t(w_t)\), choose \[\delta_t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\delta\in\mathcal U_t,\ (I-M_{S_t})\delta=0}\langle g_t,\delta\rangle,\] evaluate \(h_t=\nabla f_t(w_t+\delta_t)\), and update \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t h_t\). Here \(\mathcal U_t\) is the prescribed full perturbation set. Stop by a specified criterion and output the selected iterate. The restriction changes perturbation coverage only; unless separately masked, every coordinate may still be updated through \(h_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adversarial perturbation is supported only on selected coordinates, while the gradient evaluated at the partially perturbed point may still update all parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) is selected before solving the inner linearized problem.
\(\mathcal U_t\) is nonempty and contains a feasible masked perturbation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbation satisfies \((I-M_{S_t})\delta_t=0\), although the outer update need not be coordinate-restricted.

notation.meaning: Diagonal mask with ones on selected coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Layer-selective sharpness perturbs only parameters belonging to chosen model layers, then computes the update gradient at that partially perturbed parameter vector.
assumptions_latex: The layer sets \(L_1,\ldots,L_m\) form a disjoint partition of parameter coordinates.

children.title: Selective-Coverage Bias
children.top_down_role: Bias introduced when selected parameters do not represent full-model sharpness.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective-Coverage Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias induced when sharpness perturbations cover only selected parameter coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,d\}\), let \(P_S\) be the coordinate projector, and define \(\Phi_S(w)=\max_{\|P_S\delta\|_2\leq\rho,\,(I-P_S)\delta=0}L(w+\delta)\). Selective sharpness controls only directions in \(\operatorname{range}(P_S)\): even if \(\Phi_S(w)-L(w)\leq\varepsilon\), the full-neighborhood gap \(\Phi(w)-L(w)\), where \(\Phi(w)=\max_{\|\delta\|_2\leq\rho}L(w+\delta)\), can be arbitrarily large. Thus selective coverage systematically ignores high-loss directions supported outside \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small sharpness on selected parameters does not imply small full-model sharpness; excluded coordinates may contain arbitrarily adverse perturbation directions.
assumptions_latex: \(L:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite on the radius-\(\rho\) neighborhood of \(w\).
\(\rho>0\) and \(S\) is a proper coordinate subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_S(w)-L(w)\leq\varepsilon\not\Rightarrow\Phi(w)-L(w)\leq C\varepsilon\) for any universal \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the arbitrarily-large-gap assertion is not quantified over a loss family and has no cited counterexample or authoritative source. A source-supported formulation must clarify that no universal bound holds over the stated class of losses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal, parameter-dependent perturbation geometry for sharpness-aware updates.

Given \(w_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), radius \(ho>0\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), and positive diagonal matrices \(D_t=D(w_t)\), compute \(g_t=

abla L_{B_t}(w_t+\epsilon_t)\) and update \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t\widetilde g_t\). After \(T\) iterations, output \(w_T\) or a prescribed averaged iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive SAM maximizes a linearized minibatch loss in a parameter-dependent ellipsoid, then descends using the gradient at that perturbed point.
assumptions_latex: \(L_{B_t}:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at the queried points.
