children.title: Surrogate-Gap Variants
children.top_down_role: Sharpness-aware variants organized around surrogate objective gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate-Gap Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variants replacing the exact robust-loss gap by a computable surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), radius \(\rho>0\), and admissible perturbation set \(U_\rho\), define the exact sharpness gap by \(G_\rho(w)=\sup_{\delta\in U_\rho}[L(w+\delta)-L(w)]\). A surrogate-gap variant chooses a tractable function \(\widehat G_\rho(w;\xi)\), possibly depending on sampled information \(\xi\), and optimizes \(L(w)+\lambda\widehat G_\rho(w;\xi)\) instead of \(L(w)+\lambda G_\rho(w)\). Its defining approximation error is \(E_\rho(w;\xi)=\widehat G_\rho(w;\xi)-G_\rho(w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surrogate-gap method replaces the exact worst-case local loss increase with a tractable estimate and optimizes the resulting regularized objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{sur}}(w;\xi)=L(w)+\lambda\widehat G_\rho(w;\xi)\) approximates \(F_{\mathrm{sharp}}(w)=L(w)+\lambda G_\rho(w)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is a plausible role for this family leaf, but the record introduces a broad surrogate-gap class without identifying a recognized variant family or source establishing this terminology and objective.

children.title: Decomposed-Sharpness Variants
children.top_down_role: Variants that partition sharpness contributions across components or scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposed-Sharpness Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise decomposition of a global local-sharpness objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w=(w^{(1)},\ldots,w^{(m)})\), let \(L:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), and assign block perturbation sets \(U_j\). Define \(G_j(w)=\sup_{u\in U_j}[L(w+E_ju)-L(w)]\), where \(E_j\) embeds block \(j\). A decomposed-sharpness surrogate has the representation \(\widehat G(w)=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_jG_j(w)\), with \(\alpha_j\geq0\), and uses \(L(w)+\lambda\widehat G(w)\). In general this sum is a surrogate, not an identity for the jointly perturbed gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposed variants aggregate blockwise worst-case loss increases, usually as a weighted surrogate rather than the exact joint sharpness.
assumptions_latex: The displayed blockwise suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat G(w)=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_jG_j(w)\), while generally \(\widehat G(w)\neq\sup_{u_j\in U_j}[L(w+\sum_jE_ju_j)-L(w)]\).

notation.meaning: embedding of block j into the full parameter space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf, and the formulas are internally coherent. However, the weighted sum is only one possible blockwise construction and no source establishes it as the defining representation of decomposed-sharpness variants.

children.title: Surrogate-Fidelity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where surrogate or decomposed quantities diverge from the targeted neighborhood behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate-Fidelity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization transfer requires uniform control of surrogate value or gradient error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(w)=L(w)+\lambda G(w)\) and \(\widehat F(w)=L(w)+\lambda\widehat G(w)\) on \(W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). If \(\sup_{w\in W}|\widehat G(w)-G(w)|\leq\varepsilon\), every \(\delta\)-minimizer \(\widehat w\) of \(\widehat F\) satisfies \(F(\widehat w)\leq\inf_{w\in W}F(w)+\delta+2\lambda\varepsilon\). Without such uniform fidelity, arbitrarily small surrogate error on sampled or visited points need not control the true objective at the returned point, so surrogate optimization need not transfer to sharpness optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform surrogate accuracy transfers approximate optimality with a quantified penalty; accuracy only on sampled points gives no general transfer guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(W\neq\varnothing\), \(\lambda\geq0\), and both objectives are bounded below on \(W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\widehat w)-\inf_{w\in W}F(w)\leq\delta+2\lambda\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Aware Sharpness-Aware Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness-aware updates corrected for stochastic-gradient uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(w_t\), draw gradient samples \(g_{t,1},\ldots,g_{t,K}\) at \(w_t\), form \(\bar g_t=K^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^K g_{t,k}\), and estimate a positive-semidefinite noise covariance \(\widehat\Sigma_t\). Choose a positive-definite metric \(M_t=h(\widehat\Sigma_t)\), set \(\epsilon_t=\rho M_t^{-1}\bar g_t/\sqrt{\bar g_t^{\mathsf T}M_t^{-1}\bar g_t}\) when \(\bar g_t\neq0\), evaluate an independent or prescribed perturbed gradient \(\widetilde g_t\) at \(w_t+\epsilon_t\), and return \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t\widetilde g_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noise-aware variants estimate gradient uncertainty, shape the adversarial perturbation with that estimate, and descend using a gradient at the perturbed parameters.
assumptions_latex: The sampled gradients have finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\epsilon_t\in\arg\max_{\epsilon^{\mathsf T}M_t\epsilon\leq\rho^2}\bar g_t^{\mathsf T}\epsilon\), followed by \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t\widetilde g_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role is plausible, but this is a generic covariance-shaped update rather than a source-identified noise-aware SAM algorithm. The choice of metric map, sampling dependence, and perturbed-gradient convention require a primary algorithm source.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Optimizer-Composed Sharpness-Aware Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of a sharpness-aware gradient transform with a base optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a base first-order optimizer have state \(s_t\) and transition \((w_{t+1},s_{t+1})=\mathcal U_t(w_t,s_t,g)\). Given \(w_t\), compute \(g_t=\nabla L_{B_t}(w_t)\), choose \(\epsilon_t\in\arg\max_{\epsilon\in U_t}\langle g_t,\epsilon\rangle\), and compute \(\widetilde g_t=\nabla L_{\widetilde B_t}(w_t+\epsilon_t)\). Apply exactly one base-optimizer transition \((w_{t+1},s_{t+1})=\mathcal U_t(w_t,s_t,\widetilde g_t)\). Initialize \((w_0,s_0)\) according to the base optimizer and output \(w_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method constructs a sharpness-aware gradient, then passes it unchanged to one transition of any specified stateful first-order optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(L_B\) is differentiable at all queried points.
Each \(U_t\) is nonempty and the linear maximization problem attains a solution.
The base transition \(\mathcal U_t\) is defined for \((w_t,s_t,\widetilde g_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((w_{t+1},s_{t+1})=\mathcal U_t(w_t,s_t,\nabla L_{\widetilde B_t}(w_t+\epsilon_t))\).

children.title: Flat-Minima Generalization Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Local Sharpness Proxies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable local measures approximating worst-case neighborhood loss increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), point \(w\), radius \(\rho>0\), and norm \(\|\cdot\|\), the local sharpness is \(S_\rho(w)=\sup_{\|\delta\|\leq\rho}[L(w+\delta)-L(w)]\). A local sharpness proxy is a computable quantity \(P_\rho(w;\mathcal I)\) formed from accessible local information \(\mathcal I\), such as gradients, Hessian-vector products, or sampled perturbations, together with a stated approximation relation to \(S_\rho(w)\), for example an upper bound or a quantified error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local sharpness proxy estimates the worst loss increase near a parameter vector using specified local derivative or perturbation information.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) contains only information available to the stated proxy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\rho(w;\mathcal I)\approx S_\rho(w)=\sup_{\|\delta\|\leq\rho}[L(w+\delta)-L(w)]\), with the approximation relation stated separately.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the leaf, but the record defines a method-dependent umbrella class and uses an unformalized approximation symbol in the conclusion. A source must identify accepted proxy constructions and the particular bound or error relation each provides.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Invariant Flatness Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flatness measures invariant under function-preserving parameter rescalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(\mathcal G\) act on parameter space \(W\), and suppose every \(g\in\mathcal G\) preserves the represented predictor: \(f_{g\cdot w}=f_w\). A flatness functional \(F:W\to[0,\infty]\) is scale invariant with respect to \(\mathcal G\) precisely when \(F(g\cdot w)=F(w)\) for all \(w\in W\) and \(g\in\mathcal G\). Consequently, \(F\) is constant on each function-preserving orbit and descends to a well-defined functional on the quotient \(W/\mathcal G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scale-invariant flatness measure assigns the same value to all parameterizations connected by predictor-preserving rescaling, so it is defined on equivalence classes.
assumptions_latex: \(f_{g\cdot w}=f_w\) for every \(g\in\mathcal G\) and \(w\in W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(g\cdot w)=F(w)\), hence \(\overline F([w])=F(w)\) is well defined on \(W/\mathcal G\).

children.title: Perturbation-Based Generalization Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between parameter perturbations, local loss behavior, and generalization analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Based Generalization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates randomized parameter perturbations to empirical and population risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\) be sampled independently from \(P\), let \(w=A(S)\), and let \(\Delta\sim Q_S\) be a possibly data-dependent parameter perturbation. For loss \(\ell\in[0,1]\), define \(\widehat R_S(Q_S)=\mathbb E_\Delta[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(w+\Delta,Z_i)]\) and \(R(Q_S)=\mathbb E_\Delta\mathbb E_{Z\sim P}\ell(w+\Delta,Z)\). A perturbation-based generalization interface combines a bound on \(R(Q_S)-\widehat R_S(Q_S)\) with control of the perturbation penalty \(\widehat R_S(Q_S)-\widehat R_S(w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalization of a perturbed predictor separates into its empirical perturbation cost and the randomized predictor’s population-to-empirical gap.
assumptions_latex: The expectations defining the risks exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(Q_S)-\widehat R_S(w)=[R(Q_S)-\widehat R_S(Q_S)]+[\widehat R_S(Q_S)-\widehat R_S(w)]\).

children.title: PAC-Bayes Generalization Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between sharpness-aware training and PAC-Bayes complexity controls.

knowledge_statements.title: PAC-Bayes Generalization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-loss PAC-Bayes-kl interface for data-dependent perturbation posteriors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\sim P^n\), let \(\ell(h,z)\in[0,1]\), and let \(\Pi\) be a prior on hypotheses independent of \(S\). For any \(\delta\in(0,1)\), with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over \(S\), simultaneously for every posterior \(Q\ll\Pi\), \[\operatorname{kl}\!\left(\widehat R_S(Q)\,\middle\|\,R(Q)\right)\leq\frac{\operatorname{KL}(Q\|\Pi)+\log(2\sqrt n/\delta)}{n}.\] Taking \(Q\) as the distribution induced by perturbing learned parameters converts empirical perturbed risk and posterior complexity into a population-risk certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PAC-Bayes bound controls perturbed population risk using perturbed empirical risk plus the posterior’s divergence from a data-independent prior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{kl}(\widehat R_S(Q)\|R(Q))\leq[\operatorname{KL}(Q\|\Pi)+\log(2\sqrt n/\delta)]/n\) simultaneously for all \(Q\ll\Pi\).

notation.meaning: posterior, possibly induced by parameter perturbation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role is correct and the hypotheses are presented in the expected bounded-loss PAC-Bayes-kl form, but the exact simultaneous bound and constant log(2 sqrt(n)/delta) require an authoritative theorem-level citation before acceptance.

children.title: Perturbation–Posterior Correspondence Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits on interpreting optimizer perturbations through posterior-based generalization arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation–Posterior Correspondence Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of identifying local parameter perturbations with PAC-Bayes posteriors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameter perturbation law \(\Delta\sim\nu\) at \(w\) induces a posterior \(Q_w=(\delta\mapsto f_{w+\delta})_{\#}\nu\) on predictors. This correspondence alone yields no PAC-Bayes guarantee: a valid bound additionally requires a specified data-independent prior \(\Pi\), absolute continuity \(Q_w\ll\Pi\), finite \(\operatorname{KL}(Q_w\|\Pi)\), and control of perturbed empirical risk. Moreover, noninjective parameterizations can map distinct perturbation laws to the same predictor posterior, so parameter-space sharpness and posterior complexity are not generally equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation defines a predictor posterior, but PAC-Bayes also needs a valid prior, finite divergence, and empirical-risk control; parameter sharpness is not posterior complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\nu\) is a probability law on admissible parameter perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_w=(\delta\mapsto f_{w+\delta})_{\#}\nu\) does not imply finite \(\operatorname{KL}(Q_w\|\Pi)\) or a generalization bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and the pushforward construction is coherent. A source is required for the claimed limits and for careful qualification of absolute continuity and finite KL as conditions for a finite, nonvacuous PAC-Bayes certificate rather than for merely writing a formally valid bound.

children.title: Algorithmic-Stability Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between sharpness-aware updates and sensitivity to training-data changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Algorithmic-Stability Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform stability supplies a sufficient generalization interface for a sharpness-aware training algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_\rho\) map a sample \(S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\) to parameters obtained using perturbation radius \(\rho\), and let \(\ell(A_\rho(S),z)\in[0,M]\). If, for every pair of samples \(S,S'\) differing in one observation, \[\sup_z\left|\mathbb{E}_{A_\rho}\ell(A_\rho(S),z)-\mathbb{E}_{A_\rho}\ell(A_\rho(S'),z)\right|\leq\beta_\rho,\] then the expected generalization gap satisfies \[\left|\mathbb{E}_{S,A_\rho}\left[R(A_\rho(S))-\widehat R_S(A_\rho(S))\right]\right|\leq\beta_\rho.\] Thus sharpness-aware perturbations support a stability-based generalization claim only after controlling how \(\beta_\rho\) depends on the radius and optimization dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform stability of the complete sharpness-aware algorithm bounds its expected generalization gap, but the stability constant may depend strongly on the perturbation radius.
assumptions_latex: The displayed uniform-stability inequality holds for \(A_\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left|\mathbb{E}[R(A_\rho(S))-\widehat R_S(A_\rho(S))]\right|\leq\beta_\rho\).

notation.meaning: Possibly randomized sharpness-aware learning algorithm with radius rho.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The randomized uniform-stability hypothesis and expected-generalization conclusion are mathematically coherent, and the property kind fits the interface container. However, the record supplies no inspectable citation for either the stability theorem or its specialization to a radius-dependent sharpness-aware algorithm.

children.title: Implicit-Bias Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between optimizer dynamics and preferences among fitted solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Bias Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the optimizer-dependent selection rule among predictors attaining the same limiting training risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(F_\rho:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), initialization \(w_0\), and update map \(T_\rho\), let \(w_{t+1}=T_\rho(w_t)\). The implicit-bias selection set is \[\mathcal B_\rho(w_0)=\left\{w:\exists\,t_k\uparrow\infty,\ w_{t_k}\to w,\ F_\rho(w_{t_k})\to\inf_u F_\rho(u)\right\}.\] For a predictor map \(p\), the predictor-level bias is \(p(\mathcal B_\rho(w_0))\). A sharpness-aware optimizer has a different implicit bias from its unperturbed counterpart when \(p(\mathcal B_\rho(w_0))\neq p(\mathcal B_0(w_0))\), even if both attain the same limiting empirical risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implicit bias is the optimizer-dependent set of limiting risk-minimizing predictors; sharpness awareness changes it when its selected predictor set differs from the unperturbed set.
assumptions_latex: The trajectory has at least one convergent subsequence attaining \(\inf F_\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(\mathcal B_\rho(w_0))\neq p(\mathcal B_0(w_0))\) characterizes a change in predictor-level implicit bias.

notation.meaning: Optimizer update map at perturbation radius rho.
Limit-point selection set attaining optimal objective value.
Map from parameters to represented predictors.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent under its stated subsequence assumption and fits the implicit-bias interface, but it is a local formalization rather than an established cited definition. An authoritative implicit-bias source and support for this sharpness-aware selection-set formulation are required.

children.title: Stability–Bias Alignment Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where stability-based and implicit-bias explanations agree or diverge.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability–Bias Alignment Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a tolerance-level condition relating optimizer-selected predictors to predictor-conditioned stability bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B_\rho\) be a nonempty set of predictors selected by an optimizer, and let \(b_\rho(p)\) be a valid upper bound on the uniform-stability coefficient of the specified algorithm conditional on selection of \(p\). For a tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), define stability–bias alignment at level \(\varepsilon\) by \[\mathcal B_\rho\subseteq\{p:b_\rho(p)\leq\varepsilon\}.\] Under this condition, every predictor in the selection set carries the prescribed stability bound. If some \(p\in\mathcal B_\rho\) satisfies \(b_\rho(p)>\varepsilon\), the selection-set description does not certify alignment at level \(\varepsilon\). A global stability bound alone does not determine which member of \(\mathcal B_\rho\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a chosen tolerance, stability and implicit bias are defined to be aligned when every optimizer-selected predictor satisfies the corresponding stability bound; a selection set or a global stability bound alone does not establish both properties.
assumptions_latex: For each \(p\in\mathcal B_\rho\), \(b_\rho(p)\) is a valid stability upper bound for the specified algorithm, conditioning convention, and data model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B_\rho\subseteq\{p:b_\rho(p)\leq\varepsilon\}\) is the defined tolerance-level alignment condition.

notation.meaning: Predictors selected by optimizer implicit bias.

children.title: Reparameterization Dependence
children.top_down_role: Changes in sharpness behavior caused by equivalent parameter transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Reparameterization Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean sharpness is generally not invariant under a smooth change of model parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(L:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), let \(h:\Theta\to h(\Theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a diffeomorphism, and define \(\widetilde L=L\circ h\). For \(\theta\in\Theta\) such that \(\theta+B_\rho\subseteq\Theta\), define \[L_\rho(h(\theta))=\max_{u\in B_\rho}L(h(\theta)+u),\qquad \widetilde L_\rho(\theta)=\max_{v\in B_\rho}L(h(\theta+v)).\] In general, \(\widetilde L_\rho(\theta)\neq L_\rho(h(\theta))\), because \(h(\theta+B_\rho)\) need not equal \(h(\theta))+B_\rho\). Mapping the two perturbation sets onto one another guarantees equality for every loss for which the maxima exist; in particular, this holds for an affine Euclidean isometry on the relevant ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general smooth reparameterization changes a Euclidean perturbation neighborhood, so the resulting robust objective need not be invariant. Equality is guaranteed when the reparameterization maps the entire perturbation ball onto the corresponding Euclidean ball, as an affine Euclidean isometry does.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is open and \(h:\Theta\to h(\Theta)\) is a diffeomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(\theta+B_\rho)\neq h(\theta)+B_\rho\) permits \(\widetilde L_\rho(\theta)\neq L_\rho(h(\theta))\).

notation.meaning: Closed Euclidean ball of radius rho centered at zero.
Robust envelopes in the two parameterizations.

children.title: Scale-Sensitivity Pathology
children.top_down_role: Changes in flatness or perturbation measures caused by parameter scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Sensitivity Pathology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scale symmetry preserves predictions while making Hessian-based sharpness arbitrarily large.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(L(a,b)=\tfrac12(ab-1)^2\). Every point satisfying \(ab=1\) is a global minimizer and represents the same scalar product. At such a point, \[\nabla^2L(a,b)=\begin{pmatrix}b^2&1\\1&a^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2L(a,b))=a^2+b^2.\] The rescaling \((a,b)\mapsto(ca,b/c)\), with \(c>0\), preserves both \(ab\) and the represented predictor, but changes the largest Hessian eigenvalue to \(c^2a^2+b^2/c^2\). This quantity is unbounded as \(c\to0\) or \(c\to\infty\), demonstrating scale-sensitive sharpness without any functional change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-factor scaling symmetry leaves the predictor and loss unchanged while making Hessian sharpness arbitrarily large.
assumptions_latex: Sharpness is measured by the largest Euclidean Hessian eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{c>0}\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2L(ca,b/c))=+\infty\) although \((ca)(b/c)=1\).

notation.meaning: Largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hessian calculation is correct at points satisfying ab=1: its eigenvalues are zero and a^2+b^2. The rescaling preserves the represented product and makes the largest eigenvalue unbounded, so the counterexample kind precisely fits the pathology container. An inspectable source is nevertheless absent.

children.title: Invariant-Measure Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of proposed corrections intended to remove coordinate or scale dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Invariant-Measure Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An invariant neighborhood statistic requires the metric and, for integral statistics, the measure to transform with coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let parameter space carry a Riemannian metric tensor \(G(w)\), with metric ball \(B_G(w_0,\rho)=\{w:d_G(w_0,w)\leq\rho\}\). Under a diffeomorphism \(w=h(\theta)\), the coordinate representation of the same geometry uses the pullback metric \[\widetilde G(\theta)=Dh(\theta)^{\mathsf T}G(h(\theta))Dh(\theta).\] Integral or probabilistic neighborhood statistics must additionally use the corresponding pullback or pushforward measure. If instead both coordinate systems independently use the identity metric and Lebesgue measure, then for a fixed center \(\theta_0\) one generally has \[h_\#\bigl(\mathbf 1_{B_I(\theta_0,\rho)}(\vartheta)\,d\vartheta\bigr)\neq \mathbf 1_{B_I(h(\theta_0),\rho)}(w)\,dw.\] Consequently, maxima can change because the neighborhoods differ, while averages and probabilities can also change because the measures differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighborhood sharpness is generally not coordinate-invariant when each parameterization independently uses Euclidean distance and Lebesgue measure. Maxima require invariant neighborhoods, and averages or probabilities additionally require the measure to be transformed.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a differentiable bijection with nonsingular Jacobian on the relevant neighborhoods.
The metric balls and measures appearing in the neighborhood statistic are well defined.
Integral statistics use measurable integrands for which the relevant integrals exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without pullback geometry and the corresponding transformed measure, Euclidean neighborhood statistics generally change under \(h\).

notation.meaning: Metric tensor and its pullback under the reparameterization.
Pushforward of a measure by h.
Metric ball of radius rho centered at w0.
Fixed center and integration variable in the original coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Radius Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed perturbation radius can dominate the local optimization scale or become ineffectively small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(w)=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}w^2\), with \(\lambda>0\), the radius-\(\rho\) robust envelope is \[L_\rho(w)=\max_{|\delta|\leq\rho}L(w+\delta)=\frac{\lambda}{2}(|w|+\rho)^2.\] For \(w\neq0\), its derivative is \(L_\rho'(w)=\lambda(w+\rho\operatorname{sign}(w))\), so the robust correction has magnitude \(\lambda\rho\) even as \(w\to0\). Thus a radius large relative to the local parameter scale dominates the original gradient; conversely, \(\rho\to0\) removes the sharpness-aware correction. A fixed radius cannot be appropriate across arbitrary curvature and scale changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a quadratic loss, an oversized radius dominates the near-optimum gradient, while a vanishing radius eliminates sharpness awareness.
assumptions_latex: The perturbation neighborhood is the one-dimensional Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\rho'(w)-L'(w)=\lambda\rho\operatorname{sign}(w)\) for \(w\neq0\).

notation.meaning: Worst-case loss over a radius-rho neighborhood.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The robust envelope and its derivative are correct for the one-dimensional quadratic, and the failure-boundary kind fits radius misspecification. The final cross-scale interpretation is plausible but lacks an inspectable sharpness-aware radius source.

children.title: Perturbation-Noise Interaction
children.top_down_role: Coupling between neighborhood perturbations and stochastic gradient variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Noise Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noise affects both the constructed perturbation and the gradient evaluated at that random perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g=
abla L(w)+\xi\), \(\widehat g=g/\|g\|_2\), and evaluate an independent unbiased stochastic gradient \(q(w+ho\widehat g)\). If \(L\) is twice continuously differentiable with locally Lipschitz Hessian, then \[\mathbb E[q(w+ho\widehat g)\mid w]=

If the same minibatch constructs and evaluates the perturbation, the required conditional independence fails and additional correlation terms may appear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbation noise enters the expected update through the normalized noisy direction; reusing a minibatch can introduce additional correlation.

The same-minibatch warning is also plausible, but neither claim has an inspectable source, so the specialized stochastic formulation cannot yet be certified.

children.title: Noise–Radius Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes determined by the relative scales of gradient noise and perturbation radius.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise–Radius Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dimensionless noise-to-gradient ratio controls whether a radius-scaled stochastic perturbation tracks its deterministic counterpart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g=
abla L(w)+\xi\), define \(\sigma(w)=\mathbb E[\|\xi\|_2\mid w]\), and suppose \(

knowledge_statements.title: Additional-Pass Compute Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order sharpness-aware updates ordinarily require an extra gradient evaluation at each iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the update \[g_t=\nabla\widehat L_{B_t}(w_t),\qquad \delta_t=\rho\frac{g_t}{\|g_t\|_2},\qquad w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t\nabla\widehat L_{C_t}(w_t+\delta_t).\] Computing the exact displayed update requires two sequential first-order oracle calls per iteration: one at \(w_t\) to construct \(\delta_t\), and one at \(w_t+\delta_t\) to update the parameters. Therefore \(T\) iterations use \(2T\) gradient-oracle calls, compared with \(T\) for a single-gradient baseline. This count excludes approximations that reuse stale gradients, linearize the second evaluation, or otherwise change the update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact sharpness-aware step uses two sequential gradient evaluations, doubling gradient-oracle calls relative to a one-gradient baseline.
assumptions_latex: \(g_t\neq0\) whenever the normalized perturbation is formed.
A gradient at each distinct query point counts as one oracle call.
The exact displayed update is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) exact iterations require \(2T\) sequential gradient-oracle evaluations.

notation.meaning: Minibatches used for perturbation construction and update evaluation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For the exact displayed update, the two sequential query points require two first-order oracle calls per iteration, so the 2T count is correct under the stated oracle model. The complexity-bound kind fits the compute-boundary container, but an authoritative source for the sharpness-aware update and its additional pass is missing.

knowledge_statements.title: Flatness–Generalization Non-Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean parameter-space flatness can change without changing the predictor or its population risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the predictor be \(p_{a,b}(x)=abx\), and suppose both empirical and population risks depend on \((a,b)\) only through \(q=ab\). For every \(c>0\), the parameter pairs \((a,b)\) and \((ca,b/c)\) represent the same predictor and therefore have identical empirical and population risks. For the training loss \(L(a,b)=\tfrac12(ab-1)^2\), every minimizer satisfying \(ab=1\) has \[\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2L(a,b))=a^2+b^2,\] whereas its rescaling has sharpness \[\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2L(ca,b/c))=c^2a^2+\frac{b^2}{c^2}.\] This value can be arbitrarily large while the predictor and its population risk remain unchanged. Hence Euclidean Hessian flatness is not invariant under function-preserving reparameterization and is not equivalent to predictor-level generalization performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Function-preserving parameter scalings can have identical predictors and population risk but arbitrarily different Euclidean Hessian flatness, so this parameter-space flatness measure is not equivalent to generalization performance.
assumptions_latex: Empirical and population risks depend on \((a,b)\) only through \(ab\).
\(a,b\in\mathbb R\) and the displayed minimizers satisfy \(ab=1\).
Flatness is measured by the largest eigenvalue of the Euclidean parameter Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical predictors and population risks can coexist with arbitrarily different values of \(\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2L)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Factor Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular polar factor defined through the compact singular-value decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r>0\) and compact singular-value decomposition \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), where \(U_r^{\mathsf T}U_r=V_r^{\mathsf T}V_r=I_r\) and \(\Sigma_r\succ0\). Its polar factor is \(Q=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), and \(A=QH\) with \(H=V_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}=(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{1/2}\). The factor \(Q\) is a partial isometry satisfying \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=V_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) and \(QQ^{\mathsf T}=U_rU_r^{\mathsf T}\). If \(A\) has full column rank, then \(Q=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar factor preserves the left and right singular subspaces of a matrix while replacing every positive singular value by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) is the partial-isometric factor in \(A=Q(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{1/2}\).

notation.meaning: compact singular-value decomposition of the matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Sign Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular matrix sign interpreted as the partial-isometric polar factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) of rank \(r>0\), define the rectangular matrix-sign map by \(\operatorname{msign}(A)=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), where \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) is a compact singular-value decomposition. Equivalently, using the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse square root, \[\operatorname{msign}(A)=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger/2}=(AA^{\mathsf T})^{\dagger/2}A.\] Thus the map preserves singular vectors, sends every positive singular value to \(1\), and leaves the null spaces unchanged. For a symmetric nonsingular matrix, this agrees with the usual spectral matrix sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rectangular matrix sign is the polar factor: it keeps singular vectors and replaces each nonzero singular value by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{msign}(A)=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger/2}\).

notation.meaning: pseudoinverse of the positive-semidefinite square root of M

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Norm Steepest-Descent Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearized matrix descent over the spectral-norm unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be nonzero with compact singular-value decomposition \(G=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\). Since the nuclear norm is dual to the spectral norm, \[\min_{\lVert D\rVert_2\leq1}\langle G,D\rangle_F=-\lVert G\rVert_* .\] The direction \(D_*=-U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}=-\operatorname{msign}(G)\) attains this minimum because \(\lVert D_*\rVert_2=1\) and \(\langle G,D_*\rangle_F=-\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_r)\). Hence a negative polar-factor update is a steepest first-order descent direction when step size is measured by the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative polar factor minimizes the gradient linearization over a spectral-norm unit ball, attaining the negative nuclear norm of the gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\operatorname{msign}(G)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lVert D\rVert_2\leq1}\langle G,D\rangle_F\), with optimal value \(-\lVert G\rVert_*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Flattening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of polar orthogonalization on the nonzero singular spectrum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r>0\), with positive singular values \(\sigma_1(A),\ldots,\sigma_r(A)\). For \(Q=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), the singular values satisfy \(\sigma_i(Q)=1\) for \(1\leq i\leq r\), while all remaining singular values are zero. Consequently, \(Q\) has the same rank, row space, column space, and left and right singular vectors as \(A\), but its positive singular spectrum is flattened to one. In particular, \(\lVert Q\rVert_2=1\) and \(\lVert Q\rVert_F=\sqrt r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar orthogonalization changes every positive singular value to one while preserving rank and singular subspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_i(U_rV_r^{\mathsf T})=1\) for \(1\leq i\leq r\), and the remaining singular values are \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Parameter Muon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core Muon update for a single matrix-valued parameter block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a differentiable objective \(f\), initialize \(W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(B_{-1}=0\). Choose \(\beta\in[0,1)\), step sizes \(\eta_t>0\), and an orthogonalization map \(\mathcal O\) approximating \(A\mapsto\operatorname{msign}(A)\). At iteration \(t\), compute \(G_t=\nabla_W f(W_t)\), form momentum \(B_t=\beta B_{t-1}+(1-\beta)G_t\), and update \[W_{t+1}=W_t-\eta_t\mathcal O(B_t).\] Stop under a prescribed gradient, loss, or iteration criterion and output the final \(W_t\). Scaling, Nesterov extrapolation, and decoupled weight decay are implementation-level variants of this core scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-parameter Muon forms gradient momentum, approximately replaces its nonzero singular values by one, and applies the resulting matrix update.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable with respect to \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{t+1}=W_t-\eta_t\mathcal O\!\left(\beta B_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\nabla_W f(W_t)\right)\).

notation.meaning: exact or approximate polar orthogonalization map

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent momentum-before-orthogonalization algorithm, but identifying it as the core Matrix-Parameter Muon scheme depends on implementation-specific momentum, scaling, Nesterov, and decay conventions. No source is supplied to establish the claimed family identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum-Before-Orthogonalization Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family characterized by accumulating raw gradients before polar orthogonalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matrix gradients \(G_t\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), initialize \(B_{-1}=0\), choose \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\), step sizes \(\eta_t>0\), and an orthogonalization map \(\mathcal O\). Define \[B_t=\beta_tB_{t-1}+(1-\beta_t)G_t,\qquad D_t=\mathcal O(B_t),\qquad W_{t+1}=W_t-\eta_tD_t.\] Thus temporal averaging occurs in the original gradient space, and singular-value flattening is applied once to the accumulated matrix. The output is the final iterate at a prescribed stopping time. Because \(\mathcal O\) is nonlinear, this ordering generally differs from averaging individually orthogonalized gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family averages raw matrix gradients first and orthogonalizes the accumulated momentum only afterward.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal O\) is an exact or approximate polar map
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_t=\mathcal O\!\left(\beta_tB_{t-1}+(1-\beta_t)G_t\right)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed ordering is internally coherent and fits an algorithm-family leaf, but no source establishes this recurrence as the intended momentum-before-orthogonalization family or fixes its momentum and normalization conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonalization-Before-Momentum Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family characterized by polar orthogonalization of each gradient before momentum accumulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matrix gradients \(G_t\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), initialize \(M_{-1}=0\), choose \(\beta_t\in[0,1)\), step sizes \(\eta_t>0\), and an orthogonalization map \(\mathcal O\). Define \[Q_t=\mathcal O(G_t),\qquad M_t=\beta_tM_{t-1}+(1-\beta_t)Q_t,\qquad W_{t+1}=W_t-\eta_tM_t.\] Hence each gradient undergoes singular-value flattening before temporal averaging. The output is the final iterate at a prescribed stopping time. In general, \(M_t\) need not be a partial isometry, and the update differs from orthogonalizing raw-gradient momentum because \(\mathcal O\) is nonlinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family orthogonalizes each current gradient first and then averages the resulting directions through momentum.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal O\) is an exact or approximate polar map
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_t=\beta_tM_{t-1}+(1-\beta_t)\mathcal O(G_t)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence correctly represents orthogonalization followed by momentum accumulation, and the nonlinearity observation is sound. However, no source establishes this as the intended named optimizer family or verifies the selected normalization convention.

children.title: Hybrid Optimizers for Nonmatrix Parameter Groups

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Optimizers for Nonmatrix Parameter Groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise optimization using Muon only on eligible matrix parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the parameters as \(\theta=(\mathcal W,z)\), where \(\mathcal W=\{W^{(j)}\}\) contains eligible matrix blocks and \(z\) contains all remaining parameters. At iteration \(t\), compute the full gradient. For every \(W^{(j)}\), form matrix momentum \(B_t^{(j)}\), orthogonalize it, and set \[W_{t+1}^{(j)}=W_t^{(j)}-\eta_{j,t}\mathcal O(B_t^{(j)}).\] Independently update \(z_{t+1}=\mathcal A_t(z_t,\nabla_z f(\theta_t))\) with a specified conventional first-order optimizer \(\mathcal A_t\). Apply each parameter exactly once per iteration, stop under a common criterion, and output the combined parameter tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hybrid optimizer applies Muon to eligible matrices and a separately specified first-order rule to biases, gains, embeddings, or other excluded groups.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta=(\mathcal W,z)\) is a disjoint parameter partition
\(f\) is differentiable in every parameter block
\(\mathcal A_t\) is defined for the nonmatrix group
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_{t+1}=\bigl(\{W_t^{(j)}-\eta_{j,t}\mathcal O(B_t^{(j)})\}_j,\mathcal A_t(z_t,\nabla_z f(\theta_t))\bigr)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic blockwise construction fits an algorithm leaf, but the Muon eligibility rules and excluded-group optimizer conventions are implementation dependent. The matrix momentum recurrence is also not fully specified, and no source supports the claimed hybrid practice.

children.title: SVD-Based Orthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalized updates computed through singular-value decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: SVD-Based Orthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact construction of the rectangular polar factor from a compact SVD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a nonzero matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and a numerical rank tolerance \(\tau\geq0\). Compute a singular-value decomposition \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\), retain indices \(I=\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}\), and output \[Q=U_I V_I^{\mathsf T}.\] With \(\tau=0\) in exact arithmetic, \(Q\) is the partial-isometric polar factor of \(A\). With \(\tau>0\), it is the polar factor of the truncated matrix \(A_\tau=U_I\Sigma_I V_I^{\mathsf T}\). No iteration is required beyond the chosen SVD routine; the output convention on discarded singular subspaces is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute an SVD, discard singular values below the chosen tolerance, and multiply the retained left and right singular-vector factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=U_IV_I^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{msign}(A_\tau)\).

children.title: Exact Polar Orthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalized updates computed through an exact polar factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Polar Orthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polar orthogonalization expressed by matrix square roots and pseudoinverses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r>0\). Its exact polar orthogonalization is \[\mathcal P(A)=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger/2}=(AA^{\mathsf T})^{\dagger/2}A.\] If \(A\) has full column rank, the first pseudoinverse can be replaced by an inverse; if it has full row rank, the second can be replaced by an inverse. For a compact singular-value decomposition \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), both formulas equal \(U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\). Thus exact polar orthogonalization is uniquely specified on the row and column spaces even when \(A\) is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact polar orthogonalization can be computed from a matrix square root or pseudoinverse square root and equals the compact-SVD factor product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P(A)=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger/2}=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: pseudoinverse square root of a positive-semidefinite matrix

children.title: SVD–Polar Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Matrix-shape and rank regimes governing agreement between the two constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: SVD–Polar Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-dependent conditions under which SVD and square-root polar formulas coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r>0\). In every rank regime, the pseudoinverse polar formula satisfies \(A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger/2}=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\). The inverse formula \(A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1/2}\) is defined and equivalent exactly when \(r=n\), while \((AA^{\mathsf T})^{-1/2}A\) is defined and equivalent exactly when \(r=m\). If \(r<\min\{m,n\}\), ordinary inverse formulas fail, but compact-SVD and pseudoinverse formulas remain equivalent. A tolerance-truncated SVD instead equals the polar factor of the truncated matrix, not necessarily that of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SVD and pseudoinverse polar formulas agree for every nonzero rank; ordinary inverse formulas require full column or full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{\dagger/2}\), with ordinary inversion valid precisely under the corresponding full-rank condition.

children.title: Initial Matrix Scaling
children.top_down_role: Input rescaling choices used before Newton–Schulz evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Initial Matrix Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling condition for entering the cubic Newton–Schulz polar iteration basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be nonzero and consider the cubic Newton–Schulz iteration \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\). Choose a scalar \(\alpha>0\) and initialize \(X_0=A/\alpha\). A sufficient basin-entry condition is \(0<\sigma_i(X_0)<\sqrt3\) for every positive singular value, equivalently \(\alpha>\lVert A\rVert_2/\sqrt3\). The conservative choice \(\alpha\geq\lVert A\rVert_2\), and hence \(\alpha=\lVert A\rVert_F\), places all positive singular values in \((0,1]\). Zero singular values remain zero throughout the iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the input so every positive singular value lies inside the scalar Newton–Schulz attraction interval; spectral- or Frobenius-norm scaling suffices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\sigma_i(A)/\alpha<\sqrt3\) for every \(\sigma_i(A)>0\) ensures scalar singular-value convergence toward \(1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For the displayed cubic Newton–Schulz variant, the stated positive-singular-value interval and scaling inequality are mathematically consistent. Nevertheless, the basin and convergence claim is nontrivial, no citation is supplied, and a source must confirm that the analyzed iteration is the exact variant intended by the parent container.

children.title: Spectral Normalization
children.top_down_role: Spectral controls used to place matrices in a suitable numerical regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling condition for entering a Newton–Schulz polar-iteration basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be nonzero and let \(\alpha>0\). Spectral normalization sets \(X_0=\alpha M\), commonly with \(\alpha=\|M\|_2^{-1}\) or any computable upper bound satisfying \(\alpha\|M\|_2\le 1\). Then every singular value of \(X_0\) lies in \([0,1]\). If \(M\) has full rank in its smaller dimension, its nonzero singular values lie in \((0,1]\), so the cubic Newton–Schulz polar iteration \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\) is initialized inside its standard convergence basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the matrix so its largest singular value is at most one; full rank then places every active singular value in the standard polar-iteration basin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_i(X_0)=\alpha\sigma_i(M)\in[0,1]\) for every singular value.

notation.meaning: spectral norm, equal to the largest singular value of M

children.title: Basin-Entry Calibration
children.top_down_role: Calibration requirements for entering a stable Newton–Schulz basin.

knowledge_statements.title: Basin-Entry Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact singular-value condition for the cubic polar Newton–Schulz map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have positive nonzero singular values and set \(X_0=\alpha M\). For the cubic map \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\), basin-entry calibration requires \(0<\alpha\sigma_i(M)<\sqrt{3}\) for every nonzero singular value. Equivalently, it suffices that \(0<\alpha<\sqrt{3}/\|M\|_2\). Under exact arithmetic, each active singular value follows \(s_{k+1}=\tfrac12s_k(3-s_k^2)\) and converges to \(1\), while zero singular values remain zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the initial scale so every nonzero singular value lies strictly between zero and square root of three; the scalar iteration then approaches one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_{k,i}\to1\) for every initially nonzero singular value, and \(s_{k,i}=0\) for every initially zero singular value.

notation.meaning: ith singular value propagated by the scalar Newton–Schulz recurrence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically plausible and appropriately placed, but the exact open basin \((0,\sqrt{3})\) and convergence conclusion have no cited source. These are substantive iteration claims requiring an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–Schulz Polynomial Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd polynomial iterations that act independently on singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Newton–Schulz polynomial family for polar orthogonalization is a sequence of odd polynomials \(p_k(s)=s q_k(s^2)\) defining matrix iterates \(X_{k+1}=p_k^{\mathrm{mat}}(X_k):=X_k q_k(X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\). If \(X_0=U\operatorname{diag}(s_{0,i})V^{\mathsf T}\), then \(X_k=U\operatorname{diag}(s_{k,i})V^{\mathsf T}\) with \(s_{k+1,i}=p_k(s_{k,i})\). A family is locally polar-convergent when \(p_k(1)=1\) and its scalar compositions send every initial singular value in a specified basin to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These are odd matrix polynomials preserving singular vectors while applying a scalar polynomial recurrence to each singular value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_{k+1,i}=p_k(s_{k,i})\) with unchanged left and right singular-vector subspaces.

notation.meaning: rectangular matrix polynomial induced by an odd scalar polynomial
polynomial in the squared singular-value argument

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed family definition. Moreover, calling every scalar iterate \(s_{k,i}\) a singular value while retaining fixed singular vectors requires nonnegativity along the scalar trajectories; a general odd polynomial can produce negative values. A source is needed to determine the intended convention and necessary hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Truncated Newton–Schulz Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-depth approximation to the polar factor used as an optimizer update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), a scale \(\alpha>0\), and an iteration budget \(K\in\mathbb{N}_0\), initialize \(X_0=\alpha M\) and compute \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\) for \(k=0,\ldots,K-1\), using the transposed form when it reduces the smaller Gram matrix. Output \(\widehat Q_K=X_K\) without iterating to convergence. If every nonzero singular value of \(X_0\) is in \((0,\sqrt3)\), then \(\widehat Q_K\) has the singular vectors of \(M\), with singular values obtained after \(K\) scalar Newton–Schulz steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a fixed number of Newton–Schulz steps and use the resulting approximate polar factor instead of converging fully.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Return \(\widehat Q_K=X_K\) as a depth-\(K\) polar approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardware-Aware Newton–Schulz Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shape-, precision-, and kernel-aware realization of polynomial polar iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), choose an orientation that forms the smaller Gram matrix: use \(G_k=X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k\) when \(n\le m\), and use \(H_k=X_kX_k^{\mathsf T}\) when \(m<n\). Initialize a basin-calibrated \(X_0=\alpha M\), then evaluate a prescribed odd polynomial either as \(X_{k+1}=X_k q_k(G_k)\) or as \(X_{k+1}=q_k(H_k)X_k\). Matrix multiplications may use reduced precision, but accumulation, scaling, and any residual test must use declared precisions. Stop after the prescribed depth and return \(X_K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the smaller Gram orientation and declared arithmetic precisions, then evaluate the same odd polar polynomial with hardware-efficient matrix multiplications.
assumptions_latex: The coefficient sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_{K-1}\) and arithmetic formats are fixed inputs.
\(X_0\) lies in the declared polynomial basin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is \(X_K\), computed with the algebraically equivalent smaller-Gram orientation in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative Matrix-Sign Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar orthogonalization represented through the sign of a symmetric dilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and form the symmetric dilation \(S=\begin{pmatrix}0&M\\M^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}\). With the scalar convention \(\operatorname{sign}(0)=0\), spectral functional calculus gives \(\operatorname{sign}(S)=\begin{pmatrix}0&UV^{\mathsf T}\\VU^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}\) when \(U\) and \(V\) contain singular vectors associated with the positive singular values. Consequently, polynomial or rational approximations \(r_K(S)\approx\operatorname{sign}(S)\) provide alternative approximations to the partial polar factor through their upper-right block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embed a rectangular matrix in a symmetric block matrix; approximating that matrix's sign yields the partial polar factor in an off-diagonal block.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has compact singular value decomposition \(M=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\operatorname{sign}(S)\bigr]_{12}=UV^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: symmetric dilation of the rectangular matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and block-sign formulation fit the terminal container, but no source with a specific locator supports the symmetric-dilation identity or the approximation claim.

children.title: RMS Calibration
children.top_down_role: Calibration of orthogonalized updates using root-mean-square magnitude.

knowledge_statements.title: RMS Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rescaling an orthogonalized direction to a prescribed entrywise RMS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonzero update block \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and a target root-mean-square magnitude \(r>0\), define \(\operatorname{rms}(D)=\|D\|_F/\sqrt{mn}\). RMS calibration returns \(\widetilde D=(r/\operatorname{rms}(D))D\). If a reference update \(R\ne0\) supplies the target, take \(r=\operatorname{rms}(R)\). The construction preserves the direction of \(D\) in Frobenius geometry and satisfies \(\operatorname{rms}(\widetilde D)=r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply a nonzero update block by one scalar so its entrywise RMS equals a chosen or reference-update RMS.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rms}(\widetilde D)=r\) and \(\widetilde D\in\{cD:c>0\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is internally consistent and fits RMS Calibration, but the optimizer-specific use of entrywise RMS and reference-update matching has no cited evidence or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Layer-Scale Calibration
children.top_down_role: Calibration of update magnitude using layer-level scale references.

knowledge_statements.title: Layer-Scale Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling an update relative to the norm of its parameter layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameter layer \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), a nonzero proposed direction \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and a prescribed relative layer scale \(\rho\ge0\), define \(s_W=\max\{\|W\|_F,\varepsilon\}\) with \(\varepsilon>0\). Layer-scale calibration returns \(\widetilde D=\rho s_W D/\|D\|_F\). Thus \(\|\widetilde D\|_F=\rho s_W\); when \(\|W\|_F\ge\varepsilon\), the update-to-layer norm ratio is exactly \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescale a direction so its Frobenius norm is a prescribed fraction of the parameter layer's stabilized Frobenius norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\widetilde D\|_F=\rho\max\{\|W\|_F,\varepsilon\}\).

children.title: Calibration-Mismatch Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by disagreement between calibration statistics and update geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Calibration-Mismatch Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of RMS matching to imply matching relative layerwise step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let equal-shaped layers have parameters \(W_1,W_2
e0\), and suppose calibrated updates satisfy \(\operatorname{rms}(D_1)=\operatorname{rms}(D_2)=r>0\). Because equal shape implies \(\|D_1\|_F=\|D_2\|_F\), their relative step sizes obey \(\|D_1\|_F/\|W_1\|_F
e\|D_2\|_F/\|W_2\|_F\) whenever \(\|W_1\|_F
e\|W_2\|_F\). Hence RMS calibration and layer-scale calibration coincide only when their target scalars satisfy the corresponding layer-norm relation; otherwise one cannot enforce both with a single common multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal update RMS does not yield equal relative layer steps when the parameter-layer norms differ; one common scaling target cannot satisfy both calibrations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind correctly captures the local phenomenon, and the displayed unequal-ratio conclusion follows from the stated equal-shape assumptions. However, the broader claim about simultaneous RMS and layer-scale calibration lacks a cited source or explicit standard-field rationale.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Optimizer Grafting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transferring reference-optimizer magnitudes onto orthogonalized update directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(t\), let \(D_t\ne0\) be an orthogonalized candidate direction and let \(R_t\) be the update proposed by a reference optimizer for the same parameter block. Choose a positive homogeneous scale functional \(g\), such as the Frobenius norm or entrywise RMS. If \(g(R_t)>0\), output \(\widetilde D_t=g(R_t)D_t/g(D_t)\); otherwise output zero. The grafted update has the direction of \(D_t\) and exactly the reference magnitude \(g(\widetilde D_t)=g(R_t)\). State variables used to construct \(R_t\) are updated according to the reference optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep the orthogonalized direction but rescale it to match a reference optimizer's blockwise magnitude, while maintaining the reference optimizer's state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\widetilde D_t)=g(R_t)\), and nonzero \(\widetilde D_t\) is a positive multiple of \(D_t\).

notation.meaning: reference-optimizer update for the same block

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is internally coherent and fits Reference-Optimizer Grafting, but the grafting rule and reference-state prescription are optimizer-specific claims without supporting evidence.

children.title: Blockwise Orthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalization applied independently to parameter blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Orthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent polar transformation of a fixed partition of an update tensor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a matrix update \(M\) be partitioned into disjoint blocks \(M^{(1)},\ldots,M^{(B)}\) whose assembly operator is \(\mathcal A\). For each nonzero block, compute a partial polar factor \(Q^{(b)}=U_bV_b^{\mathsf T}\) from a compact singular value decomposition \(M^{(b)}=U_b\Sigma_bV_b^{\mathsf T}\), or a declared approximation to it; set \(Q^{(b)}=0\) for a zero block. Return \(Q=\mathcal A(Q^{(1)},\ldots,Q^{(B)})\), followed by any declared block calibration. Orthogonality is guaranteed within each exact block, not generally across block boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition an update, polar-orthogonalize each block independently, reassemble the blocks, and claim orthogonality only within individual blocks.
assumptions_latex: The blocks form a fixed, disjoint partition of \(M\).
Each nonzero block admits the stated compact singular value decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each exact \(Q^{(b)}\) is a partial isometry, while assembled \(Q\) need not be globally orthogonal.

notation.meaning: operator reassembling blocks in their original positions
partial polar factor of block b

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the blockwise terminal container, and the distinction between block partial isometries and global orthogonality is appropriate. No source supports this optimizer variant or its assembly and calibration convention.

children.title: Periodic Orthogonalization
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalization performed only at selected update intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Orthogonalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applying orthogonalization only at a fixed iteration cadence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a cadence \(p\in\mathbb{N}\). At optimizer iteration \(t\), construct a raw or momentum direction \(M_t\). If \(t\equiv0\pmod p\), output \(D_t=\mathcal O(M_t)\), where \(\mathcal O\) is a declared exact or approximate polar-orthogonalization map. Otherwise output \(D_t=M_t\), or a separately declared cached-direction rule. Apply the optimizer's calibration and learning-rate rule to \(D_t\). Only cadence iterations inherit the orthogonality guarantees of \(\mathcal O\); no such guarantee follows for intervening raw directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonalize the update every p iterations and use raw or explicitly cached directions between those iterations; guarantees apply only when the map is invoked.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal O\) is a fixed declared orthogonalization map.
The non-cadence rule is specified in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_t=\mathcal O(M_t)\) exactly when \(t\equiv0\pmod p\) under the raw-direction variant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Periodic Orthogonalization and distinguishes raw from cached intermediate rules, but the cadence convention and associated guarantee have no source. A direct optimizer-variant reference with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Block–Cadence Interaction
children.top_down_role: Resource and fidelity effects arising from combined block selection and update cadence.

knowledge_statements.title: Block–Cadence Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for blockwise polar directions reused over several optimizer steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the square momentum matrix be block diagonal, \(M_t=\operatorname{diag}(M_t^{(1)},\ldots,M_t^{(b)})\), and let \(\mathcal P(A)=UV^{\mathsf T}\) for a compact singular value decomposition \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\). Exact blockwise orthogonalization agrees with global orthogonalization because \[\mathcal P(M_t)=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\mathcal P(M_t^{(1)}),\ldots,\mathcal P(M_t^{(b)})\bigr).\] If a direction computed at cadence time \(\tau\) is reused at time \(t\), it remains the exact blockwise polar direction precisely when \[\mathcal P(M_t^{(i)})=\mathcal P(M_\tau^{(i)})\quad\text{for every active block }i.\] Thus blocking commutes with polar extraction under block diagonality, whereas cadence reuse additionally requires preservation of each active block's polar factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Blockwise and global polar extraction coincide for block-diagonal momentum. Reusing an old direction is exact only while every active block retains the same polar factor.
assumptions_latex: \(M_t\) is square and block diagonal in a fixed partition.
Each polar factor uses the compact singular-value convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P(M_t)=\operatorname{diag}_i\mathcal P(M_t^{(i)})\), and cadence reuse is exact iff \(\mathcal P(M_t^{(i)})=\mathcal P(M_\tau^{(i)})\) for every active block.

notation.meaning: compact polar factor of a matrix

children.title: AdaMuon
children.top_down_role: The named adaptive member of the Muon optimizer family.

knowledge_statements.title: AdaMuon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate matrix-valued AdaMuon formulation; the canonical named-variant specification requires confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given gradients \(G_t\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), choose \(\beta_1,\beta_2\in[0,1)\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\).\) Initialize \(M_0=0\) and \(V_0=0\), then compute \[M_t=\beta_1M_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)G_t,\qquad V_t=\beta_2V_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)(G_t\odot G_t),\] \[Z_t=M_t\oslash(\sqrt{V_t}+\varepsilon),\qquad Q_t=\mathcal P(Z_t),\qquad X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_tQ_t.\] Square roots, addition of \(\varepsilon\), and division are entrywise. The output after \(T\) iterations is \(X_T\); bias corrections may replace \(M_t,V_t\) by their corrected versions before forming \(Z_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This candidate AdaMuon rule applies Adam-style entrywise scaling to momentum, extracts the scaled matrix’s polar factor, and updates parameters along that orthogonalized direction.
assumptions_latex: \(G_t\) and \(X_t\) have a common matrix shape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_t\mathcal P\bigl(M_t\oslash(\sqrt{V_t}+\varepsilon)\bigr)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits an AdaMuon leaf, but no source establishes that the displayed Adam-style entrywise preconditioning followed by polar extraction is the canonical AdaMuon update. Bias correction and update ordering are also left optional. A primary AdaMuon specification with an algorithm/equation locator is required.

children.title: Adaptive Orthogonalized Momentum
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalized-momentum variants with adaptive scaling or state.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Orthogonalized Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General adaptive-preconditioning template followed by matrix polar extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_t\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and choose \(\beta\in[0,1)\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), and positive preconditioning maps \(S_t\).\) Starting from \(M_0=0\), perform \[M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)G_t,\qquad Z_t=S_t(M_t),\qquad Q_t=\mathcal P(Z_t),\] \[X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_tQ_t.\] The adaptive state defining \(S_t\) may depend only on gradients observed through time \(t\). If \(Z_t=0\), set \(Q_t=0\). After \(T\) iterations return \(X_T\). This template separates adaptive magnitude or curvature estimation from the final singular-value normalization imposed by \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive orthogonalized momentum preconditions an exponential gradient average, replaces its nonzero singular values by one, and uses the resulting polar direction for the update.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) maps matrices to matrices of the same shape.
\(S_t\) is determined from information available by iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_t\mathcal P(S_t(M_t))\), with zero direction when \(S_t(M_t)=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is plausible, but positivity of an abstract map S_t is not defined and multiple incompatible adaptive-preconditioning conventions fit the template. A primary source is needed to determine the intended family and sufficient conditions.

children.title: Adaptive-State Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between adaptive statistics and orthogonalized update geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-State Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance condition ensuring adaptive preconditioning respects changes of matrix coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each orthogonal pair \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), transform a matrix state \(Z\) to \(UZV^{\mathsf T}\).\) An adaptive state rule \(\mathcal S\), with induced preconditioner \(S_{\mathcal S}\), is orthogonally compatible when its transformed state satisfies \[S_{\mathcal S'}(UZV^{\mathsf T})=U S_{\mathcal S}(Z)V^{\mathsf T}.\] Under this condition, polar equivariance gives \[\mathcal P\bigl(S_{\mathcal S'}(UZV^{\mathsf T})\bigr)=U\mathcal P\bigl(S_{\mathcal S}(Z)\bigr)V^{\mathsf T}.\] Entrywise second-moment scaling generally fails this condition under non-permutation rotations, while scalar or appropriately spectral scaling satisfies it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive state is compatible when preconditioning commutes with left and right orthogonal coordinate changes; then the orthogonalized direction transforms equivariantly as well.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S'\) is the state obtained by applying the same coordinate change to \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adaptive preconditioning is compatible iff \(S_{\mathcal S'}(UZV^{\mathsf T})=US_{\mathcal S}(Z)V^{\mathsf T}\); compatibility implies equivariance of the polar direction.

children.title: Newton–Muon Variants
children.top_down_role: Muon variants incorporating Newton-like curvature structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–Muon Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract curvature-preconditioned Muon family; named implementations may select different curvature operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G_t\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), choose \(\beta\in[0,1)\), \(\eta_t>0\), and an invertible positive linear curvature approximation \(B_t\) on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).\) Initialize \(M_0=0\) and iterate \[M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)G_t,\qquad B_t Z_t=M_t,\qquad Q_t=\mathcal P(Z_t),\] \[X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_tQ_t.\] A Newton–Muon variant is determined by the construction of \(B_t\), the accuracy used to solve for \(Z_t\), and the approximation used for \(\mathcal P\).\) Return \(X_T\) after \(T\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton–Muon variants solve a curvature-preconditioned momentum equation, polar-normalize the solution, and update along the resulting matrix direction.
assumptions_latex: \(B_t\) is positive and invertible on the parameter block.
The solve for \(Z_t\) is exact unless an explicit residual tolerance is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_t\mathcal P(B_t^{-1}M_t)\).

notation.meaning: curvature approximation acting on matrix directions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithm is the correct role for a named variant family, but no primary source confirms that Newton–Muon means applying an arbitrary positive linear curvature inverse before polar normalization. The defining curvature construction, solve accuracy, and polar approximation must come from a specific named-family source.

children.title: Curvature-Coupled Orthogonalized Momentum
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalized-momentum designs coupled to curvature estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Coupled Orthogonalized Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General positive-curvature coupling applied before orthogonalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, set \(G_t=\nabla f(X_t)\), and choose \(\beta\in[0,1)\).\) Maintain \[M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)G_t.\] Given a self-adjoint positive-definite operator \(B_t\), compute \(Z_t\) satisfying \(B_tZ_t=M_t\), form \(Q_t=\mathcal P(Z_t)\), and select \(\eta_t>0\) such that \(\langle G_t,Q_t\rangle_F>0\) whenever \(G_t\ne0\).\) Update \[X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_tQ_t.\] If the descent test fails, reject the curvature coupling or regularize \(B_t\) before updating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method preconditions momentum with a positive curvature model, polar-normalizes the result, and accepts it only when the resulting direction is descending for the current gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on the iterates’ domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted step has \(X_{t+1}=X_t-\eta_t\mathcal P(B_t^{-1}M_t)\) and \(\langle G_t,\mathcal P(B_t^{-1}M_t)\rangle_F>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the acceptance test and regularization fallback may be a newly proposed safeguard rather than part of the intended frontier method. A primary algorithm source is required to fix the canonical curvature coupling and safeguard behavior.

children.title: Curvature-Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of coupled updates to inaccurate or stale curvature information.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Approximation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of positive curvature can reverse the polar-normalized update direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Positive definiteness of the curvature approximation cannot be discarded. Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\), take \(x>0\), momentum \(M=x\), scalar curvature approximation \(B=-1\), and stepsize \(\eta>0\). With \(BZ=M\), the preconditioned direction is \(Z=-x\), so \(\mathcal P(Z)=-1\). The nominal update and objective change are \[x^+=x-\eta\mathcal P(Z)=x+\eta,\qquad f(x^+)-f(x)=\eta x+\frac{\eta^2}{2}>0.\] Hence an indefinite curvature approximation can produce a strict ascent step even when the curvature equation is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative curvature approximation reverses the preconditioned direction: on a scalar quadratic, the resulting polar-normalized step strictly increases the objective.
assumptions_latex: The scalar polar factor is \(\mathcal P(z)=\operatorname{sign}(z)\) for \(z\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(B=-1\), the update satisfies \(f(x^+)-f(x)=\eta x+\eta^2/2>0\), so descent fails.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Scaled Orthogonalized Momentum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar momentum update clipped to a Frobenius trust radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given momentum \(M_t\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), nominal stepsize \(\eta_t>0\), and trust radius \(\Delta_t>0\), compute \(Q_t=\mathcal P(M_t)\).\) If \(Q_t=0\), set \(S_t=0\); otherwise set \[\alpha_t=\min\left\{\eta_t,\frac{\Delta_t}{\lVert Q_t\rVert_F}\right\},\qquad S_t=-\alpha_tQ_t.\] Update \(X_{t+1}=X_t+S_t\).\) The step is automatically feasible because \(\lVert S_t\rVert_F\le\Delta_t\).\) If \(M_t\) has rank \(r_t>0\), then \(\lVert Q_t\rVert_F=\sqrt{r_t}\), so \(\alpha_t=\min\{\eta_t,\Delta_t/\sqrt{r_t}\}.\) Return the final iterate or stop under a prescribed stationarity test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method clips a polar-normalized momentum step to a Frobenius trust radius; the required scaling depends explicitly on the momentum rank.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) uses the compact polar factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert X_{t+1}-X_t\rVert_F\le\Delta_t\), with scale \(\alpha_t=\min\{\eta_t,\Delta_t/\sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(M_t)}\}\) when \(M_t\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Polar Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex smooth descent bound for exact polar-gradient steps with uniformly bounded gradient rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below by \(f_*\) and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient in Frobenius norm. For \(G_t=\nabla f(X_t)\), suppose \(\operatorname{rank}(G_t)\le r\) and update \[X_{t+1}=X_t-\frac{\lVert G_t\rVert_*}{Lr}\mathcal P(G_t).\] Then \[f(X_{t+1})\le f(X_t)-\frac{\lVert G_t\rVert_*^2}{2Lr}.\] Consequently, after \(T\ge1\) iterations, \[\min_{0\le t<T}\lVert\nabla f(X_t)\rVert_*\le\sqrt{\frac{2Lr\bigl(f(X_0)-f_*\bigr)}{T}}.\] Thus exact polar descent reaches nuclear-norm gradient tolerance \(\varepsilon\) within at most \(2Lr(f(X_0)-f_*)/\varepsilon^2\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth lower-bounded objectives and gradient rank at most r, exact polar-gradient descent attains nuclear-gradient tolerance epsilon in order r divided by epsilon squared iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient in Frobenius norm.
\(\operatorname{rank}(\nabla f(X_t))\le r\) for every generated iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le t<T}\lVert\nabla f(X_t)\rVert_*\le\sqrt{2Lr(f(X_0)-f_*)/T}\).

notation.meaning: compact polar factor of the gradient
uniform upper bound on gradient rank
