knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Newton–Schulz Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent regime characterized by verifiable alignment and norm bounds for an inexact polar direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) satisfy the smoothness and lower-bound assumptions of exact-polar descent, and let \(G_t=\nabla f(X_t)\) have rank at most \(r\).\) Suppose a finite Newton–Schulz computation returns \(\widehat Q_t\) satisfying, for a fixed \(\delta\in[0,1)\), \[\langle G_t,\widehat Q_t\rangle_F\ge(1-\delta)\lVert G_t\rVert_*,\qquad \lVert\widehat Q_t\rVert_F^2\le r.\] With \[X_{t+1}=X_t-\frac{(1-\delta)\lVert G_t\rVert_*}{Lr}\widehat Q_t,\] one has \[\min_{0\le t<T}\lVert G_t\rVert_*\le\sqrt{\frac{2Lr(f(X_0)-f_*)}{(1-\delta)^2T}}.\] Hence inexactness worsens the exact-polar iteration bound by at most \((1-\delta)^{-2}\) whenever both displayed certificates hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton–Schulz polar approximation preserves the exact-polar convergence rate up to an alignment penalty, provided its gradient alignment and Frobenius norm are certified.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is lower bounded and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient in Frobenius norm.
\(\operatorname{rank}(G_t)\le r\), and the two displayed inexactness certificates hold with \(\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{0\le t<T}\lVert G_t\rVert_*\le\sqrt{2Lr(f(X_0)-f_*)/((1-\delta)^2T)}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional descent bound is algebraically plausible, and complexity_bound fits the container. However, no source connects a finite Newton–Schulz iteration count or initialization regime to the two assumed certificates, so the record does not yet characterize a Newton–Schulz convergence regime rather than an abstract inexact-direction bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Sensitive Optimizer Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-dependent comparison between polar and gradient directions under an operator-norm step budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be nonzero with rank \(r\), and compare directions constrained by \(\lVert D\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le1\).\) The polar direction \(D_{\mathrm{pol}}=\mathcal P(G)\) satisfies \[\langle G,D_{\mathrm{pol}}\rangle_F=\lVert G\rVert_*.\] The operator-normalized gradient \(D_{\mathrm{grad}}=G/\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\) satisfies \[\langle G,D_{\mathrm{grad}}\rangle_F=\frac{\lVert G\rVert_F^2}{\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}.\] Their linearized-decrease ratio obeys \[1\le\frac{\lVert G\rVert_*\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lVert G\rVert_F^2}\le r.\] Equality on the left holds for rank one and also when all nonzero singular values are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the same operator-norm budget, the polar direction gives between one and r times the linearized decrease of the operator-normalized raw gradient.
assumptions_latex: Both candidate directions use the same operator-norm budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\le \langle G,D_{\mathrm{pol}}\rangle_F/\langle G,D_{\mathrm{grad}}\rangle_F\le r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Stability Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation stability of full-column-rank polar directions and its singular-value boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\), both have full column rank, and let \(\mathcal P(A)=A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1/2}.\) Their polar factors satisfy the perturbation estimate \[\lVert\mathcal P(A)-\mathcal P(B)\rVert_F\le\frac{2\lVert A-B\rVert_F}{\sigma_{\min}(A)+\sigma_{\min}(B)}.\] Consequently, on any family with \(\sigma_{\min}(A)\ge\gamma>0\), the polar map is \(1/\gamma\)-Lipschitz in Frobenius norm. No uniform constant extends to matrices approaching rank deficiency: for \(A_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\) and \(B_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,-\varepsilon)\), the inputs approach each other while their polar factors remain separated by Frobenius distance \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar directions are Lipschitz stable when the smallest singular value stays positive, but uniform stability fails as matrices approach rank deficiency.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are full-column-rank matrices of the same shape.
The polar factor is the unique column-orthonormal factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polar map is uniformly Lipschitz on sets with \(\sigma_{\min}\ge\gamma>0\), but not uniformly continuous across the rank-deficient boundary.

notation.meaning: smallest singular value of a full-column-rank matrix
uniform spectral gap from rank deficiency

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Singular-Value Underresolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-step Newton–Schulz polar iteration cannot resolve arbitrarily small nonzero singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i)V^{\mathsf T}\) with \(0\leq \sigma_i<\sqrt{3}\), and apply \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\) from \(X_0=M\). Each singular value evolves by \(s_{k+1}=\phi(s_k)\), where \(\phi(s)=\tfrac12s(3-s^2)\). For every finite \(K\), \(\phi^{\circ K}(s)\leq(3/2)^K s\) on \([0,\sqrt3]\). Hence, if \(0<\sigma_i<\varepsilon(2/3)^K\), then the corresponding singular value of \(X_K\) is below \(\varepsilon\), although its limiting polar-factor singular value is \(1\). Thus no fixed iteration count uniformly resolves all nonzero singular directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After finitely many Newton–Schulz steps, sufficiently small nonzero singular values remain arbitrarily small even though their limiting polar-factor values equal one.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a real matrix with singular values in \([0,\sqrt3)\).
The stated Newton–Schulz polar iteration is evaluated in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\sigma_i<\varepsilon(2/3)^K\implies \sigma_i(X_K)<\varepsilon\), so finite \(K\) gives no uniform resolution over nonzero singular values.

notation.meaning: K-fold composition of the scalar Newton–Schulz map

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-step underresolution claim is mathematically plausible for the stated exact-arithmetic cubic iteration and fits a failure-boundary container, but no source is cited. A specific Newton–Schulz polar-iteration source and locator are required to establish the iteration, its scalar singular-direction dynamics, and the optimizer-specific interpretation.

children.title: Newton–Schulz Basin Violation
children.top_down_role: Failure caused by initialization outside a stable iterative regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–Schulz Basin Violation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar singular-value dynamics identify the exact positive basin for the cubic polar iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Newton–Schulz polar update \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\), a singular value \(s_k\geq0\) follows \(s_{k+1}=\tfrac12s_k(3-s_k^2)\). If \(s_0=\sqrt3\), then \(s_1=0\) and the direction is permanently lost. If \(s_0>\sqrt3\), then \(s_1<0\), so the iterate leaves the nonnegative singular-value dynamics used to establish convergence to the polar factor; for \(s_0>\sqrt5\), moreover, \(|s_1|>s_0\). Consequently, scaling that permits a singular value at or beyond \(\sqrt3\) violates the standard positive convergence basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled singular value at least square root of three exits the positive Newton–Schulz basin; equality annihilates that direction, and sufficiently larger values expand.
assumptions_latex: The cubic Newton–Schulz polar update is used in exact arithmetic.
At least one initial singular value satisfies \(s_0\geq\sqrt3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_0=\sqrt3\implies s_1=0\), while \(s_0>\sqrt3\implies s_1<0\); thus the positive polar-convergence basin is violated.

notation.meaning: scalar iterate associated with one singular direction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the record conflates a signed scalar coefficient with a singular value: singular values cannot become negative. For an initial SVD direction, the polynomial coefficient becomes negative when the stated scalar map is applied beyond sqrt(3), while the corresponding singular value is its absolute value. An authoritative source with a precise locator is also needed for the claimed positive convergence basin and its relevance to the optimizer variant.

children.title: Newton–Schulz Scaling Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure caused by unsuitable matrix scaling or normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–Schulz Scaling Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A spectral underestimate can place the scaled matrix outside the Newton–Schulz basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\neq0\) and initialize the polar iteration with \(X_0=M/\widehat L\), where \(\widehat L>0\) is intended to upper-bound \(\|M\|_2\). If \(\widehat L\leq\|M\|_2/\sqrt3\), then \(X_0\) has largest singular value \(s_0\geq\sqrt3\). In particular, choosing \(M=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt3,1)\) and \(\widehat L=1\) yields \(X_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\); the leading direction is annihilated and cannot be recovered by later polynomial iterates. Thus an underestimated scaling denominator can make orthogonalization fail even for a nonsingular diagonal matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Underestimating the spectral norm by a factor of at least square root of three can annihilate a valid singular direction in one Newton–Schulz step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The initialization need not converge to the polar factor; for \(M=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt3,1)\) and \(\widehat L=1\), the first diagonal direction becomes zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal counterexample is internally computable and the counterexample kind is suitable for this scaling-failure leaf, but no source supports the selected Newton–Schulz variant, scaling convention, or optimizer interpretation. A specific source and locator are required before relying on this formulation.

children.title: Basin-Recovery Conditions
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions under which rescaling can restore stable evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Basin-Recovery Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient rescaling conditions restore every nonzero singular direction to the positive basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(L\geq\|M\|_2\), choose \(0<\eta<\sqrt3\), and set \(X_0=\eta M/L\). Then every singular value of \(X_0\) lies in \([0,\eta]\subset[0,\sqrt3)\). Under \(X_{k+1}=\tfrac12X_k(3I-X_k^{\mathsf T}X_k)\), each initially positive singular value converges to \(1\), while each zero singular value remains zero. Therefore \(X_k\) converges, on the support of \(M\), to the partial polar factor \(UV^{\mathsf T}\) for a compact singular-value decomposition \(M=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuine spectral upper bound, combined with a scale strictly below square root of three, restores Newton–Schulz convergence on every nonzero singular direction.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has compact singular-value decomposition \(U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(X_0=\eta M/L\), the iteration converges on \(\operatorname{range}(M)\) to \(UV^{\mathsf T}\), and its null singular directions remain zero.

notation.meaning: certified upper bound on the spectral norm
partial polar factor on the support of M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A recovery condition is the correct role, but the rectangular update is not fully specified: the displayed right-oriented formula uses I_n and is dimensionally valid, yet the record does not distinguish the orientation normally chosen for wide matrices. The meaning of convergence 'on the support' and the asserted partial-polar limit also require a cited convergence result with a precise locator.

children.title: Rectangular-Matrix Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalization issues caused by strongly unequal matrix dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular-Matrix Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular matrices cannot satisfy both row- and column-orthogonality when their dimensions differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\neq n\). If \(m>n\) and \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_n\), then \(QQ^{\mathsf T}\) is a rank-\(n\) projector and cannot equal \(I_m\). If \(m<n\) and \(QQ^{\mathsf T}=I_m\), then \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q\) is a rank-\(m\) projector and cannot equal \(I_n\). Hence a rectangular optimizer block must select column or row orthogonalization according to shape; applying a square-matrix specification to both sides imposes an infeasible target and may distort update magnitude across shapes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsquare matrix cannot have both orthonormal rows and orthonormal columns, so orthogonalization must choose the feasible side according to shape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most one of \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_n\) and \(QQ^{\mathsf T}=I_m\) can hold; the feasible identity is on the smaller-dimensional side.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank obstruction is standard and correctly identifies the rectangular failure boundary. However, the additional prescription that an optimizer must select an orthogonalization side and the claim about update-magnitude distortion are not established by the algebra alone. A matrix-manifold or polar-decomposition source and an optimizer-specific source with precise locators are required.

children.title: Low-Rank Matrix Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Orthogonalization issues caused by deficient or concentrated singular spectra.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Matrix Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank deficiency prevents full orthogonality and makes zero singular directions unrecoverable by polynomial iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r<\min(m,n)\), and let \(X_K=M p_K(M^{\mathsf T}M)\) for any scalar polynomial \(p_K\), as occurs after finitely many right-oriented Newton–Schulz steps. Then \(\ker(M)\subseteq\ker(X_K)\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(X_K)\leq r\). Consequently \(X_K^{\mathsf T}X_K\neq I_n\) whenever \(r<n\). The limiting object can only be a partial isometry supported on the nonzero singular subspaces; no polynomial orthogonalizer without an external rank-completion rule can create orthogonal directions in the null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial orthogonalization preserves a matrix’s null space, so a rank-deficient update cannot become fully orthogonal without an external rank-completion rule.
assumptions_latex: \(X_K=M p_K(M^{\mathsf T}M)\) for a scalar polynomial \(p_K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(M)\subseteq\ker(X_K)\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(X_K)\leq r\); full column orthogonality is impossible when \(r<n\).

notation.meaning: finite-step scalar polynomial induced by the iteration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The null-space and rank conclusions follow for the explicitly assumed polynomial form and fit a failure-boundary container. The claim that all relevant finite Newton–Schulz steps have this form, and the connection to the exact orthogonalized optimizer variant, need an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Shape–Rank Interaction
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes determined jointly by aspect ratio and effective rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Shape–Rank Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shape determines the maximal orthogonalizable rank, while actual rank determines the attainable partial isometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of rank \(r\), let \(M=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) be a compact singular-value decomposition and \(Q=U_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) its partial polar factor. Then \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=V_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) and \(QQ^{\mathsf T}=U_rU_r^{\mathsf T}\), both rank-\(r\) orthogonal projectors. Thus full column orthogonality occurs exactly when \(r=n\leq m\), and full row orthogonality occurs exactly when \(r=m\leq n\). The deficit \(\min(m,n)-r\) counts unsupported directions on the smaller side and separates pure aspect-ratio limitations from additional rank deficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partial polar factor is fully orthogonal on the smaller side exactly at maximal possible rank; any further rank deficit creates unsupported directions.
assumptions_latex: \(M=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) is a compact singular-value decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=V_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\) and \(QQ^{\mathsf T}=U_rU_r^{\mathsf T}\); smaller-side orthogonality holds exactly when \(r=\min(m,n)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partial-polar projector identities and the shape–rank characterization are mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriately classified as a property. Nevertheless, the record supplies no cited polar-decomposition source or inspectable locator, so it cannot pass the evidence requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmatrix Parameter Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix orthogonalization is not invariant to arbitrary reshaping of vector or tensor parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb R^d\) be a parameter gradient and let \(R_1:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{m_1\times n_1}\) and \(R_2:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{m_2\times n_2}\) be norm-preserving reshapes with \(m_jn_j=d\). Define \(T_{R_j}(g)=R_j^{-1}(\operatorname{polar}(R_jg))\). In general \(T_{R_1}(g)\neq T_{R_2}(g)\): for \(g=(2,0,0,1)\), reshaping as \(2\times2\) gives polar output \((1,0,0,1)\), whereas reshaping as \(1\times4\) gives \((2,0,0,1)/\sqrt5\). Thus vectorization alone does not canonically extend a matrix optimizer to nonmatrix parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a matrix polar update to a vector or tensor depends on the chosen reshape, so the extension is not representation invariant.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) preserve Euclidean/Frobenius norm but use different matrix shapes.
\(\operatorname{polar}(M)\) denotes the partial polar factor of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(g,R_1,R_2\) with \(T_{R_1}(g)\neq T_{R_2}(g)\); hence reshaping does not define a canonical nonmatrix update.

notation.meaning: reshape-dependent polar update mapped back to parameter coordinates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example demonstrates reshape dependence for the particular thin partial-polar convention implicitly used, and a failure-boundary role fits the node. For rank-deficient rectangular matrices, however, 'polar(M)' can be ambiguous unless the canonical partial isometry convention is specified explicitly. A source and precise locator are also required for the optimizer-level claim that no canonical nonmatrix extension is available.

children.title: Orthogonalization Compute Boundary
children.top_down_role: Local arithmetic costs associated with matrix orthogonalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonalization Compute Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense finite-step polar orthogonalization adds matrix-multiplication cost proportional to iteration count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and orient each Newton–Schulz step through the smaller Gram matrix: use \(X^{\mathsf T}X\) when \(n\leq m\) and \(XX^{\mathsf T}\) when \(m<n\). One dense step forms a Gram matrix and multiplies it back into \(X\), requiring \(\Theta(mn\min(m,n))\) arithmetic operations and \(\Theta(mn+\min(m,n)^2)\) working storage under classical multiplication. Therefore \(K\) steps require \(\Theta(Kmn\min(m,n))\) arithmetic operations. Orthogonalization is compute-dominated relative to an elementwise \(\Theta(mn)\) update when \(K\min(m,n)\) is not treated as a small constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With classical dense multiplication and smaller-side orientation, K Newton–Schulz steps cost order K times mn times the smaller matrix dimension.
assumptions_latex: Dense classical matrix multiplication is used.
The iteration is oriented through the smaller of \(X^{\mathsf T}X\) and \(XX^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arithmetic cost is \(\Theta(Kmn\min(m,n))\), with per-step storage \(\Theta(mn+\min(m,n)^2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arithmetic count is plausible under classical dense multiplication and smaller-side orientation, and complexity_bound is the correct kind. The storage bound depends on whether temporaries may overwrite or reuse buffers, while the compute-dominated interpretation depends on the implementation and hardware model. A specific algorithmic-complexity source and locator are required.

children.title: Orthogonalization Communication Boundary
children.top_down_role: Distributed data movement and synchronization costs for orthogonalized updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonalization Communication Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed Gram-based orthogonalization requires repeated aggregation of a dense smaller-side Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(n\leq m\) is partitioned by rows over \(P\) workers, so worker \(p\) stores \(X_p\). A right-oriented Newton–Schulz step requires \(G=X^{\mathsf T}X=\sum_{p=1}^P X_p^{\mathsf T}X_p\). Any implementation that explicitly materializes \(G\) identically on all workers must perform a collective reduction of \(n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)\) independent symmetric entries per step. Thus \(K\) steps communicate \(\Theta(Kn^2)\) matrix words per worker up to collective-algorithm factors, plus \(K\) collective synchronizations. The analogous column-partitioned case communicates \(\Theta(Km^2)\) words.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit distributed Gram formation communicates a dense square matrix and synchronizes once per orthogonalization step, even when the parameter matrix itself is sharded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is row-partitioned over \(P\) workers and \(n\leq m\).
Each step explicitly replicates the exact Gram matrix \(X^{\mathsf T}X\).
Communication counts matrix words, excluding collective topology factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each step aggregates \(\Theta(n^2)\) words and incurs one collective synchronization; \(K\) steps incur \(\Theta(Kn^2)\) words and \(K\) synchronizations.

notation.meaning: row shard stored by worker p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gram aggregation identity is correct for row partitioning, and a communication complexity bound fits the leaf. The asserted per-worker Theta(n^2) communication and one synchronization per step depend on the collective algorithm, accounting convention, replication requirement, and latency model; the assumptions do not fully determine that bound. A distributed-algorithms source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Compute–Communication Frontier
children.top_down_role: System regimes where local approximation cost trades against distributed communication.

knowledge_statements.title: Compute–Communication Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto minimality formalizes the resource frontier among admissible orthogonalization implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) be a family of implementations whose output \(Q_A(M)\) satisfies a prescribed orthogonality error \(e(Q_A(M))\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(M\) in a fixed input class. Associate to each \(A\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon\) its worst-case compute cost \(C(A)\) and communication cost \(W(A)\). The compute–communication frontier is
\[\mathcal F_\varepsilon=\{(C(A),W(A)):A\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon,\;\nexists B\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon\text{ with }C(B)\leq C(A),\;W(B)\leq W(A)\text{ and one strict inequality}\}.\]
An implementation outside \(\mathcal F_\varepsilon\) is resource-dominated at accuracy \(\varepsilon\); changing \(\varepsilon\), the sharding model, or the cost model changes the frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed accuracy and deployment model, the frontier contains exactly those orthogonalizers for which neither compute nor communication can improve without worsening the other.
assumptions_latex: All compared implementations satisfy the same uniform error tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
Compute and communication are measured under one fixed arithmetic, sharding, and collective-cost model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_\varepsilon\) is precisely the set of nondominated attainable pairs \((C(A),W(A))\).

notation.meaning: worst-case compute cost of implementation A
worst-case communication cost of implementation A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed set is a definition of the nondominated attainable cost pairs, not merely a representation; content_kind should be definition for this exact frontier leaf. The formalization also needs a source with a precise locator establishing the relevant compute–communication cost and admissibility model.

knowledge_statements.title: Frontier-Variant Evidence Maturity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dominance claim requires uncertainty-aware evidence across the declared workload and resource domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variants \(A_1,\ldots,A_J\) be evaluated on a declared workload set \(\mathcal D\). For each resource or quality metric \(\ell\), let \([L_{j\ell d},U_{j\ell d}]\) be a simultaneous confidence interval for the expected metric of \(A_j\) on \(d\in\mathcal D\), with smaller values preferred. A statistically certified dominance claim \(A_a\preceq A_b\) requires \(U_{a\ell d}\leq L_{b\ell d}\) for every declared metric and workload, with at least one strict inequality. If any required intervals overlap, workloads are omitted, or resource accounting differs between variants, the evidence does not certify frontier dominance and the comparison remains provisional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frontier claim is mature only when simultaneous uncertainty intervals establish dominance across every declared workload and consistently measured metric.
assumptions_latex: All variants use identical workload definitions and resource-accounting conventions.
The intervals are simultaneous at a declared coverage level.
Smaller values are preferred for every transformed metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(U_{a\ell d}\leq L_{b\ell d}\) for all \(\ell,d\), with one strict, certify dominance; otherwise no dominance certificate is issued.

notation.meaning: simultaneous confidence interval for a variant, metric, and workload
variant a weakly dominates variant b under the declared comparison

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A certificate is a plausible role for this evidence-maturity leaf, but simultaneous confidence intervals do not yield an unconditional dominance fact: the separation rule certifies dominance only at the declared joint confidence level and under the sampling and interval-validity assumptions. Moreover, overlapping intervals imply failure of this particular certificate, not evidence of nondominance. A statistical methodology source and a domain-specific frontier-evaluation source with precise locators are required.

knowledge_statements.title: General Convex Stochastic Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected stochastic subgradient rate for nonsmooth convex objectives on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex with minimizer \(x_\star\). Suppose the oracle returns \(g_t\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial F(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|g_t\|^2\mid x_t]\leq G^2\). If \(\|x_1-x_\star\|\leq R\), projected stochastic subgradient descent \(x_{t+1}=\Pi_C(x_t-\eta g_t)\), with \(\eta=R/(G\sqrt{T})\) and \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\), satisfies \[\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq \frac{RG}{\sqrt{T}}.\] Thus achieving expected error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires at most \(\lceil R^2G^2/\varepsilon^2\rceil\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected stochastic subgradient descent attains expected convex suboptimality of order RG divided by the square root of the oracle-call count.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is convex and attains its minimum on \(C\).
The oracle is conditionally unbiased with conditional second moment at most \(G^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq RG/\sqrt{T}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Stochastic Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected rate for stochastic gradient descent on an unconstrained smooth convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L,R,\sigma>0\), let \(T\) be a positive integer, and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer \(x_\star\). Suppose \(\|x_1-x_\star\|\leq R\) and the stochastic gradient \(g_t\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|g_t-\nabla F(x_t)\|^2\mid x_t]\leq\sigma^2\). Set \(\eta=\min\{1/(2L),R/(\sigma\sqrt{T})\}\), iterate \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta g_t\), and define \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\). Then \[\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq \frac{2LR^2}{T}+\frac{2\sigma R}{\sqrt{T}}.\] Consequently, expected error at most \(\varepsilon>0\) is attained using \(O(LR^2/\varepsilon+\sigma^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) stochastic-gradient evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth convex objective, averaged stochastic gradient descent has a deterministic term proportional to LR squared over T and a noise term proportional to sigma R over the square root of T.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is convex, differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and has a minimizer \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq 2LR^2/T+2\sigma R/\sqrt{T}\).

notation.meaning: arithmetic average of the first T iterates

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Stochastic Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected stochastic subgradient rate under strong convexity and bounded oracle second moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex with minimizer \(x_\star\). Suppose \(g_t\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial F(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|g_t\|^2\mid x_t]\leq G^2\). Projected stochastic subgradient descent with \(\eta_t=2/(\mu(t+1))\) and the weighted average \(\bar x_T=2(T(T+1))^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T t x_t\) satisfies \[\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq C\frac{G^2}{\mu T},\] for a universal constant \(C>0\). Hence \(O(G^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\) stochastic-oracle calls suffice for expected error \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity improves the bounded-subgradient stochastic rate from inverse square root to inverse linear dependence on the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\) and attains its minimum.
The oracle is conditionally unbiased with second moment at most \(G^2\).
The iterates use Euclidean projection and \(T\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]=O(G^2/(\mu T))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation-Sensitive Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-step SGD rate when every sampled loss shares a common minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}_\xi[f_\xi(x)]\), where every \(f_\xi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth. Assume there is \(x_\star\) such that \(\nabla f_\xi(x_\star)=0\) almost surely. For independent samples \(\xi_t\), set \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta\nabla f_{\xi_t}(x_t)\), where \(0<\eta<1/(2L)\), and \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\). Then \[\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq \frac{\|x_1-x_\star\|^2}{2\eta(1-2\eta L)T}.\] Thus exact interpolation removes the persistent variance term and yields an expected \(O(1/T)\) objective rate with a constant stepsize.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all sampled losses have the same minimizer, stochastic gradients vanish there and constant-step SGD recovers an expected 1/T convex rate.
assumptions_latex: Each sampled loss is convex and \(L\)-smooth.
\(\nabla f_\xi(x_\star)=0\) almost surely for a common point \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[F(\bar x_T)-F(x_\star)]\leq \|x_1-x_\star\|^2/[2\eta(1-2\eta L)T]\).

notation.meaning: common minimizer of all component losses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interpolation-sensitive complexity bound fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no citation is supplied for the exact constant-step theorem and displayed denominator. Source verification is required before choosing among closely related interpolation and expected-smoothness variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Stationarity Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected squared-gradient rate for stochastic gradient descent on smooth nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and bounded below by \(F_\inf\). Put \(\Delta=F(x_1)-F_\inf\), and suppose \(g_t\) is conditionally unbiased with \(\mathbb{E}[\|g_t-

abla F(x_R)\|^2\leq  rac{2\Delta}{\eta T}+L\eta\sigma^2.\] Optimizing the stepsize gives \(O(L\Delta/T+\sqrt{L\Delta\sigma^2/T})\), so obtaining \(\mathbb{E}\|
abla F(x_R)\|^2\leq\varepsilon^2\) costs \(O(L\Delta/\varepsilon^2+L\Delta\sigma^2/\varepsilon^4)\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconvex SGD reaches small expected squared gradient with a deterministic 1/T term and a noise-driven 1/square-root-T term.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic gradient is conditionally unbiased with variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
The output index is uniform and independent of the oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq2\Delta/(\eta T)+L\eta\sigma^2\).

notation.meaning: initial objective gap to the lower bound
finite lower bound on the objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind and expected-stationarity formulation fit the leaf, and the displayed rate is standard under the stated variance model. No source with a theorem, section, or page locator is supplied, so the exact bound and resulting oracle-complexity statement require evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability oracle complexity for smooth nonconvex stationarity under sub-Gaussian noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(L\)-smooth, bounded below, and let \(\Delta=F(x_1)-\inf_xF(x)\). Assume access to independent unbiased stochastic gradients whose noise is conditionally sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(\sigma^2\). There exist clipped or suitably mini-batched stochastic first-order methods which, for \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), return \(\widehat x\) satisfying \[\mathbb{P}\{\|\nabla F(\widehat x)\|\leq\varepsilon\}\geq1-\delta\] using \[O\!\left(\frac{L\Delta}{\varepsilon^2}+\frac{L\Delta\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^4}\log\frac1\delta\right)\] stochastic-gradient evaluations, with universal constants suppressed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sub-Gaussian noise permits an epsilon-stationary point with confidence 1−delta at a logarithmic confidence overhead in stochastic oracle complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and has finite initial gap \(\Delta\).
Oracle noise is conditionally centered and sub-Gaussian with proxy \(\sigma^2\).
Independent oracle samples and confidence parameter \(\delta\in(0,1)\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}\{\|\nabla F(\widehat x)\|\leq\varepsilon\}\geq1-\delta\) within the displayed oracle complexity.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity bound is appropriate for this leaf, but the existence claim ranges over unspecified clipped or mini-batched methods and does not define whether vector sub-Gaussianity is directional, norm-based, or coordinatewise. A precise source is needed to fix the algorithm, noise model, confidence dependence, and any dimension factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum Nonconvex Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected stationarity rate for stochastic heavy-ball momentum with fixed momentum parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(L\)-smooth and bounded below, with \(\Delta=F(x_1)-\inf_xF(x)\). Suppose \(g_t\) is conditionally unbiased and has conditional variance at most \(\sigma^2\). Fix \(\beta\in[0,1)\), initialize \(m_0=0\), and iterate \(m_t=\beta m_{t-1}+(1-\beta)g_t\), \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta m_t\). For a horizon-dependent \(\eta\leq c(1-\beta)/L\) and a suitable randomized output \(x_R\), \[\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq C_\beta\left(\frac{L\Delta}{T}+\sqrt{\frac{L\Delta\sigma^2}{T}}\right),\] where \(c>0\) is universal and \(C_\beta\) depends only on \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a stable stepsize and fixed momentum, stochastic heavy-ball methods retain the standard nonconvex expected-stationarity order, with momentum-dependent constants.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is \(L\)-smooth, bounded below, and has finite initial gap.
Stochastic gradients are conditionally unbiased with variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
The fixed momentum satisfies \(0\leq\beta<1\) and the stepsize obeys the stated stability scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2=O_\beta(L\Delta/T+\sqrt{L\Delta\sigma^2/T})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind matches the momentum-rate leaf, but no source supports the stated heavy-ball theorem. The randomized-output law, admissible horizon-dependent stepsize, transient terms, and dependence on the momentum parameter must be resolved from a specific theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Method Nonconvex Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: AMSGrad-type stationarity rate under bounded gradients and standard momentum compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, lower bounded, and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Consider AMSGrad with unbiased stochastic gradients bounded coordinatewise almost surely, stepsizes \(\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt{t}\), first-moment parameter \(\beta_1\), second-moment parameter \(\beta_2\), and nondecreasing coordinatewise denominator \(\widehat v_t^{1/2}\). If \(0\leq\beta_1<\sqrt{\beta_2}<1\) and the iterates remain in a bounded domain, then for an output index \(R\) sampled according to the analysis weights, \[\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq C\frac{1+\log T}{\sqrt{T}},\] where \(C\) depends on the smoothness, bounds, initialization, dimension, and algorithmic parameters but not on \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under boundedness and compatible momentum parameters, an AMSGrad-type method attains an expected nonconvex stationarity rate of order log(T)/sqrt(T).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is lower bounded and \(L\)-smooth on the iterate domain.
Stochastic gradients are unbiased and bounded coordinatewise almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_R)\|^2\leq C(1+\log T)/\sqrt T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rate belongs in this leaf and complexity_bound is the correct role, but the AMSGrad recursion and analysis-weighted output distribution are not fully defined. A theorem-level citation is required to establish the logarithmic rate and its dependence on dimension, gradient bounds, denominator initialization, and momentum parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic First-Order Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case lower bound for deterministic first-order minimization of smooth convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every deterministic first-order method, every \(L>0\), \(R>0\), and integer \(T\geq1\), in sufficiently large dimension there exist a convex function \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, a minimizer \(x_\star\), and an initial point satisfying \(\|x_1-x_\star\|\leq R\), such that after \(T\) sequential first-order oracle calls the method's output \(x_T^{\mathrm{out}}\) obeys \[F(x_T^{\mathrm{out}})-F(x_\star)\geq c\frac{LR^2}{(T+1)^2},\] for a universal constant \(c>0\). Therefore every such method requires \(\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) oracle calls to guarantee objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No deterministic sequential first-order method can improve the worst-case 1/T² smooth-convex objective order in sufficiently high dimension.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and receives only sequential first-order oracle answers.
The adversarial objective is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
The dimension is large enough relative to the query horizon \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x_T^{\mathrm{out}})-F(x_\star)\geq cLR^2/(T+1)^2\) for some admissible instance.

notation.meaning: algorithm output after T oracle calls

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound statement has the correct content kind and local subject, but a resisting-oracle result depends on the precise deterministic oracle model, output convention, and dimension threshold. No source is provided for those details or the universal constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Oracle Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax lower bound for convex optimization with a bounded-second-moment stochastic subgradient oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a universal constant \(c>0\) such that, for every integer \(T\geq1\) and every possibly randomized algorithm using at most \(T\) sequential stochastic first-order queries, in sufficiently large dimension there exist a closed convex set \(C\), points in \(C\) within distance \(R\) of a minimizer, a convex objective \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}\), and an unbiased stochastic subgradient oracle with second moment at most \(G^2\), for which the output \(\widehat x_T\) satisfies \[\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat x_T)-\min_{x\in C}F(x)]\geq c\frac{RG}{\sqrt{T}}.\] Hence expected error \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(R^2G^2/\varepsilon^2)\) stochastic-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only unbiased bounded-second-moment subgradients, every sequential method has worst-case expected convex error at least order RG/sqrt(T).
assumptions_latex: The algorithm may randomize and adapt each query to the complete preceding transcript.
Oracle replies are unbiased subgradients with second moment at most \(G^2\).
The dimension may scale with the query horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_{(F,\mathcal O)}\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat x_T)-F_\star]\geq cRG/\sqrt T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A minimax complexity bound fits the stochastic-oracle lower-bound leaf, but the hard-instance class and radius condition are not stated with enough precision to identify a particular theorem. A source must establish the conditional oracle model, feasible-set geometry, algorithm class, dimension requirement, and claimed rate.

children.title: Adaptive-Oracle Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Complexity barriers for methods whose queries adapt to observed oracle information.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Oracle Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lower bound allowing queries to depend on the full stochastic-oracle transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(T\geq1\). An adaptive stochastic first-order algorithm chooses \(x_t\) measurably from its internal randomness and the transcript \((x_s,Y_s)_{s<t}\), where \(\mathbb{E}[Y_t\mid x_t]\in\partial F(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|Y_t\|^2\mid x_t]\leq G^2\). There exists a universal \(c>0\) such that, in sufficiently large dimension, every such algorithm has an admissible convex instance with a minimizer within distance \(R\) of its initial query and \[\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat x_T)-F_\star]\geq c\frac{RG}{\sqrt T}.\] Thus transcript-adaptive query selection alone does not beat the \(\Omega(R^2G^2/\varepsilon^2)\) minimax oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even full adaptation to previous stochastic gradients cannot improve the worst-case nonsmooth convex oracle order beyond inverse square root.
assumptions_latex: Each query is measurable with respect to the algorithm's prior transcript and internal randomness.
Oracle replies are conditionally unbiased subgradients with second moment at most \(G^2\).
The hard-instance dimension is allowed to depend on \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{(F,\mathcal O)}\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat x_T)-F_\star]\geq cRG/\sqrt T\) for every adaptive algorithm.

notation.meaning: stochastic oracle reply at query t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the adaptive-oracle lower-bound leaf, and the transcript-adaptive formulation is locally relevant. No cited theorem establishes that the stated lower bound holds for exactly this measurability, second-moment, output, radius, and dimension model.

children.title: Online-Optimization Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Performance barriers under sequential decision and feedback protocols.

knowledge_statements.title: Online-Optimization Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax regret lower bound for online linear optimization on a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\|x\|_2\leq R\}\). In each round \(t\), an online algorithm selects \(x_t\in C\) before observing a linear loss \(\ell_t(x)=\langle g_t,x\rangle\), where \(\|g_t\|_2\leq G\). For every possibly randomized algorithm and every \(T\geq1\), there exists an obliviously chosen loss sequence such that \[\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(x_t)-\min_{x\in C}\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(x)\right]\geq cRG\sqrt T,\] where \(c>0\) is universal and expectation is over the algorithm's randomness. Hence worst-case average regret cannot decay faster than order \(RG/\sqrt T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online linear optimization over a Euclidean ball has unavoidable worst-case cumulative regret of order RG times the square root of T.
assumptions_latex: The decision is selected before the current loss vector is revealed.
The comparator set is the radius-\(R\) Euclidean ball.
Each linear-loss vector has Euclidean norm at most \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_{g_{1:T}}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Regret}_T]\geq cRG\sqrt T\).

notation.meaning: cumulative loss minus best fixed comparator loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax regret lower bound is an appropriate complexity bound for the online-optimization leaf and the mathematical order is standard. A theorem-level source is nevertheless required for the claim covering randomized algorithms against an oblivious loss sequence, including its dimension convention and universal constant.

children.title: Feedback-Structure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence of lower bounds on feedback timing, adaptivity, or adversarial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Feedback-Structure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between round-adaptive parallel feedback and sequential within-round feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rounds \(t=1,\ldots,T\), a \(K\)-parallel first-order algorithm selects the batch \((x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,K})\) measurably with respect to \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), the sigma-field generated by all oracle responses from rounds preceding \(t\). It then observes \((O(x_{t,1}),\ldots,O(x_{t,K}))\) and enlarges the transcript to \(\mathcal F_t\). The feedback-structure boundary is the prohibition of dependence of \(x_{t,j}\) on responses from the same batch. If such dependence is admitted, the batch may implement up to \(K\) sequential adaptive queries, so a lower bound expressed only in parallel depth \(T\) need not remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel-round lower bounds require every query in a batch to be chosen before any response from that batch is observed; within-batch feedback changes the effective adaptive depth.
assumptions_latex: The oracle response \(O(x)\) contains permitted first-order information at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Same-round adaptivity crosses the model boundary and can invalidate lower bounds depending only on \(T\).

notation.meaning: number of simultaneous queries per round

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and round-adaptive model fit the boundary leaf, and the notation is internally coherent. An inspectable source is required for the precise parallel-oracle model and the claim that same-round adaptivity invalidates depth-only lower bounds.

children.title: Parallel-Oracle Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Complexity barriers under bounded rounds of simultaneous oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Oracle Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax lower bound for synchronous parallel stochastic first-order optimization of smooth convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\|x\|_2\le R\}\). For sufficiently large \(d\), there is a universal constant \(c>0\) such that every algorithm using at most \(T\) adaptive rounds and at most \(K\) simultaneous oracle calls per round has a problem instance with convex, \(L\)-smooth objective \(f\), minimizer \(x^\star\in\mathcal X\), and unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle satisfying \(\mathbb E[O(x)\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E\|O(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\le\sigma^2\), for which its output \(\widehat x\) obeys \[\mathbb E[f(\widehat x)-f(x^\star)]\ge c\left(\frac{LR^2}{(T+1)^2}+\frac{\sigma R}{\sqrt{KT}}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With K parallel queries over T rounds, worst-case error retains an accelerated deterministic term in T and a sampling term governed by the total KT oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth on the Euclidean ball of radius \(R\).
The oracle is unbiased with conditional variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
The dimension is large enough for the resisting-oracle construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[f(\widehat x)-f(x^\star)]\ge c\bigl(LR^2/(T+1)^2+\sigma R/\sqrt{KT}\bigr)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but the exact additive minimax lower bound, its uniformity in K and T, the necessary dimension, and the stochastic-oracle conventions require an authoritative theorem-level source.

children.title: Minibatch Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Complexity barriers governing gains from batched stochastic samples.

knowledge_statements.title: Minibatch Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound when each iteration observes independent gradients at one common query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(t\), let a minibatch algorithm choose \(x_t\) from its preceding transcript and receive \(K\) conditionally independent gradients \(g_{t,1},\ldots,g_{t,K}\) at that same point. Over convex \(L\)-smooth objectives on \(\mathcal X=\{x:\|x\|_2\le R\}\), with \(\mathbb E[g_{t,j}\mid x_t]=\nabla f(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb E\|g_{t,j}-\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\le\sigma^2\), sufficiently high dimension admits a universal \(c>0\) such that after \(T\) iterations some instance satisfies \[\mathbb E[f(\widehat x)-f(x^\star)]\ge c\left(\frac{LR^2}{(T+1)^2}+\frac{\sigma R}{\sqrt{KT}}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minibatch of K independent gradients can reduce the sampling term by square-root averaging, but it cannot remove the deterministic lower bound in the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: All \(K\) samples in iteration \(t\) are conditionally independent and evaluated at \(x_t\).
The objective and oracle satisfy the displayed smoothness, radius, unbiasedness, and variance conditions.
The ambient dimension is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case error is at least order \(LR^2/T^2+\sigma R/\sqrt{KT}\).

notation.meaning: j-th stochastic gradient in minibatch t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minibatch model and complexity-bound kind fit the container. The exact two-term minimax lower bound and the dimension and oracle-independence conditions require a theorem or page-level source before the mathematical claim is reliable.

children.title: Parallel-Speedup Saturation
children.top_down_role: Regimes where additional parallel queries or batch elements cease to improve complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Speedup Saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saturation of batch-size gains when adaptive round complexity becomes dominant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the applicable minimax lower bound after \(T\) rounds with batch size \(K\) is \(c(LR^2/(T+1)^2+\sigma R/\sqrt{KT})\). Increasing \(K\) affects only the stochastic term. In particular, \[\liminf_{K\to\infty}\ \inf_A\sup_{f,O}\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_A)-f(x^\star)]\ge c\frac{LR^2}{(T+1)^2}.\] Consequently, achieving expected error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(T=\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\), regardless of batch size. For fixed \(T\), the onset of saturation occurs when \(\sigma R/\sqrt{KT}\lesssim LR^2/(T+1)^2\); beyond this scale, further parallel sampling cannot improve the lower-bound order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel speedup saturates once sampling error falls below the deterministic round-complexity term; arbitrarily large batches cannot replace adaptive rounds.
assumptions_latex: The parallel-oracle lower bound has deterministic term \(LR^2/(T+1)^2\) and stochastic term \(\sigma R/\sqrt{KT}\).
Queries within each batch are nonadaptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Batch growth cannot reduce the required adaptive depth below \(\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The saturation calculation is algebraically consistent and the failure-boundary kind is appropriate, but every conclusion depends on the unsourced parallel-oracle lower bound being uniform in batch size.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Variance Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform conditional second-moment model for unbiased stochastic first-order oracles in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(f:\mathcal X	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable, and let \(g(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^d\) be a stochastic first-order oracle. The oracle is in the bounded-variance regime with parameter \(\sigma\ge 0\) when, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[\mathbb E[g(x,\xi)\mid x]=
abla f(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\|g(x,\xi)-
abla f(x)\|_2^2\mid x]\le \sigma^2.\] The bound is uniform over \(\mathcal X\) and does not scale with \(\|
abla f(x)\|_2\). If \(g_1(x),\ldots,g_K(x)\) are conditionally independent oracle calls at the same point \(x\), each having conditional mean \(
abla f(x)\) and satisfying the displayed variance bound, then their average \( ar g_K(x)=K^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^K g_j(x)\) satisfies \[\mathbb E[\| ar g_K(x)-
abla f(x)\|_2^2\mid x]\le  rac{\sigma^2}{K}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased Euclidean stochastic-gradient oracle has bounded variance when its conditional mean-square deviation from the true gradient is uniformly bounded. Averaging K conditionally independent calls at the same point divides this variance bound by K.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is equipped with the Euclidean norm.
The \(K\) calls used in the average are conditionally independent given \(x\), share conditional mean \(\nabla f(x)\), and each obey the same variance bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\|\bar g_K(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\mid x]\le \sigma^2/K\).

notation.meaning: average of K conditionally independent oracle calls at x

children.title: Growth-Condition Noise Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic regimes where noise magnitude varies with objective or gradient scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth-Condition Noise Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine growth bound relating oracle variance to local gradient magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x,\xi)\) be an unbiased stochastic gradient for differentiable \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\). An affine growth-condition noise regime is specified by constants \(\sigma_0\ge0\) and \(\rho\ge0\) such that, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[\mathbb E[\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|_*^2\mid x]\le \sigma_0^2+\rho\|\nabla f(x)\|_*^2.\] The additive term permits irreducible noise near stationary points, while the multiplicative term permits variance to grow with the first-order signal. Setting \(\rho=0\) recovers uniform bounded variance; setting \(\sigma_0=0\) gives a purely relative-noise condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A growth-condition oracle has variance bounded by an additive noise floor plus a term proportional to the squared gradient norm.
assumptions_latex: The conditional second moment is finite at every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes \(\rho=0\) and \(\sigma_0=0\) reduce respectively to bounded and purely relative noise.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine variance-growth condition is mathematically coherent and the condition kind fits the leaf. Because both the name and parameterization vary across the literature, a source with a specific definition, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Relative-Noise Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic regimes where error is controlled relative to the underlying signal.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Noise Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely multiplicative stochastic-gradient noise measured relative to the gradient signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal X	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable. An unbiased oracle \(g(x,\xi)\) is in a relative-noise regime with coefficient \(ho\ge0\) if, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[\mathbb E[\|g(x,\xi)-
abla f(x)\|_*^2\mid x]\leho\|
abla f(x)\|_*^2.\] Equivalently, at points with nonzero gradient, the root-mean-square noise-to-signal ratio is at most \(\sqrtho\). At every stationary point \(x\) with \(
abla f(x)=0\), the inequality forces \(g(x,\xi)=0\) almost surely, so this regime contains no additive variance floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative noise scales with gradient magnitude and vanishes almost surely at stationary points; its root-mean-square noise-to-signal ratio is uniformly bounded.
assumptions_latex: The conditional second moment exists for every query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\nabla f(x)=0\), then \(g(x,\xi)=0\) almost surely.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: purely multiplicative specialization of the growth condition

children.title: Noise-Regime Transition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Parameter regions where growth-based or relative-noise characterizations become dominant.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Regime Transition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise crossover between additive and gradient-relative components of affine growth noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the affine growth bound \(V(x)\le\sigma_0^2+ho\|
abla f(x)\|_*^2\), where \(V(x)=\mathbb E[\|g(x,\xi)-
abla f(x)\|_*^2\mid x]\), the pointwise transition boundary is \[ho\|
abla f(x)\|_*^2=\sigma_0^2.\] When \(ho>0\), this is equivalently \(\|
abla f(x)\|_*=\sigma_0/\sqrtho\). Above the boundary, the relative component is at least the additive component; below it, the additive component dominates the variance bound. Thus purely relative-noise reasoning ceases to describe the guaranteed local behavior once the gradient norm falls below this threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The crossover occurs when additive and relative variance terms are equal; below that gradient scale, the additive noise floor controls the available guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition gradient scale is \(\sigma_0/\sqrt\rho\).

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Oracle Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased oracle model with a finite fractional moment but no required finite variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in(1,2)\). An unbiased stochastic first-order oracle \(g(x,\xi)\) is in a \(q\)-moment heavy-tailed regime with scale \(M\ge0\) if, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[\mathbb E[g(x,\xi)\mid x]=\nabla f(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\|g(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\|_*^q\mid x]\le M^q.\] No finite conditional second moment is assumed. Hence the regime includes oracle distributions with infinite variance, and analyses relying on variance reduction by ordinary averaging are not justified without additional tail control or robust gradient aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heavy-tailed oracle has a uniformly bounded moment of order strictly between one and two, while its variance may be infinite.
assumptions_latex: The oracle error has a finite conditional \(q\)-th moment uniformly over \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite conditional variance is not implied by the \(q\)-moment condition.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical finite-q-moment heavy-tailed oracle model
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-q-moment formulation is mathematically sound, correctly does not imply finite variance, and fits the condition leaf. Heavy-tailed oracle definitions vary, so this exact uniform conditional-moment model requires an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased-Oracle Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order oracle whose conditional mean differs controllably from the true gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathcal X	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and define the conditional oracle mean \(m(x)=\mathbb E[g(x,\xi)\mid x]\). The oracle is in an additive-relative biased regime with parameters \(b_0,b_1\ge0\) if, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[\|m(x)-
abla f(x)\|_*\le b_0+b_1\|
abla f(x)\|_*.\] The case \(b_1=0\) gives uniformly bounded additive bias, while \(b_0=0\) gives relative bias. Independent averaging can reduce centered sampling variance but leaves \(m(x)-
abla f(x)\) unchanged, so bias is not removed merely by increasing batch size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biased oracle has a conditional mean separated from the true gradient by an additive-relative bound; minibatch averaging does not remove this systematic error.
assumptions_latex: The conditional mean \(m(x)\) exists for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
The displayed bias bound holds uniformly on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Averaging independent calls preserves the conditional bias \(m(x)-\nabla f(x)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive-relative bias condition is coherent and the averaging conclusion is correct for repeated calls sharing conditional mean m(x). The exact bias parameterization and its regime terminology require an authoritative definition or theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Acceleration Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-order accelerated first-order rate for smooth convex deterministic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(x^\star\) minimize \(f\), and suppose \(\|x_0-x^\star\|_2\le R\). A deterministic accelerated gradient method can generate iterates satisfying \[f(x_T)-f(x^\star)\le \frac{C LR^2}{(T+1)^2}\] for a universal constant \(C\). Conversely, in sufficiently high dimension, every deterministic first-order method has some convex \(L\)-smooth objective for which its error after \(T\) oracle calls is at least \(cLR^2/(T+1)^2\), with universal \(c>0\). Thus the deterministic oracle complexity for error \(\varepsilon\) is \(\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth convex deterministic problems, acceleration achieves and cannot improve upon order one over the squared iteration count in the worst case.
assumptions_latex: The lower bound permits sufficiently large dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal deterministic first-order complexity is \(\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Limited Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossover where stochastic sampling error overtakes accelerated deterministic decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For smooth convex stochastic optimization with radius bound \(R\), smoothness \(L\), and an unbiased oracle of variance at most \(\sigma^2\), the optimal-order error decomposition has the form \[\mathbb E[f(x_T)-f(x^\star)]\asymp \frac{LR^2}{(T+1)^2}+\frac{\sigma R}{\sqrt T}.\] Deterministic acceleration governs only while \(LR^2/(T+1)^2\gtrsim\sigma R/\sqrt T\). Ignoring universal constants and the harmless unit shift, equality occurs at \(T_{\mathrm{cross}}\asymp(LR/\sigma)^{2/3}\). Beyond this boundary, the stochastic term dominates, so faster deterministic decay does not yield a correspondingly accelerated total-error rate unless variance is reduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration controls early error, but after roughly (LR/σ)^(2/3) iterations the stochastic square-root term dominates unless variance is reduced.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic-gradient oracle is unbiased with variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
The stated two-term optimal-order bound applies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The noise-dominance crossover is \(T_{\mathrm{cross}}\asymp(LR/\sigma)^{2/3}\).

notation.meaning: iteration scale where deterministic and stochastic terms balance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crossover calculation is correct conditional on the displayed two-term optimal-order rate, and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. The stochastic acceleration rate and its precise oracle assumptions need an authoritative theorem or page-level source.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum Stability Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-stability region for constant-parameter heavy-ball dynamics on strongly convex quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be symmetric positive definite with \(\operatorname{spec}(H)\subseteq[\mu,L]\), where \(0<\mu\leq L\), and apply \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha Hx_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\). Along an eigenvector of eigenvalue \(\lambda\), the error satisfies \(e_{k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)e_k-\beta e_{k-1}\), with characteristic polynomial \(r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta\). Every mode converges to zero for every initialization exactly when \(|\beta|<1\), \(\alpha\lambda>0\), and \(\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\) for every \(\lambda\in[\mu,L]\). Equivalently, the uniform stability region is \(-1<\beta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<2(1+\beta)/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball iteration is stable on every eigenmode precisely when its momentum magnitude is below one and its step size lies below the stated momentum-dependent spectral limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho<1\) for every modal recurrence if and only if \(-1<\beta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<2(1+\beta)/L\).

notation.meaning: largest modulus of the modal characteristic roots

knowledge_statements.title: False-Acceleration Phenomena
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stable momentum method can be strictly worse than gradient descent, even after reaching the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\), choose \(0<\beta<1\), and initialize \(x_{-1}=x_0\neq0\). Gradient descent with step \(\alpha=1\) gives \(x_1=0\) and remains at the minimizer. The heavy-ball update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\nabla f(x_k)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\) also gives \(x_1=0\), but then \(x_2=-\beta x_0\), so \(f(x_2)=\beta^2f(x_0)>0\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(r^2-\beta r+\beta\), whose roots have modulus \(\sqrt{\beta}<1\). Thus asymptotic stability—and even an initially perfect step—does not imply acceleration relative to gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a scalar quadratic, stable heavy-ball momentum leaves the minimizer after reaching it, while unit-step gradient descent reaches it once and stays there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_2^{\mathrm{HB}})=\beta^2f(x_0)>0=f(x_2^{\mathrm{GD}})\), although the heavy-ball recurrence is asymptotically stable.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frank–Wolfe gap as a computable upper certificate for convex differentiable minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(f\) be convex and differentiable on an open set containing \(C\). For \(x\in C\), define \(g_C(x)=\max_{z\in C}\langle
abla f(x),x-zangle\), and choose \(z_x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\langle
abla f(x),zangle\). If \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}f(z)\), then \(f(x)-f(x^*)\leq\langle
abla f(x),x-x^*angle\leq g_C(x)=\langle
abla f(x),x-z_xangle\). Consequently, \(g_C(x)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(f(x)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function differentiable on a neighborhood of a compact convex feasible set, the Frank–Wolfe gap computed by linear minimization upper-bounds the objective error.

\(f\) is convex and differentiable on an open set containing \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Norm Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained differentiable first-order stationarity measured in the ambient Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable function \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\), a reported point \(x\) and the scalar \(c(x)=\|
abla f(x)\|_2\) form a gradient-norm certificate. The certificate is directly verifiable by evaluating the gradient and its norm. If \(c(x)\leq\varepsilon\), then \(x\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-first-order stationary point in the convention \(\|
abla f(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\); when \(\varepsilon=0\), it satisfies the unconstrained necessary stationarity equation \(
abla f(x)=0\). This certificate makes no objective-suboptimality claim without additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small gradient norm directly certifies approximate first-order stationarity for an unconstrained differentiable objective, but not generally a small objective gap.

The gradient can be evaluated with the accuracy required by the certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Mapping Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite stationarity certificate for a smooth term plus a proper closed convex nonsmooth term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\), where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define \(x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{\eta h}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\) and \(G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}(x-x^+)\). The pair \((x,x^+)\) makes \(\|G_\eta(x)\|_2\) directly computable. Moreover, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\). Thus \(\|G_\eta(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\) is the gradient-mapping certificate of \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity under this residual convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For composite optimization, the norm of one proximal-gradient displacement certifies approximate stationarity and vanishes exactly at first-order stationary points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), and \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\eta>0\), and the proximal point \(x^+\) is evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\eta(x)=0\iff0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial h(x)\), while \(\|G_\eta(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\) certifies the stated residual tolerance.

notation.meaning: proximal operator of the scaled nonsmooth term
one proximal-gradient update from the reported point

children.title: Certificate-Applicability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Problem classes where gradient norms or gradient mappings provide the appropriate stopping signal.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Applicability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary gradient norms are not generally valid constrained-stationarity certificates, while projected-gradient mappings cover active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)=x\) over \(C=[0,\infty)\), equivalently minimizing \(F=f+\iota_C\). The unique minimizer is \(x^*=0\), but \(\|\nabla f(x^*)\|_2=1\), so no tolerance \(\varepsilon<1\) makes the ordinary gradient norm certify this constrained optimum. For every \(\eta>0\), however, \(\operatorname{proj}_C(x^*-\eta\nabla f(x^*))=\operatorname{proj}_C(-\eta)=0\), and hence \(G_\eta(x^*)=0\). Thus a small raw gradient norm is not a generally applicable constrained-stationarity certificate, whereas the projected-gradient mapping correctly detects stationarity in this active-constraint example.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a boundary optimum the raw gradient need not vanish, while a projected-gradient mapping can still vanish and certify constrained stationarity.
assumptions_latex: The gradient mapping uses \(h=\iota_C\) and an arbitrary \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x^*)\|_2=1\) but \(G_\eta(x^*)=0\), so the raw gradient norm is not generally an applicable constrained-stationarity certificate.

notation.meaning: indicator function of the feasible set
projected-gradient mapping for the indicator formulation

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Stationarity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability gradient-norm certificate obtained from an independent validation batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x,\xi_1),\ldots,g(x,\xi_m)\) be conditionally independent validation gradients at a point \(x\), with \(\mathbb E[g(x,\xi_i)\mid x]=
abla f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|g(x,\xi_i)-
abla f(x)\|_2^2\mid x]\leq\sigma^2\). Define \( ar g_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m g(x,\xi_i)\). For any \(0<\delta<1\), Markov's inequality applied to \(\| ar g_m-
abla f(x)\|_2^2\) yields, with conditional probability at least \(1-\delta\), \(\|
abla f(x)\|_2\leq\| ar g_m\|_2+\sigma/\sqrt{m\delta}\). The displayed upper bound is therefore a stochastic stationarity certificate when the variance bound is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent batch mean plus a variance-based confidence radius upper-bounds the true gradient norm with the prescribed probability.
assumptions_latex: The validation gradients are conditionally independent and unbiased given \(x\).
Each validation gradient has conditional mean-square noise at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\!\left(\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\leq\|\bar g_m\|_2+\sigma/\sqrt{m\delta}\mid x\right)\geq1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on gradient-noise second moment

Neither cited locator specifically identifies the independent validation-batch certificate or its high-probability formula, so authoritative source alignment is required before candidate-review acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Certificate Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle-gap interface converting feasible primal and dual outputs into an objective-gap bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty convex sets and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). For a feasible pair \((\hat x,\hat y)\), define \(P(\hat x)=\sup_{y\in Y}L(\hat x,y)\), \(D(\hat y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\hat y)\), and \(\Gamma(\hat x,\hat y)=P(\hat x)-D(\hat y)\). Weak duality gives \(\Gamma(\hat x,\hat y)\geq0\). If a saddle value \(v^*\) exists, then \(P(\hat x)-v^*\leq\Gamma(\hat x,\hat y)\) and \(v^*-D(\hat y)\leq\Gamma(\hat x,\hat y)\). Hence \(\Gamma\leq\varepsilon\) simultaneously certifies primal and dual errors at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal–dual pair exposes a nonnegative saddle gap that simultaneously upper-bounds its primal and dual value errors.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is convex–concave on nonempty convex sets \(X\times Y\).
The displayed supremum and infimum are finite at the reported pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq P(\hat x)-v^*\leq\Gamma(\hat x,\hat y)\) and \(0\leq v^*-D(\hat y)\leq\Gamma(\hat x,\hat y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Online Regret Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hindsight-comparator certificate for finite-horizon online convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty decision set, let \(x_t\in K\) be the decision made before observing \(\ell_t:K\to\mathbb R\), and fix a horizon \(T\). Define \(L_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(x_t)\) and compute a hindsight comparator \(u_T^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(u)\). The pair consisting of the logged decisions and a verifiably optimal comparator certifies static regret \(R_T=L_T-\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(u_T^*)\). Consequently, an evaluated value \(R_T\leq B_T\) certifies average regret at most \(B_T/T\); if \(B_T=o(T)\), the certified average regret converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logged online losses and a certified best fixed hindsight decision determine static regret and its average exactly.
assumptions_latex: Each decision \(x_t\) belongs to the common comparator set \(K\).
All realized loss functions can be evaluated after the horizon.
The hindsight comparator is solved with a verifiable global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T\leq B_T\) certifies \(T^{-1}R_T\leq B_T/T\), and \(B_T=o(T)\) implies \(R_T/T\to0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The static-regret identity and average-regret consequence are mathematically standard, and certificate fits the leaf, but the record supplies no citation. A specific authoritative online-optimization definition or theorem locator is required, particularly for the proposed comparator-optimality certificate interface.
