children.title: Optimizer-State Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Logical decomposition of optimizer state across parameter or state dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract coordinate partition of persistent optimizer state across distributed owners.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the persistent optimizer state be \(s=(s_j)_{j\in I}\), indexed by a finite coordinate set \(I\), and let \(W\) be a finite set of workers. An optimizer-state partition is a family \((I_w)_{w\in W}\) satisfying \(I=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}I_w\), together with ownership maps assigning worker \(w\) the substate \(s|_{I_w}\). Each state coordinate has exactly one primary owner, although temporary communicated copies may exist. A distributed optimizer update respects the partition when every updated coordinate \(s_j^+\) is computed by its owner from the required parameter, gradient, and prior-state data, after which the global state is the disjoint assembly \(s^+=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}s^+|_{I_w}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizer-state partitioning assigns every persistent state coordinate to exactly one primary worker and reconstructs the global update from disjoint owned substates.
assumptions_latex: Every persistent state coordinate has exactly one primary owner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}I_w\) and \(s^+=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}s^+|_{I_w}\).

notation.meaning: coordinates primarily owned by worker w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract partition formalization is coherent and definition is the appropriate content kind, but no source supports the exact ownership, temporary-copy, or owner-computed-update conventions. These conventions are system-dependent and require an authoritative distributed optimizer-state locator.

children.title: Optimizer-State Sharding
children.top_down_role: Physical distribution of optimizer-state fragments across workers or devices.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Sharding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonreplicated distributed storage of optimizer-state partitions, optionally balanced across workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an optimizer-state partition \(I=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}I_w\), a sharded placement stores each persistent substate \(s|_{I_w}\) at its primary owner and does not persist a complete copy of \(s\) at every worker. If coordinate \(j\) requires \(b_j\) storage units, the persistent optimizer-state load of worker \(w\) is \(M_w=\sum_{j\in I_w}b_j\). The sharding is \(\rho\)-balanced when \(\max_{w\in W}M_w\leq\rho(\sum_{j\in I}b_j)/|W|\), where \(\rho\geq1\). Sharding concerns physical storage and communication of a partition; the coordinate partition alone does not determine whether state is replicated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharding physically stores disjoint optimizer-state pieces across workers without full persistent replication; a balance factor quantifies the largest worker load.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No worker is required to persist all of \(s\), and \(\rho\)-balance means \(\max_w M_w\leq\rho(\sum_jb_j)/|W|\).

notation.meaning: persistent optimizer-state memory on worker w
storage size of state coordinate j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between coordinate partitioning and nonreplicated physical placement is coherent, and definition fits the sharding leaf. No source supports the exact persistence convention or the introduced rho-balance definition, so the record requires a specific distributed optimizer-state sharding reference.

children.title: State-Placement Topology
children.top_down_role: Placement choices linking state layout to device and network topology.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Placement Topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation of optimizer-state ownership and the communication paths required by updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a distributed platform by a directed communication graph \(G=(W,E)\), an optimizer-state partition \((I_w)_{w\in W}\), and a placement map \(p:I\to W\) satisfying \(p(j)=w\) exactly when \(j\in I_w\). For each state coordinate \(j\), let \(R_j\subseteq W\) be the workers producing or consuming data required for its update. The placement is communication-feasible when, for every \(u\in R_j\), the graph contains a directed path from \(u\) to \(p(j)\) for required inputs and a directed path from \(p(j)\) to every required consumer. Thus \((G,p,(R_j)_{j\in I})\) specifies both state location and update-data reachability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A communication graph, ownership map, and per-coordinate producer–consumer sets jointly represent where optimizer state lives and whether update data can reach it.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(W,E)\) is the directed worker communication graph.
Each \(R_j\) lists the workers requiring communication for coordinate \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The topology is feasible exactly when every required producer-to-owner and owner-to-consumer directed path exists.

notation.meaning: workers participating in coordinate j's update dataflow

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the appropriate kind for the graph-based state-placement model, and its variables are introduced consistently. The producer/consumer set and bidirectional reachability interface is a proposed formalization with no cited support, so it cannot be accepted without an inspectable distributed-systems or optimizer-state placement source.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Offloading
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational semantics for moving inactive optimizer state to slower storage while preserving the logical first-order update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the optimizer state at step \(t\) be \(S_t=(x_t,u_t)\), where \(x_t\) is the parameter vector and \(u_t\) contains auxiliary accumulators. Choose encoding and decoding maps \(E\) and \(D\), and a residency policy \(R_t\). After completing step \(t\), store \(E(u_t)\) on the offload device whenever \(R_t=0\). Before step \(t+1\), retrieve and decode it, requiring \(D(E(u_t))=u_t\) under the declared numerical equivalence. Compute \(S_{t+1}=\Phi(S_t,g_t)\) only after all required components are resident; otherwise the update is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Offloading stores auxiliary optimizer state remotely and restores it before use, with decoding required to preserve the state under a declared numerical equivalence.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t=(x_t,u_t)\) is sufficient to determine the next update together with \(g_t\).
\(E\) and \(D\) are defined on every offloaded state component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(E(u_t))\equiv u_t\) and \(S_{t+1}=\Phi(S_t,g_t)\) uses the restored state.

notation.meaning: Complete logical optimizer state at step t.
Offload encoding and restoration decoding maps.
Residency indicator or policy at step t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the operational offloading leaf, but no citation supports the protocol. The domains of E and D, the type of R_t, and the declared numerical equivalence are not defined precisely enough to assess the exact-restoration requirement.

children.title: Optimizer-State Checkpointing
children.top_down_role: Persistence of optimizer state for recovery, resumption, or archival use.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Checkpointing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A restart-complete representation of parameters, optimizer auxiliaries, progress variables, and serialization metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimizer transition \(S_{t+1}=\Phi(S_t,g_t;h_t)\), a restart-complete checkpoint at step \(t\) is a serialized tuple \(C_t=(V,E(S_t),h_t,r_t,m_t)\). Here \(V\) identifies the schema, \(h_t\) contains update hyperparameters and schedules, \(r_t\) contains random-generator state needed for reproducibility, and \(m_t\) describes tensor names, shapes, dtypes, and ordering. A loader \(D_V\) is valid when \(D_V(C_t)=(S_t,h_t,r_t)\) under the checkpoint’s declared equivalence and when continuation applies \(\Phi\) from step \(t\), not from an earlier or partially restored state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restart-complete checkpoint serializes all state and metadata needed to reconstruct the optimizer and continue from the recorded step.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) contains every persistent variable read by a subsequent optimizer update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_V(C_t)\equiv(S_t,h_t,r_t)\), so continuation begins from the recorded optimizer state.

notation.meaning: Serialized checkpoint recorded at step t.
Loader associated with schema version V.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind for a checkpoint payload, but the asserted restart-complete field set is implementation-dependent and unsupported. The transition uses g_t to form S_{t+1}, while continuation is described as starting from step t, leaving the checkpoint timing convention ambiguous.

children.title: Optimizer-State Migration
children.top_down_role: Transfer of optimizer state across devices, layouts, or training configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Migration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of a live optimizer state between implementations, devices, or distributed placements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let source implementation \(A\) hold optimizer state \(S_t^A\). Quiesce updates after step \(t\), serialize \(C_t=E_A(S_t^A)\), transfer \(C_t\), validate its metadata and integrity, and construct the target state \(S_t^B=D_B(M(C_t))\), where \(M\) is any required schema conversion. Resume exactly once at step \(t+1\). Migration is semantics-preserving for an admissible gradient sequence when the source and target continuations satisfy \(\Phi_B(S_t^B,g_t)\equiv T(\Phi_A(S_t^A,g_t))\), where \(T\) is the declared state correspondence and equivalence includes the permitted rounding tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migration quiesces updates, transfers and converts a checkpoint, validates it, and resumes once only when target updates correspond to source updates.
assumptions_latex: \(E_A\), \(M\), and \(D_B\) are defined for the migrated state schema.
No optimizer update overlaps the migration cut at step \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_t^B\equiv T(S_t^A)\) and target continuation preserves the declared update semantics.

notation.meaning: Semantic correspondence between source and target states.
Source and target optimizer transition maps.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the migration leaf, but no source supports this protocol or equivalence criterion. “Admissible gradient sequence” is undefined, and the displayed first target transition uses g_t even though the procedure says to resume at step t+1.

children.title: Checkpoint Compatibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits involving optimizer versions, tensor layouts, precision, or distributed topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Checkpoint Compatibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary loading and continuation conditions across checkpoint and runtime schemas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A checkpoint \(C\) is compatible with runtime \(B\) precisely within the declared boundary \(\mathcal K_B\) consisting of checkpoints for which: the schema version is accepted or has a total migration map; every required state key has a unique target; tensor shapes and parameter identities agree; stored dtypes admit the declared conversion; hyperparameters and step counters have defined semantics; and all mandatory invariants validate. Formally, \(C\in\mathcal K_B\) only if decoding produces a complete state \(D_B(C)=S^B\) and the first resumed transition \(\Phi_B(S^B,g)\) is defined for every admissible next gradient \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatibility ends wherever schema, identity, shape, dtype, counter, hyperparameter, or invariant mismatches prevent complete decoding and a defined resumed update.
assumptions_latex: Runtime \(B\) publishes its required state fields, conversions, and validation invariants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\in\mathcal K_B\) if and only if complete decoding and the declared resumed transition are defined.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits the compatibility-boundary leaf, but the runtime-specific checklist has no cited specification. The statement initially gives only necessary conditions and then concludes an if-and-only-if characterization, so sufficiency cannot be assessed without a complete runtime contract.

children.title: Migrated-State Integrity
children.top_down_role: Preservation of optimizer-state semantics during relocation or format conversion.

knowledge_statements.title: Migrated-State Integrity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate that transferred optimizer bytes are authentic, complete, and structurally valid before resumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be the source checkpoint and \(C'\) the received checkpoint. An integrity certificate is \(\pi=(d,n,V,q)\), where \(d=H(C)\) is a collision-resistant digest, \(n\) is the expected byte count, \(V\) is the schema version, and \(q\) is a manifest of required tensors with shapes and dtypes. Verification accepts only when \(H(C')=d\), the byte count equals \(n\), schema \(V\) is supported, every manifest entry occurs exactly once with matching metadata, and deserialization satisfies all finite-value and structural invariants. Acceptance certifies transfer and structural integrity, but not semantic equivalence of different optimizer implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A digest, size, schema, and tensor manifest can certify transfer completeness and structural validity, but not cross-implementation semantic equivalence.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is collision resistant for the threat model.
The manifest \(q\) enumerates every state component required for resumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful verification certifies \(C'=C\) up to the digest guarantee and validates the declared checkpoint structure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct role for this leaf, but the proposed certificate and threat model lack a security source. A bare collision-resistant digest establishes neither authenticity nor trusted provenance, and mandatory finite-value validation is optimizer- and policy-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Precision Optimizer States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical optimizer state whose components are intentionally represented in different floating-point formats.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-precision optimizer state is a tuple \(S_t=(x_t^{(p)},\bar x_t^{(q)},u_{1,t}^{(r_1)},\ldots,u_{k,t}^{(r_k)})\) whose components use at least two distinct numerical formats. The working parameters \(x_t^{(p)}\) may be used by forward and backward kernels, while the master parameters \(\bar x_t^{(q)}\) and accumulators \(u_{i,t}^{(r_i)}\) are updated in their declared formats. Each optimizer transition must specify casts and rounding explicitly: compute \((\bar x_{t+1}^{(q)},u_{t+1})=\Phi_q(\bar x_t^{(q)},u_t,C_q(g_t))\), then synchronize \(x_{t+1}^{(p)}=C_p(\bar x_{t+1}^{(q)})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed-precision state stores optimizer components in multiple formats and makes every cast, update format, and parameter synchronization part of the transition.
assumptions_latex: Every format has a specified rounding rule and representable range.
The optimizer identifies which state copy is authoritative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state transition and synchronization casts determine \(S_{t+1}\) unambiguously.

notation.meaning: Numerical formats assigned to state components.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the topic, but the first sentence defines mixed-format state generally while the prescribed transition requires a higher-precision master-parameter architecture that is not universal. An authoritative mixed-precision source is needed to select and scope the intended variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Scaling Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic cancellation required between scaled backpropagation and optimizer-state updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a loss and let a positive scale \(s_t\) produce the computed gradient \(\tilde g_t=\nabla(s_tL)(x_t)=s_tg_t\). For an optimizer whose intended transition is \(S_{t+1}=\Phi(S_t,g_t)\), loss scaling is update-neutral only when the optimizer receives \(g_t=\tilde g_t/s_t\) before clipping, regularization, moment accumulation, or parameter updating, unless those operations are explicitly transformed to commute with scaling. If \(\tilde g_t\) is nonfinite, the step and all associated optimizer-state mutations must be rejected before increasing the step counter; otherwise contaminated accumulators may persist after the scale changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loss scaling preserves an optimizer update only when gradients are unscaled before non-scale-invariant operations, and rejected nonfinite steps must not mutate persistent state.
assumptions_latex: \(s_t>0\) is known when the scaled gradient is consumed.
\(\Phi\) denotes the update defined for the unscaled gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Using \(\tilde g_t/s_t=g_t\) yields the intended transition whenever all intervening operations respect the declared scaling transformation.

notation.meaning: Gradient obtained from the scaled loss.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property fits the interaction leaf, but the universal requirement to unscale before regularization is not reliable without distinguishing coupled L2 regularization from decoupled weight decay and other transformed operations. The rejected-step mutation and counter policy is framework-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Optimizer Accumulator Precision
children.top_down_role: Precision choices for accumulated optimizer statistics, including effects on retained numerical information.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer Accumulator Precision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability and rounding requirements for persistent sums, moments, and preconditioner statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a persistent accumulator updated by \(a_{t+1}=Q_r(\rho a_t+\psi(g_t))\), where \(Q_r\) rounds into format \(r\), \(0\leq\rho\leq1\), and \(\psi\) is the accumulated statistic. Format \(r\) is adequate on a horizon \(0\leq t\leq T\) only if every exact intermediate \(z_t=\rho a_t+\psi(g_t)\) lies within its finite range and the rounding error satisfies \(|Q_r(z_t)-z_t|\leq\varepsilon_t\) for the prescribed error budget. If nonzero \(\psi(g_t)\) repeatedly rounds away relative to \(\rho a_t\), the stored state stagnates and no longer represents the intended recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulator precision is adequate only when intermediates remain representable and rounding stays within budget; repeatedly lost increments cause state stagnation.
assumptions_latex: \(a_0\) and all \(g_t\) for \(t\leq T\) lie in the declared input domain.
\(Q_r\) has a specified overflow and rounding policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Range safety and \(|Q_r(z_t)-z_t|\leq\varepsilon_t\) are required for the declared finite-precision recurrence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is plausible for this precision leaf, but the stated range and per-step error inequalities are merely imposed checks, not a sourced characterization of adequate accumulator precision. The prescribed error budget and its relationship to accumulated recurrence error are undefined.

children.title: Matrix-Kernel Arithmetic Precision
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic formats used by matrix-oriented optimizer kernels across supported execution backends.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Kernel Arithmetic Precision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit model separating operand, product, accumulation, and output formats of matrix kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-precision matrix kernel for \(Y=AB+C\) is represented by four formats \((p_A,p_B,p_{	imes},p_{m acc},p_Y)\) and the recurrence \(s_{ij}^{(0)}=C_{ij}\), \(s_{ij}^{(k)}=Q_{p_{m acc}}(s_{ij}^{(k-1)}+Q_{p_{\times}}(A_{ik}B_{kj}))\), followed by \(Y_{ij}=Q_{p_Y}(s_{ij}^{(n)})\). Operand loads are first rounded to \(p_A\) and \(p_B\). Thus an advertised input dtype does not determine arithmetic precision: product and accumulator formats, contraction order, subnormal handling, and final conversion jointly define the numerical kernel consumed by the optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-kernel precision is determined separately by operand, product, accumulation, ordering, and output formats, not merely by the input dtype.
assumptions_latex: Each \(Q_p\) has a specified rounding, overflow, and subnormal policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rounded recurrence defines the kernel’s arithmetic result \(Y\).

notation.meaning: Rounding or conversion into format p.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the arithmetic-precision leaf, but the text says “four formats” while listing five. It also says operand loads are rounded to p_A and p_B without including those conversions in the recurrence, and the simple multiply-then-add model does not cover fused or backend-specific contraction semantics without qualification and sources.

children.title: Cross-Kernel Precision Transitions
children.top_down_role: Casting boundaries encountered as optimizer data moves between accumulation, matrix processing, storage, or update execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Kernel Precision Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed conversion protocol for tensors passed between kernels with different arithmetic contracts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let kernel \(K_i\) output a tensor \(y_i\) in format \(p_i\), and let \(K_{i+1}\) require format \(q_i\). A cross-kernel transition applies an explicit conversion \(z_i=C_{p_i\to q_i}(y_i)\), records whether the conversion rounds, saturates, flushes subnormals, or rejects nonfinite values, and supplies \(z_i\) to \(K_{i+1}\). If a higher-precision logical value must survive a lower-precision kernel, it must be retained separately rather than reconstructed from \(z_i\). Correct execution requires every edge in the kernel graph to have exactly one declared conversion and forbids an implicit reinterpretation of the stored bit pattern as another numerical format.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every tensor edge between kernels needs one explicit conversion contract; precision discarded at an edge cannot later be reconstructed from the converted tensor.
assumptions_latex: Each kernel publishes its input and output formats.
Conversion behavior is defined for finite, subnormal, infinite, and undefined values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_i=C_{p_i\to q_i}(y_i)\) is the unique value consumed across the kernel boundary.

notation.meaning: Kernel i in an execution graph.
Declared conversion from format p to format q.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes an interface condition or representation more than an algorithm, so the selected kind is questionable for this leaf. No system specification supports the exactly-one-conversion rule, and “undefined values” is not a defined numerical category alongside finite values, subnormals, and infinities.

children.title: Precision-Mismatch Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure regimes caused by incompatible numerical ranges or accuracy levels across optimizer components.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Mismatch Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete thresholds at which a lower-precision state update overflows, underflows, or loses its increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a binary floating-point format have largest finite value \(M\), smallest positive representable value \(m\), and unit roundoff \(u\). For the stored update \(a^+=Q(a+\delta)\), three failure boundaries are immediate: if \(|a+\delta|>M\), finite representation fails by overflow; if \(0<|a+\delta|<m\) and subnormals are unavailable or flushed, the result becomes zero; and under round-to-nearest, if \(|\delta|<u|a|\) away from binade boundaries, the increment may satisfy \(Q(a+\delta)=a\). Consequently, using a lower-precision accumulator than the update’s scale requires can create nonfinite state, erase small state, or freeze adaptation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A precision mismatch fails when updates exceed range, fall below the minimum retained magnitude, or are too small to change the stored accumulator.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) uses binary floating-point rounding with declared subnormal behavior.
\(a\) and \(\delta\) are exact inputs to the analyzed rounding operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Overflow, underflow-to-zero, or \(Q(a+\delta)=a\) occurs at the corresponding displayed boundary.

notation.meaning: Largest finite and smallest retained positive magnitudes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure-boundary is the correct kind, but the stagnation threshold |δ|<u|a| is only a rough sufficient regime and is not the exact local half-ulp boundary; cancellation, sign, and binade position matter. The meaning of m also shifts between smallest representable and smallest retained positive value, so authoritative floating-point sourcing and corrected qualifications are required.

children.title: Overflow Prevention
children.top_down_role: Range-management safeguards that prevent optimizer values from exceeding the active numerical format.

knowledge_statements.title: Overflow Prevention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient range condition for keeping scaled gradients and optimizer intermediates finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a floating-point format with largest finite magnitude \(M_F\), and let \(z_{j,t}(s_t)\) denote every intermediate produced at step \(t\) when loss scale \(s_t>0\) is used. A sufficient overflow-prevention condition is \(\max_j |z_{j,t}(s_t)|\leq M_F/\gamma\) for a safety factor \(\gamma>1\), together with pre-operation range checks for products, squares, reductions, and casts. If the condition fails or any intermediate is nonfinite, reject the update without mutating persistent optimizer state and choose a smaller scale or a wider format before retrying. Clipping only after an overflowing operation does not prevent that overflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prevent overflow by bounding every intermediate before it is formed; reject nonfinite attempts without state mutation and retry with smaller scaling or wider precision.
assumptions_latex: All relevant kernel intermediates are included among \(z_{j,t}\).
The format’s overflow and nonfinite propagation rules are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_j|z_{j,t}(s_t)|\leq M_F/\gamma\) keeps the enumerated intermediates within the finite range.

notation.meaning: Largest finite magnitude in format F.
Loss scale used at step t.
Range safety factor greater than one.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits the overflow-prevention leaf, but bounding every already-produced intermediate does not itself provide executable pre-operation conditions ensuring those values can be formed without overflow. The required product, square, reduction, and cast bounds and the no-mutation retry policy are backend-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Underflow Preservation
children.top_down_role: Safeguards for retaining small gradients, moments, corrections, or update contributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Underflow Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-precision safeguard preserving small optimizer signals before parameter updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be a gradient, let \(s_t>0\) be a scaling factor, and let \(Q\) denote rounding into a finite format whose smallest positive representable magnitude is \(u_{\min}\). Underflow preservation requires scaling before quantization and unscaling after accumulation: \(\widehat g_t=s_t^{-1}Q(s_tg_t)\). For every coordinate satisfying \(|s_tg_{t,i}|\ge u_{\min}\) and lying below the overflow threshold, \(\widehat g_{t,i}\neq0\). The scaling policy must therefore keep informative coordinates inside the representable interval while all optimizer-state accumulation and the final update use the unscaled quantity \(\widehat g_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale gradients before low-precision rounding and unscale afterward so informative small coordinates remain representable without causing overflow.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) rounds into a finite numerical format.
Scaled coordinates considered in the conclusion do not overflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|s_tg_{t,i}|\ge u_{\min}\Rightarrow \widehat g_{t,i}=s_t^{-1}Q(s_tg_{t,i})\neq0\).

notation.meaning: Smallest positive magnitude representable in the working format.
Rounding or quantization map into the working format.
Positive dynamic scaling factor at iteration t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the Underflow Preservation leaf, but the nonzero-rounding implication depends on the precise rounding rule and representable-number convention. The prescribed placement of scaling, accumulation, and unscaling is also a deployment design requiring an authoritative mixed-precision source.

children.title: Nonfinite-State Detection
children.top_down_role: Detection coverage for invalid values arising in gradients, optimizer states, matrix intermediates, or parameter updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonfinite-State Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-level certificate for detecting NaN or infinite optimizer state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the deployed optimizer state at iteration \(t\) be \(z_t=(x_t,g_t,m_t,v_t,\eta_t)\), with absent components omitted. Define the finite-state predicate \(F(z_t)=\bigwedge_{a\in z_t}\bigwedge_i \operatorname{isfinite}(a_i)\). The Boolean value \(F(z_t)=0\) is a directly verifiable certificate of numerical failure: at least one stored scalar is NaN or infinite. A guarded implementation evaluates \(F\) after gradient production, after state recurrence, and before committing the parameter update; it commits iteration \(t\) only if every required check returns one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check every gradient, parameter, optimizer-state, and step-size scalar; any NaN or infinity certifies numerical failure and blocks update commitment.
assumptions_latex: All components of \(z_t\) are stored as finite-format scalars.
Every state component influencing the committed update is included in the check.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(z_t)=0\Rightarrow\) the iteration contains a nonfinite numerical state and must not be committed.

notation.meaning: Complete optimizer state relevant to iteration t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the detection leaf, and the finiteness predicate is mathematically clear. However, the mandatory check locations and prohibition on committing the iteration are deployment-policy claims with no cited source.

children.title: Numerical-Failure Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery policies after numerical-range safeguards report compromised optimizer state or update validity.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Failure Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transactional rollback and retry after a detected nonfinite optimizer iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a last-known-finite checkpoint \(z_{t-1}\), a proposed transition \(T_{\eta_t}\), a contraction factor \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and retry limit \(R\in\mathbb{N}\). For \(r=0,\ldots,R\), form \(z_t^{(r)}=T_{\rho^r\eta_t}(z_{t-1})\) without overwriting the checkpoint and test every component for finiteness. Stop at the first finite proposal, commit \(z_t=z_t^{(r)}\), and record the retry count. If no proposal is finite, output the unchanged checkpoint \(z_{t-1}\) together with a failure status and terminate or escalate according to deployment policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rollback to a finite checkpoint, retry transactionally with geometrically reduced step sizes, and commit only the first wholly finite state.
assumptions_latex: \(z_{t-1}\) has passed a complete finiteness check.
Proposals can be evaluated without mutating the checkpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm either commits a finite \(z_t\) or returns the unchanged finite checkpoint with failure status.

notation.meaning: Optimizer transition evaluated with step size eta.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the recovery leaf, and the transactional procedure has a well-defined finite-output guarantee under its assumptions. Geometric step-size reduction, rollback semantics, retry limits, and escalation behavior constitute one particular recovery policy and require a supporting source.

children.title: Anisotropic Curvature
children.top_down_role: Directional curvature imbalance affecting first-order optimizer progress across parameter-space directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local spectral condition expressing direction-dependent curvature for a smooth objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x\), and suppose its Hessian \(H(x)=\nabla^2f(x)\) is positive definite. The curvature at \(x\) is anisotropic at ratio \(\kappa>1\) when \(\lambda_{\max}(H(x))/\lambda_{\min}(H(x))\ge\kappa\). Equivalently, there exist unit directions \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \(u^{\mathsf T}H(x)u\ge\kappa v^{\mathsf T}H(x)v\). Thus a single scalar step size is constrained by the high-curvature directions while progress along low-curvature directions can be proportionally slower.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature is anisotropic when directional second derivatives differ by at least a prescribed spectral ratio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}(H(x))/\lambda_{\min}(H(x))\ge\kappa\), equivalently for suitable unit \(u,v\), \(u^{\mathsf T}H(x)u\ge\kappa v^{\mathsf T}H(x)v\).

notation.meaning: Hessian of the objective at x.

children.title: Ill-Scaled Parameter Blocks
children.top_down_role: Layerwise or blockwise parameter groups whose characteristic gradient scales differ materially.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Scaled Parameter Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise spectral condition identifying incompatible curvature scales within parameter groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(B)})\) and let \(H_{bb}(x)=\nabla^2_{x^{(b)}x^{(b)}}f(x)\) be a positive-definite diagonal Hessian block. Block \(b\) is ill-scaled at threshold \(\kappa_b>1\) when \(\lambda_{\max}(H_{bb}(x))/\lambda_{\min}(H_{bb}(x))\ge\kappa_b\). Under the local quadratic model, any unpreconditioned step size stable in the block's largest-curvature direction yields a contraction deficit governed by this ratio in its smallest-curvature direction. The predicate concerns within-block scaling and does not require comparison with any other parameter block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter block is ill-scaled when the ratio of its largest to smallest positive curvature exceeds a prescribed threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Block \(b\) is ill-scaled exactly when \(\lambda_{\max}(H_{bb}(x))/\lambda_{\min}(H_{bb}(x))\ge\kappa_b\).

notation.meaning: Within-block Hessian for parameter block b.

source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms II: Advanced Theory and Bundle Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blockwise spectral predicate fits the leaf, but the statement that a stable unpreconditioned step has a contraction deficit 'governed by' the ratio is not quantitatively specified. The cited second-order differentiability section is not clearly sufficient evidence for this optimization-dynamics claim.

children.title: Cross-Block Scale Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Optimizer behavior when shared hyperparameters span parameter blocks with incompatible scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Scale Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of characteristic curvature magnitudes across parameter blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(B)})\), assume every diagonal Hessian block \(H_{bb}(x)\) is positive definite, and define its characteristic scale by \(s_b=\lambda_{\max}(H_{bb}(x))\). The blocks exhibit cross-block scale mismatch at threshold \(\Gamma>1\) when \(\max_b s_b/\min_b s_b\ge\Gamma\). For the block-diagonal quadratic model, any global step size satisfying \(0<\eta\le 1/\max_b s_b\) is no greater than \(1/\Gamma\) times the natural reciprocal-curvature scale \(1/\min_b s_b\) of the least-curved block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-block mismatch occurs when characteristic curvature scales of different parameter blocks differ by at least a prescribed factor; a conservative global step then undershoots the least-curved block's reciprocal-curvature scale by that factor.
assumptions_latex: The local quadratic model is block diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_b s_b/\min_b s_b\ge\Gamma\) implies \(\eta\le (1/\Gamma)(1/\min_b s_b)\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal Hessian block for parameter block b.

source_refs.source_title: Parallel and Distributed Computation: Numerical Methods

children.title: Preconditioning Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where diagonal, factored, or matrix-aware scaling fails to compensate for adverse geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioning Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral boundary beyond which a fixed symmetric positive-definite preconditioner cannot meet a local conditioning target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\succ0\) be the Hessian of a local quadratic model and let \(P\succ0\) be a fixed symmetric preconditioner used in the update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta P\nabla f(x_t)\). Define the effective curvature \(M=P^{1/2}HP^{1/2}\). For a target \(K\ge1\), the preconditioner fails to attain the target whenever \(\kappa(M)=\lambda_{\max}(M)/\lambda_{\min}(M)>K\). No scalar choice of \(\eta>0\) changes \(\kappa(M)\); scalar tuning may enforce stability but cannot remove the residual spectral disparity. Preconditioners that are not symmetric positive definite lie outside this certificate's stated scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed symmetric positive-definite preconditioner misses its conditioning target when the transformed Hessian remains too ill-conditioned, and scalar step-size tuning cannot change that condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(P\succ0\) is symmetric and fixed during the analyzed update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(P^{1/2}HP^{1/2})>K\Rightarrow\) the target conditioning is not attained for any scalar \(\eta>0\).

children.title: Vanishing-Gradient Regimes
children.top_down_role: Training regions where usable gradient signals become too small for effective optimizer progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Gradient Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-based regime in which gradient magnitude is negligible relative to the optimization scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_t=\nabla f(x_t)\in\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(G_{\mathrm{ref}}>0\) be a problem-dependent reference magnitude, choose \(\varepsilon_g\in(0,1)\), and let \(\eta_t\ge0\). Iteration \(t\) lies in a vanishing-gradient regime when \(\lVert g_t\rVert_2\le\varepsilon_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\) while the optimization residual used by the task remains above its termination tolerance. For the first-order update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t\), the displacement satisfies \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2\le\eta_t\varepsilon_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\). The residual clause distinguishes pathological vanishing from legitimate approach to a stationary solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradients are pathologically vanishing when their norm is tiny relative to a reference scale although the task has not reached its stopping criterion; with a nonnegative step size, the resulting gradient-step displacement is correspondingly small.
assumptions_latex: The task residual exceeds its stopping tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert g_t\rVert_2\le\varepsilon_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2\le\eta_t\varepsilon_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative step size at iteration t.

children.title: Exploding-Gradient Regimes
children.top_down_role: Training regions where gradient magnitudes destabilize optimizer states or parameter updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Exploding-Gradient Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-based regime of excessively large gradient norms and proposed updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_t=\nabla f(x_t)\in\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(G_{\mathrm{ref}}>0\), choose \(M_g>1\), and let \(\eta_t\ge0\). Iteration \(t\) lies in an exploding-gradient regime when \(\lVert g_t\rVert_2\ge M_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\). For the unmodified update \(x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t\), the displacement obeys \(\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2\ge\eta_tM_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\). Consequently, a deployment limit \(U_{\max}\ge0\) on update magnitude is violated whenever \(\eta_tM_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}>U_{\max}\), unless a safeguard alters or rejects the proposed update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradients are exploding when their norm exceeds a reference scale by a large factor; with a nonnegative step size, the proposed update can then exceed its deployment limit unless a safeguard intervenes.
assumptions_latex: The proposed update is \(-\eta_tg_t\) before safeguards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert g_t\rVert_2\ge M_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\Rightarrow\lVert x_{t+1}-x_t\rVert_2\ge\eta_tM_gG_{\mathrm{ref}}\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative step size at iteration t.

children.title: Gradient Dynamic-Range Transitions
children.top_down_role: Temporal or architectural shifts between weak-signal, ordinary-scale, or extreme-gradient behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Dynamic-Range Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detects abrupt changes between gradient-magnitude regimes over consecutive iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For gradients \(g_{t-1},g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and a threshold \(\tau>0\), define \(r_t=\log(\lVert g_t\rVert_2/\lVert g_{t-1}\rVert_2)\) when both norms are positive. An upward dynamic-range transition occurs when \(r_t\ge\tau\), and a downward transition occurs when \(r_t\le-\tau\); equivalently, the positive norms differ by a multiplicative factor of at least \(e^\tau\). If only \(g_t\) is zero, set \(r_t=-\infty\); if only \(g_{t-1}\) is zero, set \(r_t=+\infty\). If both gradients are zero, classify the pair as having no dynamic-range transition and leave \(r_t\) undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic-range transition is an iteration-to-iteration gradient-norm change exceeding a prescribed multiplicative factor; one-sided zero norms represent infinite transitions, while two zero norms represent no transition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For positive consecutive norms, \(|r_t|\ge\tau\) exactly when the norms differ by a factor of at least \(e^\tau\); the zero-norm cases follow the stated extended convention.

notation.meaning: Logarithmic ratio of consecutive positive gradient norms, extended for one-sided zero norms.

children.title: Optimizer-State Consequences
children.top_down_role: Persistence of extreme gradient scales in momentum, moment, accumulator, or preconditioner state.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of extreme gradients through exponential first- and second-moment optimizer states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider coordinatewise states \(m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t\) and \(v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^{\odot2}\), where \(0\le\beta_1,\beta_2<1\), and assume \(v_{t-1}\) is coordinatewise nonnegative. If \(g_t=0\), then \(m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}\) and \(v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}\), so stored history decays geometrically rather than vanishing immediately. If \(G\ge0\) and \(|g_{t,i}|\ge G\), then \(v_{t,i}\ge(1-\beta_2)G^2\). Consequently, after \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\) subsequent zero-gradient iterations, \(v_{t+k,i}\ge\beta_2^k(1-\beta_2)G^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero gradients geometrically decay exponential optimizer history, while a large gradient coordinate injects a nonnegative second-moment contribution that persists through later zero-gradient iterations.
assumptions_latex: The state recurrences are evaluated coordinatewise.
The relevant state and gradient values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(g_t=0\), stored states decay by their respective factors; if \(|g_{t,i}|\ge G\), then after \(k\) subsequent zero-gradient iterations, \(v_{t+k,i}\ge\beta_2^k(1-\beta_2)G^2\).

children.title: Gradient-Variance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Variation in stochastic gradient estimates across batches, examples, parameters, or training phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Variance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-noise classification for unbiased stochastic first-order oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(x,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be a stochastic gradient estimator satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]=\nabla f(x)\). Define its conditional total variance by \(V(x)=\mathbb{E}[\lVert G(x,\xi)-\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\mid x]\). Relative to thresholds \(0\le V_{\mathrm{low}}<V_{\mathrm{high}}\), the oracle is in a low-variance regime when \(V(x)\le V_{\mathrm{low}}\), an intermediate regime when \(V_{\mathrm{low}}<V(x)<V_{\mathrm{high}}\), and a high-variance regime when \(V(x)\ge V_{\mathrm{high}}\). These predicates require the second conditional moment to exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle by its conditional mean-square noise using explicit low- and high-variance thresholds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities involving \(V(x)\), \(V_{\mathrm{low}}\), and \(V_{\mathrm{high}}\) partition all finite-variance oracle states into three regimes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and conditional mean-square-noise definition fit the stochastic gradient-variance leaf, and the inequalities form a valid partition under the finite-second-moment assumption. An authoritative stochastic-optimization source is still required for the oracle model, while the low/high thresholds must be identified as locally calibrated conventions.

children.title: Outlier-Dominated Updates
children.top_down_role: Update behavior driven disproportionately by rare samples, coordinates, layers, or gradient events.

knowledge_statements.title: Outlier-Dominated Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-batch averaging becomes nonrobust when a small subset controls most of the update magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mini-batch of vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_b\in\mathbb{R}^d\), define the averaged update \(u=-\eta b^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^b g_i\), where \(\eta>0\). Given \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and \(\rho\in(0,1]\), the batch is \((\varepsilon,\rho)\)-outlier dominated if there exists \(O\subseteq\{1,\ldots,b\}\) with \(|O|\leq\varepsilon b\) such that \(\sum_{i\in O}\|g_i\|\geq\rho\sum_{i=1}^b\|g_i\|\). For a fixed index \(j\) and unit vector \(v\), let \(u_M\) be the averaged update after replacing \(g_j\) by \(Mv\), where \(M\geq0\). Then \(\|u_M-u_0\|=\eta M/b\), so the ordinary mean has unbounded single-sample influence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch is outlier dominated when a small subset supplies a prescribed fraction of total gradient magnitude; replacing one gradient by an arbitrarily large vector can change the mean update without bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{M\geq0}\|u_M-u_0\|=\infty\), so mean aggregation is not uniformly robust to an unrestricted outlier.

notation.meaning: Index set of outlying gradient samples.
Mini-batch update after replacing one selected gradient by M times a unit vector.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-sample mean aggregation has unbounded influence under unrestricted contamination

children.title: Heavy-Tailed Gradient Noise
children.top_down_role: Gradient-noise regimes where extreme observations materially influence optimizer statistics.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Gradient Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional stochastic-gradient noise with finite lower moments but no finite variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be a stochastic gradient at iterate \(x_t\), and let \(\mathcal F_t\) denote the history before sampling \(g_t\). Write \(\xi_t=g_t-\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\). A heavy-tailed gradient-noise regime of order \(p\in(1,2)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^p\mid\mathcal F_t]\leq \sigma_p^p<\infty\) almost surely, while a uniform conditional second-moment bound is unavailable; in the strict infinite-variance version, \(\mathbb E[\|\xi_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]=\infty\) on an event of positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-tailed gradient noise has a controlled moment below order two but lacks the finite-variance bound used by standard stochastic-gradient analyses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi_t\) has a finite conditional \(p\)-th moment but need not have a finite conditional second moment.

notation.meaning: Optimization and sampling history before step t.
Uniform scale bound for the conditional p-th moment.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-p-moment noise with p below two is the standard heavy-tailed stochastic-gradient model
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and distinguishes a finite-p-moment model from a strict infinite-variance variant, but no inspectable source establishes that this is the intended heavy-tailed stochastic-gradient convention. A dedicated source is needed to validate the exact conditional-moment formulation.

children.title: Robustness Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which clipping, averaging, normalization, or adaptive scaling no longer limits outlier influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Breakdown boundary of untrimmed mean-gradient aggregation under arbitrary contamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(b\geq1\), let \(A(g_1,\ldots,g_b)=b^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^b g_i\). Under replacement contamination, an adversary may replace at most \(m\) inputs by arbitrary vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). The finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction of \(A\) is \(1/b\): with \(m=0\), its output is fixed by the clean batch, whereas with \(m=1\), replacing \(g_j\) by \(Mv\), where \(\|v\|=1\), makes \(\|A\|\to\infty\) as \(M\to\infty\). Thus no positive contamination fraction independent of \(b\) permits a uniform output bound for untrimmed averaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary batch mean breaks down after one arbitrary replacement, so its finite-sample robustness threshold is exactly one over the batch size.
assumptions_latex: Contaminated vectors may have unrestricted norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_b^*(A)=1/b\), and therefore \(\varepsilon_b^*(A)\to0\) as \(b\to\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the arithmetic mean has finite-sample replacement breakdown fraction one over sample size
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and arithmetic-mean claim are mathematically plausible, but finite-sample replacement breakdown has convention-dependent definitions and normalizations. A robust-statistics source with a specific definition or theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Gradient Statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-varying conditional means or covariances of stochastic gradients along an optimization trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be adapted to \(\mathcal F_{t+1}\). Define its pre-sampling conditional mean and covariance by \(\mu_t=\mathbb E[g_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\) and \(\Sigma_t=\mathbb E[(g_t-\mu_t)(g_t-\mu_t)^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_t]\). The gradient statistics are nonstationary on a horizon \(T\) if either \(\mu_t\) or \(\Sigma_t\) is not almost surely constant in \(t\). Their cumulative drift may be quantified by \(V_T^\mu=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|\mu_{t+1}-\mu_t\|\) and \(V_T^\Sigma=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|\Sigma_{t+1}-\Sigma_t\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient statistics are nonstationary when their conditional mean or covariance changes over time; cumulative variation records the magnitude of that drift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonstationarity holds when \(V_T^\mu+V_T^\Sigma>0\) with positive probability.

notation.meaning: Conditional mean gradient at step t.
Conditional covariance of the sampled gradient.
Cumulative mean and covariance drift budgets.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional moment variation is a standard mathematical representation of nonstationary stochastic observations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the node, and the conditional-moment drift quantities are coherent. However, the proposed criterion is one possible finite-horizon definition rather than a uniquely standard definition of nonstationary gradient statistics, so a specific optimization or stochastic-process source is required.

children.title: Biased Sampling Effects
children.top_down_role: Optimizer consequences of unequal, selective, stale, or otherwise nonrepresentative example sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Sampling Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling probabilities alter the expected component gradient unless inverse-probability correction is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable. If index \(I\) is sampled with probabilities \(q_i>0\), then the unweighted estimator \(g(x)=
abla f_I(x)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[g(x)]=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i
abla f_i(x)\). Its bias for the uniform empirical objective is \(b_q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n(q_i-1/n)
abla f_i(x)\). In contrast, \(\widetilde g(x)=
abla f_I(x)/(nq_I)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\widetilde g(x)]=

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonuniform sampling biases an unweighted component gradient toward frequently sampled components; inverse-probability weighting restores unbiasedness for the uniform objective.

children.title: Data-Order Effects
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of optimizer trajectories to example, batch, task, or shard presentation order.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Order Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential component-gradient maps generally do not commute, making epoch endpoints order dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For quadratic components \(f_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}H_i x+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\), with symmetric \(H_i\), define \(T_i(x)=x-\eta\nabla f_i(x)\). Processing components \(1\) then \(2\) gives \(T_2(T_1(x))\), while reversing them gives \(T_1(T_2(x))\). Their difference is \[T_2(T_1(x))-T_1(T_2(x))=\eta^2\bigl((H_2H_1-H_1H_2)x+H_2a_1-H_1a_2\bigr).\] Hence the two-step endpoint depends on data order whenever the displayed vector is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential component updates are order dependent when their gradient maps do not commute; for quadratics, the discrepancy is an explicit second-order term in the step size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \((H_2H_1-H_1H_2)x+H_2a_1-H_1a_2\neq0\), then \(T_2\circ T_1(x)\neq T_1\circ T_2(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct composition of affine gradient maps establishes the order-dependence identity

children.top_down_role: Finite-pass sampling behavior where examples are visited without independent replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Without-Replacement Sampling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Within an epoch, the next sampled component is conditionally uniform only over unseen indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi\) be a uniformly random permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(I_t=\pi_t\), and define \(\mathcal H_{t-1}=\sigma(I_1,\ldots,I_{t-1})\). If \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal H_{t-1}\)-measurable, then \[\mathbb E[
abla f_{I_t}(x_t)\mid\mathcal H_{t-1}]= rac{1}{n-t+1}\sum_{i
otin\{I_1,\ldots,I_{t-1}\}}
abla f_i(x_t).\] This generally differs from \(
abla F(x_t)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
abla f_i(x_t)\), although equality holds at \(t=1\) before any index is revealed.

For \(t>1\), \(\mathbb E[
abla f_{I_t}(x_t)\mid\mathcal H_{t-1}]

children.title: Curriculum-Induced Distribution Drift
children.top_down_role: Changes in optimizer statistics caused by staged, difficulty-based, or adaptive data presentation.

knowledge_statements.title: Curriculum-Induced Distribution Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A time-varying sampling curriculum may induce a moving optimization objective or gradient field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_t\) be the data distribution selected by a curriculum at step \(t\), and define \(F_t(x)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_t}[\ell(x;Z)]\). Assuming differentiation and expectation may be interchanged, \(
abla F_t(x)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_t}[
abla_x\ell(x;Z)]\). The curriculum exhibits distribution drift on a horizon \(T\) when \(P_{t+1}
eq P_t\) for some \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\). Its optimization-relevant gradient drift over a domain \(X\) is \(D_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sup_{x\in X}\|
abla F_{t+1}(x)-
abla F_t(x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curriculum exhibits distribution drift when its sampling distribution changes over time. Such drift may move the expected objective or gradient field; the quantity D_T measures cumulative change of the expected gradient field over X.
assumptions_latex: \(P_t\) is a probability distribution for each \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), where \(T\geq2\).
The interchange \(\nabla_x\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_t}[\ell(x;Z)]=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_t}[\nabla_x\ell(x;Z)]\) is valid for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_T>0\) implies that the curriculum changes the expected gradient field on \(X\) at least once during the horizon.

notation.meaning: Curriculum-selected data distribution at step t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: time-indexed sampling distributions induce time-indexed expected losses and gradients

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Evaluation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle cost counts individual component-gradient evaluations separately from optimizer arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), suppose iteration \(t\) evaluates a nonempty mini-batch \(B_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and forms \(g_t=|B_t|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_t}\nabla f_i(x_t)\). In the component-gradient oracle model, its evaluation cost is \(|B_t|\), and the cumulative cost through \(T\) iterations is \(N_{\mathrm{grad}}(T)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}|B_t|\). Thus constant batch size \(b\) costs \(bT\) component-gradient calls, while exact full-gradient iterations cost \(nT\). This count excludes optimizer-side vector and matrix operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-evaluation cost is the number of component-gradient oracle calls: a nonempty batch of size b costs b calls per iteration and bT calls over T iterations.
assumptions_latex: Each evaluation of one \(\nabla f_i(x)\) has unit oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{grad}}(T)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}|B_t|\), giving \(N_{\mathrm{grad}}(T)=bT\) when \(|B_t|=b\) for every \(t\).

notation.meaning: Nonempty mini-batch evaluated at iteration t.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Memory Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent auxiliary state is measured separately from parameters, gradients, and transient workspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an optimizer for \(d\) parameters that persistently stores \(s\) dense state vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), in addition to the parameter vector. Its optimizer-state memory is exactly \(sd\) scalar slots. If every slot uses \(w\) bytes, the state requires \(wsd\) bytes, excluding parameters, gradients, and temporary buffers. A stateless gradient method has \(s=0\); one-moment and two-moment methods have \(s=1\) and \(s=2\), respectively, before accounting for scalar counters or factored states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimizer storing s dense auxiliary vectors for d parameters uses sd scalar slots, or wsd bytes at w bytes per scalar.
assumptions_latex: \(d\geq1\) parameters and \(s\geq0\) persistent dense state vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mathrm{state}}=sd\) scalar slots and \(M_{\mathrm{state}}^{\mathrm{bytes}}=wsd\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Operation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense, diagonal, and low-rank optimizer transformations have distinct arithmetic and storage scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an optimizer transform \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) using a preconditioner. Applying a dense stored matrix \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) as \(Pg\) requires \(\Theta(d^2)\) arithmetic operations and \(\Theta(d^2)\) stored scalars; forming a generic dense factorization costs \(\Theta(d^3)\). A diagonal preconditioner requires \(\Theta(d)\) arithmetic and storage. A rank-\(r\) factorization \(P=D+UV^{\mathsf T}\), with diagonal \(D\) and \(U,V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\), can be applied and stored using \(\Theta(dr)\) resources when \(1\leq r\ll d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense preconditioning costs quadratic work and storage, diagonal preconditioning costs linear resources, and rank-r factorizations cost order dr.
assumptions_latex: Dense arithmetic uses the classical matrix-vector and matrix-factorization models.
\(1\leq r\ll d\) for the low-rank representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense, diagonal, and rank-\(r\) applications cost respectively \(\Theta(d^2)\), \(\Theta(d)\), and \(\Theta(dr)\) arithmetic operations.

children.title: Communication Cost Profiles
children.top_down_role: Communication volume, frequency, synchronization pressure, or topology sensitivity introduced by optimizer state processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Cost Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-step distributed cost is characterized by transmitted scalars, synchronization rounds, and collective structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In synchronous data-parallel optimization with \(p\geq2\) workers and a dense gradient of \(d\) scalars per worker, a ring all-reduce implemented by reduce-scatter followed by all-gather uses \(2(p-1)\) sequential communication rounds. Each worker sends \(2(p-1)d/p\) scalar values and receives the same amount, ignoring padding and protocol metadata. Under the latency-bandwidth model, its per-worker communication time is modeled by \(2(p-1)\alpha+2(p-1)d\beta/p\), where \(\alpha\) is per-round latency and \(\beta\) is transfer time per scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ring all-reduce uses two times p minus one rounds and sends two times (p−1)d/p scalars per worker, yielding the stated latency-bandwidth profile.
assumptions_latex: \(p\geq2\) workers each hold a dense vector of \(d\) scalars.
The vector is evenly partitioned across workers, with protocol overhead ignored.
Communication follows a ring reduce-scatter and all-gather implementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=2(p-1)\), \(V_{\mathrm{send}}=2(p-1)d/p\), and \(T_{\mathrm{comm}}=2(p-1)\alpha+2(p-1)d\beta/p\).

notation.meaning: Per-round latency and per-scalar transfer-time parameters.
Scalar values transmitted by each worker.
