children.title: Optimizer-State Sharding
children.top_down_role: Partitioning compatibility for optimizer vectors, matrices, statistics, or auxiliary state across workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-State Sharding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact data-parallel sharding of coordinate-separable first-order optimizer state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the parameter coordinates be partitioned as \(\{1,\ldots,d\}=I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_p\). An optimizer state \(s_t=(s_{t,1},\ldots,s_{t,d})\) is sharded across \(p\) workers when worker \(r\) stores exactly \(s_{t,I_r}\), and the update is coordinate-separable: \(s_{t+1,i}=U_i(s_{t,i},g_{t,i})\) and \(x_{t+1,i}=V_i(x_{t,i},s_{t+1,i},g_{t,i})\). After the required gradient coordinates have been communicated, the workers compute their local updates and collectively assemble \(x_{t+1}\). The sharding is exact when this distributed result equals the corresponding unsharded update for every admissible \((x_t,s_t,g_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizer state is sharded when workers hold disjoint coordinate blocks and their local updates, after gradient communication, exactly reproduce the unsharded optimizer step.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t,g_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and the optimizer state is indexed by parameter coordinates.
\(I_1,\ldots,I_p\) are disjoint and cover all coordinates.
The state and parameter update maps are coordinate-separable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Assemble}_{r=1}^p(x_{t+1,I_r})=x_{t+1}^{\mathrm{unsharded}}\).

notation.meaning: Coordinate block assigned to worker r.
Coordinatewise state and parameter update maps.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Optimizer-State Sharding leaf and is internally consistent for coordinate-separable state, but it supplies no inspectable source for the distributed-system model or the asserted exact equivalence with unsharded execution.

children.title: Collective-Operation Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility with distributed aggregation, reduction, broadcast, gather, or exchange primitives.

knowledge_statements.title: Collective-Operation Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication condition for exact distributed execution of a first-order optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For worker-local gradients \(g_t^{(1)},\ldots,g_t^{(p)}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), let the required aggregate be \(\bar g_t=p^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^p g_t^{(r)}\). A distributed optimizer is collective-operation compatible with a communication interface \(\mathcal C\) when every nonlocal quantity used by its update can be produced by a finite composition of operations in \(\mathcal C\), with the same value on every worker that consumes it. For ordinary synchronous data parallelism, compatibility holds if \(\mathcal C\) can compute \(\bar g_t\) before the update; for sharded updates it must additionally route each required block \(\bar g_{t,I_r}\) to its owning worker and assemble the resulting parameter blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimizer is compatible when the available collectives can construct and deliver every nonlocal quantity required to reproduce its distributed update exactly.
assumptions_latex: The optimizer update is deterministic given its parameters, state, and aggregated inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is compatible exactly when its operations realize every required aggregate and routing map before that quantity is consumed.

notation.meaning: Gradient computed by worker r at iteration t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the Collective-Operation Compatibility leaf, and its notation and quantification are adequate. An authoritative locator is required to validate the communication model, the finite-composition criterion, and the stated collective requirements for replicated and sharded execution.

children.title: Partitioning Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Optimizer structures or execution regimes that resist efficient sharding or require excessive synchronization.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural boundary beyond which coordinatewise optimizer-state partitioning is not exact without extra communication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a sharding partition \(I_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_p=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Purely local sharded execution fails to reproduce an unsharded update whenever some owned output coordinate depends on unavailable remote data: there exist \(r\), \(i\in I_r\), and admissible inputs differing only outside \(I_r\) for which \(U_i(s_t,g_t)\) or \(V_i(x_t,s_{t+1},g_t)\) differs. Exactness can then be restored only by communicating a sufficient statistic that resolves this dependence, replicating the coupled state, or changing the partition. Global norm clipping, dense preconditioning, and parameter-coupled regularization exhibit this obstruction unless their global quantities are communicated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local sharding ceases to be exact when an owned update depends on remote coordinates that are neither replicated nor summarized through communication.
assumptions_latex: The distributed implementation restricts worker \(r\) to data indexed by \(I_r\) plus explicitly communicated messages.
The reference optimizer may couple different parameter coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If two globally admissible inputs are locally indistinguishable to worker \(r\) but require different outputs on \(I_r\), no purely local rule on that worker is exact.

notation.meaning: Reference state and parameter update components.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the local-indistinguishability criterion is mathematically plausible. No source supports the impossibility formulation or verifies that the listed examples fall within it under the intended distributed execution model.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperparameter-Budget Confounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimizer comparisons under unequal or insufficient hyperparameter-search resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(o,h)\) be the evaluation loss of optimizer \(o\) with hyperparameters \(h\in H_o\), and let a tuning procedure with budget \(B\) return a tested set \(S_o(B)\subseteq H_o\). The reported score is \(\widehat L_B(o)=\min_{h\in S_o(B)}L(o,h)\), whereas the target tuned score is \(L^*(o)=\inf_{h\in H_o}L(o,h)\). Hyperparameter-budget confounding occurs when an observed ordering \(\widehat L_{B_1}(o_1)<\widehat L_{B_2}(o_2)\) cannot be attributed to optimizer identity because \(B_1\ne B_2\), or because changing the common budget or search rule can reverse the ordering while \(L^*(o_1)\) and \(L^*(o_2)\) remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizer rankings are confounded when unequal or limited tuning searches, rather than optimizer identity, can determine or reverse the reported ordering.
assumptions_latex: Each optimizer \(o\) has a specified hyperparameter domain \(H_o\).
Evaluation loss \(L(o,h)\) is measured under otherwise fixed experimental conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A comparison of \(\widehat L_B\) identifies tuned optimizer quality only relative to the declared search procedure and budget, not automatically the ordering of \(L^*\).

notation.meaning: Configurations evaluated under tuning budget B.
Best attainable loss over the declared domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but no methodological source supports the proposed formalization. In particular, the conditions under which unequal or finite tuning budgets prevent attribution, rather than merely weaken it, require authoritative validation.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule–Optimizer Confounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-identifiability of optimizer effects when learning-rate schedules differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(o,\eta)\) denote a performance metric obtained using optimizer \(o\) and schedule \(\eta=(\eta_t)_{t=0}^{T-1}\). Schedule–optimizer confounding occurs when optimizers \(o_1,o_2\) are compared using different schedules \(\eta^{(1)},\eta^{(2)}\), so the contrast \(M(o_1,\eta^{(1)})-M(o_2,\eta^{(2)})\) combines an optimizer effect with a schedule effect. In particular, optimizer identity is not isolated if there exist admissible schedules \(\tilde\eta^{(1)},\tilde\eta^{(2)}\) for which the sign of this contrast reverses. A valid conditional comparison must fix a common schedule or separately optimize schedules under the same declared tuning protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimizer comparison is schedule-confounded when differing learning-rate schedules contribute to, or can reverse, the measured optimizer ranking.
assumptions_latex: Both runs share the same task, architecture, data protocol, initialization law, and horizon \(T\).
Each schedule belongs to a declared admissible schedule class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The paired contrast identifies an optimizer effect only conditional on a common schedule or a symmetric schedule-tuning rule.

notation.meaning: Performance for optimizer o under schedule eta.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record matches Schedule–Optimizer Confounding and uses a suitable failure-boundary kind. A source is needed for the identification claim and for the assertion that a common schedule or symmetric tuning protocol suffices for a valid optimizer-effect comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Architecture–Optimizer Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonadditive dependence of optimizer performance on model architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(o,a)\) be the expected evaluation metric for optimizer \(o\) and architecture \(a\), after applying a fixed training and tuning protocol. Optimizer and architecture interact when there exist optimizers \(o_1,o_2\) and architectures \(a_1,a_2\) such that the optimizer contrast depends on architecture: \[\bigl(M(o_1,a_1)-M(o_2,a_1)\bigr)-\bigl(M(o_1,a_2)-M(o_2,a_2)\bigr)\ne 0.\] A qualitative interaction occurs when the two optimizer contrasts have opposite signs. Consequently, an optimizer ranking established on one architecture does not determine its ranking on another architecture without an assumption excluding interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Architecture–optimizer interaction means the performance difference between two optimizers changes with architecture; it is qualitative when their ranking reverses.
assumptions_latex: \(M(o,a)\) is an expectation over the declared sources of training randomness.
Training, tuning, data, and evaluation protocols are fixed across optimizer–architecture pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonzero difference-in-differences implies that optimizer and architecture effects are not additive on the scale of \(M\).

notation.meaning: Expected metric for optimizer o and architecture a.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-in-differences formula correctly expresses nonadditivity on the declared metric scale, and the property kind is compatible with this leaf. No inspectable source is supplied for the interaction criterion, qualitative-interaction terminology, or its application to optimizer comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Training-Horizon Performance Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise optimizer ranking reversal as the training horizon changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_o(t)\) be a metric for optimizer \(o\) after exactly \(t\) units of a declared training resource, with larger values preferred. A training-horizon performance reversal between optimizers \(o_1\) and \(o_2\) occurs when there exist \(0<t_1<t_2\) such that \(M_{o_1}(t_1)>M_{o_2}(t_1)\) but \(M_{o_1}(t_2)<M_{o_2}(t_2)\). The resource unit must be fixed across optimizers, such as update count, processed examples, elapsed time, or floating-point work. Thus a ranking reported at \(t_1\) cannot be extrapolated to \(t_2\) without an additional no-crossing assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A horizon reversal occurs when one optimizer leads at an earlier matched training budget but trails another optimizer at a later matched budget.
assumptions_latex: Both optimizers are evaluated on the same task and metric.
The training resource \(t\) is measured identically for both optimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordering of \(M_{o_1}(t)\) and \(M_{o_2}(t)\) is horizon-dependent whenever their performance curves cross.

notation.meaning: Performance of optimizer o at resource horizon t.
Earlier and later matched training horizons.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition precisely matches Training-Horizon Performance Reversal, with consistent LaTeX and plain text. An authoritative source with a specific locator is still required for the matched-resource convention and the interpretation of crossing learning curves in optimizer comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark-to-Scale Transfer Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an optimizer ranking to persist under a declared scaling transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\) denote a training configuration and \(\sigma(b)\) a scaled configuration obtained by changing declared scale variables, such as model width, parameter count, batch size, data volume, or compute budget. For a metric \(M(o,b)\) with larger values preferred, benchmark-to-scale transfer fails for optimizers \(o_1,o_2\) when \(M(o_1,b)>M(o_2,b)\) but \(M(o_1,\sigma(b))\le M(o_2,\sigma(b))\), after each optimizer is evaluated under the same scale-specific tuning protocol. More generally, a benchmark ranking is not transferable unless its ordering is invariant over the stated target family of scaled configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark-to-scale transfer fails when an optimizer’s advantage on a reference configuration disappears or reverses after model, data, batch, or compute scale changes.
assumptions_latex: The reference configuration \(b\) and scaling map \(\sigma\) are explicitly declared.
The same metric and symmetric scale-specific tuning protocol are used for both optimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A ranking at \(b\) alone does not identify the ranking at \(\sigma(b)\) when optimizer performance interacts with scale.

notation.meaning: Performance of optimizer o on configuration b.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and ranking-change formulation fit the leaf. No source validates the proposed transfer-failure criterion, the admissible scaling variables, or the requirement that scale-specific tuning makes the two evaluations comparable.
